en: Preface to the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, composed by the śramaṇa Jizhen, successor to the Patriarchs at Huading Peak on Mount Tiantai.
The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* is the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden One Vehicle; it is the true school of all Buddhas, wondrous and transcendent.
The various scriptures encompass all phenomena; by setting aside the provisional to reveal the ultimate, they fully realize the merit achieved after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

By entrusting extinction to discourse upon the eternal, they first deploy the vanguard of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. They uniquely expound the profound intent of the five periods and generously bestow the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter).

To transcend all stages instantaneously requires nothing more than a single prior awakening; that all sentient beings may attain it together—how could there be any distinction between superior and inferior?

The two roots—ordinary and sage—are equal in their fundamental state; wisdom and folly share the same path. This is truly the secret key for Bodhisattvas to benefit sentient beings, and the essential pivot for all beings to attain Buddhahood.
To seal the mind with this Dharma, nothing surpasses it. Is not true cultivation and esoteric practice found herein?
Beginning at Vulture Peak, the Buddha revealed his entire capacity through silence, manifesting the wordless truth. A bhikṣu spoke on his behalf, chanting a verse to earnestly exhort and inquire.
From this, the teaching was initiated; all arose in reliance upon wisdom. Liberation opened the Dharma-gate of formlessness, and awakening to Prajñā transcended the three realms.
The Mind-King realized the Dharma-patience of non-arising; speech was extinguished as one attained silent resonance within the One Mind.

Abiding nowhere, one attains the benefit of the transformation of original enlightenment; the various consciousnesses become a sea of nature without waves. With great power, one enters the ruins of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
possessing wisdom and eloquence, the source of the mind flows pure. Attaining the true nature, the essence is empty; Śāriputra alone bears the burden as the ground is filled.
Entering the ocean of the Tathāgatagarbha, one dwells in the Brahma-conduct of equal enlightenment. Retention (*dhāraṇī*) serves as the foundation for all.

The meaning and essence of this chapter consist in the perfect realization of wondrous contemplation and true awakening. At the end of the chapter, the Dharma-eye for propagation is revealed, with this sutra alone being entrusted.
Truly, for those who obtain it, all external seeking is forever severed; for those who awaken to it, both the beginning and the end return to a single consistency.
Examining its origin and tracing its conclusion, its systematic analysis is like flowers strung into a garland, brilliant and magnificent.

Contemplate this: like a pearl rolling upon a platter, its radiant brilliance is difficult to gaze upon directly. It has been protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas and shall not fall into the hands of other sentient beings.
For this reason, it has long remained sealed within the secret treasury and was not recklessly proclaimed; those who know it are rare, and even those who hear of it find it difficult to believe.

Moreover, its phrasing is extraordinary and its meaning is profound; though the words are concise, the principles are complete. Yet, in barely eleven thousand five hundred characters, it encompasses the entirety of—

The ocean of meaning within the entire Great Canon of the Teachings, which moreover is able to encompass the school of the separate transmission that does not rely on written words—this is truly the excellent guide for transcending the world amidst the Semblance Dharma.
I, Zhen, having fortunately encountered these holy words, have studied them with a profound mind;
though I am unable to fathom their deep mysteries, I vow to circulate them, establishing a course of practice for this life and future lives. For...

This is the sublime practice of benefiting both oneself and others. May all who see or hear it suddenly awaken to the emptiness of the mind, so that in this life and in future lives, they may forever be nourished by the milk of the Dharma. Thus it is said.

Discriminating the Pronunciation and Meaning of Characters (In all cases where there are actual entities that appear similar or where there are shifting pronunciations, notes shall first be provided for ease of reference).

*Qí* (pronounced *zhī*. Also means "only. In words such as *qírú* (just like) and *qǐyǒu* (merely has), this [reading] is used. Nowadays it is written as *zhǐ*; furthermore, it is pronounced *qí*, as in *shénqí* (deities). All instances of *qíyè* (geya) and *qítuó* (jetavana) derive from this). *Dǐ* (pronounced *zhǐ*. To lean against; to strike. In the word *dǐduì* (to face/counter), this [reading] should be used.

This is because one strikes the joints with the hand while facing [the other]. Nowadays it is written as *zhǐ* or *qí*; both are errors). *Bié* (read with the entering tone as *bié*. To distinguish; to separate. In the sense of "separation," it is the same character. Furthermore, it is pronounced *biè*, as in "to analyze" or "to discriminate").

Chēng (In all cases of praise or eulogy, it is pronounced in the level tone; in all cases of "name matching" or correspondence, it is pronounced in the departing tone). Háng (As in "walking," "stopping," or "operation," it is pronounced héng; as in "virtuous conduct" or "words and deeds," it is pronounced xìng; as in "rows" or "arrayed," it is pronounced háng; when meaning "to practice such deeds for the benefit of others," it is pronounced hàn).

Jiě (In all cases of "untying knots" or "explanation," it is pronounced in the rising tone; it may also be pronounced in the departing tone as xiè, meaning "to understand. For example, to clearly comprehend and thereby liberate oneself is called *vimokṣa* [liberation]; to awaken to its meaning is called "understanding the meaning" [artha-viniścaya]).

*Zhì* (pronounced *chí* and *zhì*; when meaning "to cultivate" something that has not yet been cultivated, it is pronounced in the level tone; when meaning "that which has already been cultivated," it is pronounced in the departing tone). *Qiè* (pronounced *qiè*; this refers to the "proper and earnest" sense of *qiè*, and also in the departing tone as *qì*, meaning "multitude").

Furthermore, regarding general usage: *Li* (to separate): *li fan* (separate from the ordinary), *bie li zhi li* (branching off). All are level tone (*píngshēng*). Also, with departing tone (*qùshēng*), it sounds like *lì*, meaning "gradually diverging. Both "leaving desire" (*li yù*) and "leaving defilement" (*li gòu*) derive from this. *Xuan* (to revolve):

As in *zhouxuan* (revolve), *zhexuan* (turn), *xuánzhuǎn* (rotate). All are level tone. Also, with departing tone, it is the *xuan* of "following along" (*zhúxúan*). *Dù* (to deliver): In "deliverance" (*jìdù*), it is departing tone. Also, with entering tone (*rùshēng*), it sounds like *duó*; in "calculation" (*jìdù*), it is the *dù*. *Nà*: Level tone, *nuó*; *chán nà* (dhyāna) and *tán nà* (dāna) derive from this. Also, with rising tone (*shàngshēng*), pronounced as *nú kě*;

it is the *nà* in "where" (*nà lǐ*) or "that matter" (*nà shì*). Also, with rising tone, pronounced as *nú wò*; it is the trailing sound at the end of a phrase. *yǎng*: To provide for those below or serve those above is called *yǎng*; it is departing tone. In "nurturing life" (*shēngyǎng*), "raising livestock" (*chùyǎng*), or "self-nurturing" (*zìyǎng*), it is level tone.

All [the following] are in the rising tone (shǎngshēng). Qù (in the sense of "departing" or "coming and going," it is in the departing tone [qùshēng]; in the sense of "removing" or "excluding," it is in the rising tone). Yǔ (rising tone; meaning "speech. Also, when using words to inform others, it is called yǔ; in this case, it is in the departing tone).
Preface to the *Tongzong Ji* (Record of the Penetrating School) of the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, composed by the diligent student Wei Xuequ.
In perusing the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I read where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara says: "In the past, I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara."
That Buddha bestowed upon me the Illusion-like Vajra Samādhi, through which I attained awakening to the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing. He further said:
"The true essence of the teaching in this land is pure within sound and hearing. This speaks to those who study the Way in the Eastern Land: they must certainly enter through the faculty of hearing.
Since the teachings arrived from the West, the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon have hung like the sun and stars, ever-present; they flow through the land like rivers.
Apart from these, what could serve as the steps for ascending to sagehood or the candle for dispelling darkness?

The First Patriarch pointed directly at the human mind, seeing one's nature to become a Buddha—transcending gradual stages and swiftly accomplishing the Perfect and Sudden. Thus, the style of this school flourished, and the Mahayana [attained its full expression].

People [divided] into two schools stood side by side. While the school (zong) flourished, the teaching (jiao) declined; yet with only a partial understanding, they failed to perceive the true reality (shixiang), and thus the school itself also fell into decay.
Those who practice Chan seek realization through karmic conditions (jiyuan), while those who study the teachings seek it through the Buddha’s words.

Certainly, karmic conditions can lead to awakening; how could the Buddha’s words ever deceive people? One must ensure that the school and the teaching are harmonized, so that they naturally become perfect and complete.

Dunli arrived. The Elder Zibo said: "In studying the teachings, take the Buddha’s words as the foundation. In clarifying the essence (the *zong*), take the karmic conditions (*jīyuán*) as the foundation.
In propagating and expounding the teachings and the essence, take moral virtue (*dàodé*) as the foundation. Support this with preceptual conduct (*jièxíng*) and expand it through learning (*xuéwèn*).
Otherwise, though one may occupy the throne of the Dharma King, don the robes of the Tathāgata, and transmit the words of our Buddha," [one would be a fraud].
This is what is meant by the "fox’s howl. I have long borne these words in mind, yet I had not encountered such a person.

Hearing that there was the Great Master Renshan, a true dragon-elephant of our time, my heart privately yearned for him. In the middle month of winter in the Guihai year, I passed through the ancient Baiyun Temple at T'ien-p'ing and suddenly met him there.
Dwelling in a desolate cottage of but a few rafters, wearing tattered robes and eating coarse food, he appeared as tranquil and unassuming as the mountain air. We conversed...
Next, he brought forth the *Jingang Sanmei Tongzong Ji* (Record of the General Lineage of the Vajrasamādhi) for my inspection. I read one or two sections;

the prose was concise yet the meaning was rich, the indications were brief yet the principles were comprehensive. It was exactly like taking a single drop of water from the great ocean—the flavor of which encompasses that of all its hundred rivers.

Consequently, he transmitted this scripture to me and requested that I provide a preface for its opening. The general purport of the sutra synthesizes the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*;
its subtle words and elegant expressions bear a resemblance to the *Śūraṅgama*. Is it not here that the path of hearing, contemplating, and cultivating is truly found?
This Sanskrit manuscript has traveled from afar, gathered primarily to transform and guide all sentient beings so that they may come to know the Buddha-way. However, fearing that...
There is the danger of becoming attached to existence. When the First Patriarch faced the wall and did not establish written texts, he feared that people might become attached to non-existence.

Consequently, Tiantai and Xianshou composed commentaries and sub-commentaries, not sparing themselves as they analyzed the teachings in minute detail to provide explanations for them. Now, this Master’s composition of this record is driven by a profound heart of compassion;
his sole aim is to cause the Dharma lineage to resound greatly once more and for the rain of the Teachings to fall in torrents, ensuring that one neither clings to existence nor...
Attachment to non-existence is unattainable; attachment to existence is unattainable; attachment to both existence and non-existence is likewise unattainable.
If this is so, then the Buddha’s words are present herein, and the karmic conditions for enlightenment are present herein. How could the Perfect and Sudden Teaching be difficult to attain?
I have thus composed this preface to bring it all home.

Now, when the teachings of the Platform [School] explain the sutras, they expound the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*): namely, that through names the essence (*dharmatā*) is revealed; by means of the essence, the core principle (*śāstra-artha*) is clarified;

based on the core principle, the function (*kāritra*) is distinguished; and finally, the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*) are elucidated. When Fazang (Xianshou) commented on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, he first opened with ten gates of differentiation;
these are the principles established by these two schools for their respective teachings. Now, the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra* fully encompasses these.

Within the *Avataṃsaka*, the profound mysteries of the final five stages shall be briefly expounded according to ten gates: first, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, the classification and inclusion within the Piṭakas and teachings;
third, the profundity of its principles and meanings; fourth, the suitability of the Dharma for various capacities; fifth, the essence and function of its doctrinal divisions;
sixth, the chronological sequence of the traces of the teaching; seventh, the periods of the translations; eighth, the spiritual resonance regarding commentaries and annotations; ninth...
Explaining the title of the sutra: the ten commentaries clarify that its meaning accords with the fundamental school.

First, regarding the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching: when our Buddha appeared in the world, he preached over three hundred assemblies of sutras solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition—to awaken all sentient beings and lead them into the ground of the Buddha’s wisdom. This is just as it was with the sages of this land [China].
The intention behind bequeathing the Six Classics to demonstrate to future generations is the same [as that of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*]. As for the Six Classics:

the *Book of Changes* (*Yi*) exhausts the profound and investigates the subtle, setting forth the principles of heaven and earth, yin and yang, the four seasons, and the five elements; the *Book of Documents* (*Shu*) records the deeds of sage-kings in governing the world;

the *Book of Poetry* (*Shi*) strengthens human relations, glorifies education and transformation, and shifts customs and manners; the *Book of Rites* (*Li*) provides a framework for the order of social relations; and the *Book of Music* (*Yue*)... [is intended to harmonize the mind and unify the people].
This brings forth the ultimate harmony of Heaven and Earth. Through the Spring and Autumn Annals, evil is punished and goodness encouraged;

by propagating the virtues of the Three Dynasties, it serves as a model for the world—this is the business of governing the world. Now, the Tathāgata acts for the great matter of transcending the world.

Observing the capacities of beings and adapting the teachings accordingly, from the shallow to the profound, the World-Honored One expounded the teachings for a single lifetime over forty-nine years, each with its own causal origin.

For instance, at the very beginning upon attaining enlightenment, while in the Hall of the Path of Quiescent Extinction, he was surrounded by the forty-one ranks of Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body, as well as those whose roots had matured in past lives, and the eight classes of devas and dragons, all gathered at once. The World-Honored One...

Manifesting the body of the ten-thousand-fathom Vairocana, he preached for them the Dharma of the Ten Abodes, the Ten Practices, the Ten Transferences, the Ten Grounds, as well as the two awakenings of Equality and Subtlety;
this is named the *Avataṃsaka*. This constitutes the beginning of the Great Transformation.

Xianshou (Fazang) classified it as the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), while the Tiantai school classified it as the Sudden Teaching (*tun jiao*). Furthermore, they maintain that it combines the Separate Teaching while preaching the Perfect, as stated in the sutra:
At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening; for those of complete capacity, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is preached.
Furthermore, in various places, the sequential progression of practice is taught; for those of provisional capacity, the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) is preached.
At that time, the Śrāvakas of the Two Vehicles were like the deaf and mute, neither hearing nor seeing. Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says: "When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, I observed..."
He walked in meditation beneath a tree for twenty-one days, contemplating and recollecting how all the Buddhas of the past had, through skillful means, taught the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
For this reason, in order to cause all sentient beings to cast off their precious [attachments] and discard their coarse [delusions], he preached the Four Āgamas (translated here as "The Peerless").
First, the *Ekottarika Āgama* clarifies the causes and effects for humans and devas. Second, the *Madhyama Āgama* clarifies the profound meaning of true quiescence.
Third, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* clarifies the various dhyāna concentrations. Fourth, the *Dīrgha Āgama* clarifies the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.

Master Xianshou classified these as the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings, while the Tiantai school classified them as the Tripitaka Teaching (*Zangjiao*). These were taught during the second period at the Deer Park; subsequently, they were used to critique the partial (one-sided) teachings.

He censures the Small [Vehicle] and extols the Great, praising the Perfect. Thus, he expounds more than forty scriptures, including the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Saṃghāṭa*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and the *Śrīmālā*.
The Tiantai teachings refer to this as the third period, the "Period of the Shared Equivalence" (*fāngděng shí*).

Within it, the four teachings (namely, the *Zàng*, *Tōng*, *Bié*, and *Yuán*) are discussed extensively; they are called "Shared" (*fāng*) because they are equally bestowed upon all capacities. Xianshou’s judgment [is as follows]:
The *Sudden Teaching* (*dun jiao*) consists of the subsequent preaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and others. Xianshou classifies this as the Initial Teaching of Mahāyāna.
The Tiantai school classifies it as the fourth period, while the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* are combined as the fifth period; Xianshou classifies this as the Final Teaching of Mahāyāna.
However, the *Lotus Sūtra* bestows predictions upon the śrāvakas that they shall become Buddhas, and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies the permanence of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

The meaning of "abiding" (*sthiti*) marks the conclusion of the beginning of the Mahāyāna. This present sutra truly brings together the entire Great Canon (*Tripitaka*), synthesizing the teachings of the five periods and five flavors.

It may thus resolve the disputes regarding the division into eight [categories]—as classified by the Tiantai school into the Sudden, Gradual, Esoteric, Indeterminate, Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect—or the division into five—as classified by Xianshou into the Small, Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect. Therefore, within it, it is neither the Tripitaka, nor the Shared, nor the Distinct; therein...
It is gradual yet sudden; sudden yet perfect; beginning yet ending; provisional yet ultimate.

It enables those of both sharp and dull faculties to attain realization, and allows practitioners of both small and great capacities to achieve enlightenment together. Furthermore, there are five reasons for the arising of this sutra:

first, for the sake of Bodhisattvas on the current stages who have deeply entered the One Vehicle and understand the fundamental principles of the Buddha-dharma; second, for the sake of those who are about to... [text continues]
First, it is for bodhisattvas who come to study Prajñāpāramitā to transcend the latter five stages instantaneously, thereby attaining the dharmas of both Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment.
Second, it is to enable sentient beings of the末代 (final age) to obtain a direct and swift path of practice, as each stage is perfectly encompassed therein.
Third, it is to manifest the single-flavor, true, and unsurpassed *amṛta* (clarified butter) of the genuine Bodhisattva Vehicle. Fourth, it is for... [the fifth point follows].

To sever the proliferation of words and phrases, to harmonize the teachings and penetrate the essence, and to attain the wondrous wisdom that accords with a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*) by awakening to the true meaning—for these reasons, it is said in the *Huayan He lun* (Treatise on the Compendium of the Avataṃsaka): "Accord in a single thought-moment, and in a single thought-moment one attains Buddhahood;
accord for a single day, and in a single day one attains Buddhahood. There is no need to practice through gradual stages over the course of kalpas. These are the five meanings. Thus...

Regarding the classification of this sutra within the two collections (*piṭaka*) of the teachings: since the dependent origination has already been clarified, one must understand that the doctrines and meanings spoken by the Tathāgata are subsumed within the three collections and twelve divisions of the teachings (formerly called the twelvefold scriptures). Now, this *Vajrasamādhi* is fundamentally [a teaching on] cultivation...
The *Tara-piṭaka* (that is, the Sūtra-piṭaka) contains within it the three clusters of precepts (*tri-śikṣā*), which thus subsume the Vinaya-piṭaka.

Furthermore, as its beginning and end consist of responses to inquiries that investigate and analyze profound principles, it also concurrently subsumes the Abhidharma-piṭaka; therefore, all three piṭakas are contained therein.

Among the twelve divisions of the teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*), this sutra encompasses nine of them. Its direct revelation of the true reality (*tattva*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) constitutes the *sūtra* (discourse) division, the fundamental source of the Dharma.
Its verses, dialogues, and non-redundant meanings constitute the *geya* (versified response) division.

The Tathāgata’s proclamation upon emerging from meditative absorption constitutes the *vyākaraṇa* (prophecy/self-proclamation) division. The questions posed by bodhisattvas constitute the *nidāna* (causal narrative) division, as it is extensively taught for the sake of sentient beings in the final age.
To teach the Dharma of a single flavor that brings about vast benefit and happiness is Vaipulya (Extensive Teaching).
To bestow upon Śāriputra the prophecy of his attainment of Bodhi is Vyākaraṇa (Prophecy). To speak now what was not previously spoken is Adbhutadharma (Marvelous Event).
To apply the metaphor to the Dharma and the Dharma to the metaphor is Avadāna (Parable). To investigate and interrogate through the profoundness of ultimate truth is Upadeśa (Treatise).

[The commentary] deliberates that [this scripture] does not include three categories: the *itivṛttaka* (accounts of past events), the *jātaka* (accounts of former births), and the *geya* (verses reiterating the meaning).
Furthermore, it states that while the doctrinal characteristics established by various schools differ from one another, this scripture harmonizes and synthesizes them all.

This merely reveals the perfect and true [teaching]. For instance, when the Great Master Xianshou established the teachings of the Hīnayāna, he relied upon the six consciousnesses and the three poisons to briefly explain the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena, yet he did not do so clearly.

The Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna speaks only of the emptiness of the characteristics of all phenomena, without exhausting the meaning of the Mahāyāna dharma-nature. The Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna is also called the True Teaching (*śāstramata*). Slightly...

It explains the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) and predominantly explains the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Even when it speaks of the characteristics of phenomena, it ultimately converges upon the nature of phenomena;

this constitutes the ultimate teaching of the Mahāyāna from beginning to end. Nevertheless, these two teachings—beginning and end—involve progressive cultivation according to stages; they are gradual, not sudden.
The fifth is the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This refers to the ocean-like nature of the *dharmadhātu*, wherein all things are perfectly interfused and mutually inclusive.

For example, upon reaching the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one immediately encompasses the five stages of abiding, practice, direction, the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*), and equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) to achieve perfect awakening.
Furthermore, according to the Fourfold Teachings of the Great Master Zhiyi, the Tathāgata preached the Tripitaka for those śrāvakas who were fixed in their resolve.
The Teaching: The *Tongjiao* (Teaching of Commonality) is taught for the sake of regressing Mahāśrāvakas; the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching) is taught for the sake of gradual Bodhisattvas;

and the *Yuanjiao* (Perfect Teaching) is taught for the sake of sudden-awakening Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, the *Sijiaoyi* (Outline of the Four Teachings) states: "Generally, all Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras that do not share the stages and positions of the Three Vehicles belong entirely to the Perfect Teaching.
It further cites the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "At the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one immediately becomes..."
The Perfectly Awakened One. Vimalakīrti enters the Dharma-gate of non-duality; Prajñāpāramitā elucidates the Supreme Vehicle. As for the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:

suppose there is a person who enters the great ocean to bathe, having already used the waters of all rivers, and furthermore, the Sāgara Dragon pours down rain as thick as chariot axles—only the great ocean can receive it, while other lands cannot endure it. Furthermore, it is like pounding ten thousand kinds of...
Incense is made into pellets; when one pellet is burned, all fragrances are fully present. Such categories as these all belong to the Complete Teaching (Yuanjiao).

The meaning of the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* precisely accords with what is explained in the *Fourfold Teaching Ritual*. Furthermore, it correctly corresponds to the teaching of the Complete Teaching for Bodhisattvas of the Sudden Teaching (Dun jiao).
Moreover, since the sūtra repeatedly speaks of the One Vehicle and the Single Flavor, there is no need to apply the "opening" (kai) [of the provisional].
"Three reveal one. Furthermore, the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) states:
"From the opening of the provisional at the Deer Park, passing through various sūtras and teachings until reaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, one finally attains union with the Real.

Now, observing the meaning of the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, the principle of the single reality (*eka-artha*) of the *Lotus Sūtra* only here reaches its ultimate perfection. Moreover, it is further able to encompass all Mahāyāna sūtras..."
Regarding its meaning: if one fully cultivates the six perfections, it is rooted in the *Prajñāpāramitā*; if one elucidates the five dharmas, it is consistent with the *Laṅkāvatāra*;
if one realizes the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), it is subsumed within the *Vimalakīrti*; and if one clarifies the stages and positions (*bhūmi*), it is identical to the *Avataṃsaka*.
In explaining the nine consciousnesses, it resembles the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*; in citing the One Vehicle, it accords with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;

and in supporting the Vinaya while discussing the eternal, it represents the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Furthermore, in discussing characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it truly encompasses the *Vijñaptimātratā* school;

in discussing nature (*svabhāva*), it includes the *Awakening of Faith*. Thus, there are no dharmas of the Mahāyāna that are not subsumed within it; it is therefore fitting to call it the "Compendium of the Mahāyāna" (*Mahāyānasaṃgraha*).
This is the school of the meaning of the *Pramāṇa*.

Regarding the three points that "the principles are profound and deep": since one already knows what is subsumed within the *piṭaka* teachings, one should further understand the intent behind the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.

Specifically, the Initial Teaching (Śāstra) discards the real and reveals the provisional, differentiating the gradual progression of the Three Vehicles; the Final Teaching discards the provisional...
Establishing the reality [of the teachings], he synthesizes the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle; that is to say, the earlier stages are shallow and the later stages are deep.
Nevertheless, the Tiantai teaching regards the *Lotus Sūtra* as the final teaching and the final flavor.

Furthermore, it is said that the *Lotus Sūtra* was taught for those śrāvakas whose faculties had matured, while for others with dull faculties who were not yet mature, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* serves as the final teaching and the final flavor.
This present sutra serves as the pivotal key for the two sutras of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*. It is the essential core of the final teaching and the final flavor (*rasa*).

Its meaning is profound and deep, difficult to comprehend through mere intellectual understanding. Furthermore, according to the Tiantai teachings, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is designated as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which opens up the preceding sudden and gradual teachings and brings them together into that which is neither sudden nor gradual, thereby manifesting the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). In terms of flavors, it is called "ghee" (*ghṛta*, *ti-hu*); therefore, it is said to "open."

He reveals, awakens, and leads [beings] into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; he bestows upon the śrāvakas the prediction of their attainment of Buddhahood, thereby fully manifesting the Tathāgata’s fundamental intention.
Yet, he provisionally sets forth the three vehicles as a skillful means and grants the śrāvakas the prediction of attaining Buddhahood after distant kalpas.
This is precisely because he wishes to induce them to practice the bodhisattva path and urge them to enter the Buddha’s nirvana without remainder. Now, this sutra...

He elucidated the perfect principle of the One Vehicle, the single flavor, and the single reality of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, clarifying the practices performed by Bodhisattvas throughout the stages and levels, and realizing the dharmas of the two awakenings—Equal and Wondrous.
Beyond this, there is nothing further to be added. As for Xianshou [Fazang], he regarded the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as the One Vehicle of sudden and perfect realization;
it is like the great ocean encompassing the hundred rivers, wherein a single dharma is cited [to represent all].
Yet, every dharma is fully present therein; thus, the text is abundant and the meaning is vast, leaving scholars no choice but to feel as bewildered as one gazing out at the ocean.

This present sutra is precisely the teaching on the latter five stages (*bhūmi*) and the two levels of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) from within the *Daśabhūmika* chapter of the *Avataṃsaka*.
However, its phrasing is concise while its meaning is comprehensive; its sentences and words are ancient and simple, incomparable to other sutras.
For the "dharma of signlessness" mentioned in this sutra refers to the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) and one’s own mind.

Furthermore, it clarifies that the six *pāramitās* are all signless and unconditioned—the dharma of liberation and the practice of non-arising, which is the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena). The meaning of attaining this patience constitutes the central tenet [of this teaching].
The "gate" refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). A single stroke cuts it off; this is the sharpness of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

One immediately transforms the eighth consciousness of original enlightenment into *amala-vijñāna* (the ninth, pure white consciousness). This is precisely attaining the sharpness that emerges from within original enlightenment.
Entering the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one cultivates the wisdom of the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) to benefit sentient beings. True nature is empty; directly, below—
This reveals the cultivation of the five stages, so that sentient beings of future generations may each attain the stage of perfected wisdom in a single lifetime.
Through the Tathāgatagarbha, they realize and witness the Tathāgata’s own nature, the pure treasury;
by exhausting the subtle characteristics within the ālayavijñāna, they become one essence with Vairocana. This "Chapter on Total Retention" summarizes the preceding six chapters.

The Dharma perfectly accords with the Buddha’s mind, thereby clarifying that the fundamental essence of wisdom is shared by both sentient beings and Buddhas; this is precisely the fulfillment of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment.

Regarding the fourth point, "the Dharma reaching those whose capacities are appropriate": now that the profound and mysterious principle of this sutra has been clarified, for what kind of capacity is it intended?
As for the "vessel," there are two types according to the Dharma: first, those intended for Mahayana bodhisattvas who are currently ready to transform and deliver sentient beings;
second, those intended for sentient beings of future末代 (final ages) who cultivate supramundane causes and thereby attain supramundane fruits.

As for the "causes," these refer to the Introductory Chapter (*Nidāna-parivarta*), which inspires right faith in sentient beings and reveals the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*) Dharma. As for the "fruits," these refer to the textual passages of the subsequent seven chapters.

First, it demonstrates the Dharma of *prajñā* within the sixth stage; second, it demonstrates the realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) within the seventh stage;
third, it demonstrates the transformation of the various consciousnesses into the *amala-vijñāna* Dharma within the eighth stage;

fourth, it demonstrates the entry into the Dharma of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) within the ninth stage; and fifth, it demonstrates the true nature of emptiness as the essence, whereby the Dharmas of the ten stages are brought to full completion.

Sixth, it demonstrates entry into the Tathāgatagarbha, because one realizes the stage of the Dharma-position of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Seventh, it demonstrates the Dharma of Sublime Enlightenment, because the fruit of Buddhahood is perfected.
Furthermore, in the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when Sudhana first beheld Mañjuśrī, he awakened to the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa;
yet Mañjuśrī further directed him to travel south to consult more than fifty spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Sudhana said:
"I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how to study the conduct of a bodhisattva or cultivate the path of a bodhisattva.

At that time, each of those spiritual friends, having individually instructed me in the Dharma of self-realization and self-awakening, further said: "I have only attained this Dharma-gate of liberation. As for all other bodhisattvas..."
"This is what is practiced by the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; how could I possibly know or recognize their meritorious conduct?

These are the words from the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter. Now, these teachings on the stages from the sixth to the tenth bhūmis, as well as the Dharma of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment, spoken directly from the mouth of the Tathāgata, are truly for those who study the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path in this final age.
The Dharma procedure. Yet, apart from this, the great meritorious practices of a Bodhisattva can ultimately not be attained.

Regarding the five schools that distinguish essence (*ti*) and function (*yong*): once one knows the capacities of those to be converted, one must know the fundamental tenets of the Dharma, which possess both essence and function.
Now, the Tiantai teachings first present the names of essence, tenet, and function, and subsequently demonstrate the characteristics of the teaching; this [present case] is not so.
Indeed, in the past, when the World-Honored One first beheld the morning star and attained perfect enlightenment, he exclaimed:
"All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata; it is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they do not realize it.

This clarifies that the Buddha’s initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) and the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) of sentient beings are of one essence and non-dual. Yet, it is only after the Buddhas have realized this that [they manifest...].
There is the name of the "Treasury Teachings" (Zangjiao). Furthermore, it is truly from beholding the stars that one realizes its essence, and from observing the tree that one attains its function.

Moreover, when the Tathāgata entered meditative absorption and emitted light, this was the "Patriarchal Penetration" (Zongtong); to use verbal explanation to elucidate the meaning of entering absorption and emitting light belongs to the "Explanatory Penetration" (Shuotong).
Furthermore, the Patriarchal Penetration is the plucking of the flower to show the assembly; the Explanatory Penetration is the Way of the World-Honored One.
"I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana, the subtle and sublime Dharma-gate of the true mark which is markless.
It does not rely on words and letters; it is a separate transmission outside the teachings, entrusted to Mahākāśyapa. This is it.

Therefore, this sutra takes the two types of awakening—the fundamental and the initial—as its core principle (*zong*); the true mark which is markless as its essence (*ti*); and the penetration of the principle and the penetration of the teaching as its function (*yong*). Its essence is...
By means of mutual exposition, both the thesis and the explanation are fully elucidated; this is the most supreme and subtle Dharma within the Great Treasury of the Buddha’s Teachings.

Regarding the sequence of the traces of the six teachings, since the fundamental tenets have been established to distinguish essence and function, one must also determine the temporal period of this sutra.
According to the Tiantai classification of the teachings, there are five periods: first, the Huayan period; second, the Deer Park period; third, the Vaipulya period; fourth, the Prajñā period;
and fifth, the Nirvāṇa period. Furthermore, eight teachings are established:

the four teachings of sudden, gradual, secret, and indefinite are designated as the "teachings of method" (huayi), while the four teachings of Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect are designated as the "teachings of content" (huafa). Moreover, the sudden teaching is divided into two types: the first...
The *Avataṃsaka* is designated as "Sudden," while other teachings are said to be "Complete" (perfect).

Second, the Vaipulya Mahāyāna section—whose temporal sequence is not fixed—is considered "Sudden" in its manifestation of the essence according to the capacities of beings, and thus belongs to the "Indeterminate Teaching.

Furthermore, the three periods of the Deer Park (the Four Āgamas), the Vaipulya, and the Prajñāpāramitā are classified as the "Gradual Teaching. Moreover, within these aforementioned four periods, some teachings are also described as "Sudden."
Alternatively, it is said that [the teachings] are gradual; that beings do not know one another's [intentions], yet are able to derive benefit—this is the secret teaching (*guhyaka*).
Furthermore, during the first four periods, the Buddha preached the Dharma with a single voice, and sentient beings attained understanding according to their respective types.

Some attained the gradual through the sudden, while others attained the sudden through the gradual; as they mutually benefited one another in different ways, this is also called the indeterminate teaching (*aniyata-vyākaraṇa*). This...

These constitute the four teachings of the pedagogical method (*sāṃketika-dharma*). Furthermore, the preaching of the *Āgamas* at the Deer Park is designated as the Tripitaka Teaching of the Hīnayāna.

Moreover, the Vaipulya and Prajñā sections are designated as the Shared Teaching; this is because it is shared with the preceding Tripitaka Teaching and shared with the subsequent Distinct and Perfect Teachings.

Furthermore, the sequential stages of the bodhisattva path—such as the practices, dwellings, directions, and grounds—as found in the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Ratnakūṭa*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* sūtras, all belong to the provisional vehicle (*upāyayāna*) and constitute the Separate Teaching (*pṛthagvidya*).
This means it is distinct from the preceding Tripitaka and Shared Teachings, and distinct from the subsequent Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpannayāna*).

Finally, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is established as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of true reality (*dharmatā*), wherein the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are revealed and the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) is bestowed.
To become a Buddha—this is the sudden and the perfect. This refers to the Tathāgata’s teaching throughout his entire life;

it was only upon reaching the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that it finally attained full completion, and is therefore termed the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). These constitute the four teachings regarding the methods of transformation.

In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is combined to form the fifth period. It is designated as "clarified butter" (*tíhú*) in terms of its flavor, clarifying that the realization of the Buddha-nature is its essential meaning. Furthermore...

In the teachings, five periods are mentioned: primarily based on twelve years for the *Āgama* period, eight years for the *Vaipulya*, twenty-two years for the *Prajñāpāramitā*, seven years for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and one day at midnight for the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.

If one examines the various sūtras according to what the Buddha taught, the circumstances regarding the Śākya clan being slaughtered by King Virūḍhaka actually occurred during the seventh year of the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

The five-year period is instead recorded in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, and the account of King Udayana’s creation of an image—occurring within the three months prior to the Parinirvāṇa—is instead recorded in the *Ekottara Āgama*.
If one were to claim that these were collected among the Āgama sections, [it would be inconsistent].
This is acceptable. It need not necessarily refer to the assembly at the *Āgama*, which concludes after twelve years.

As for the remaining four periods, one should likewise not be dogmatically attached to their specific explanations. Regarding the claim that during the final seven years he preached only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
even the *Śuddhodana-rāja-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* was delivered during the fourth year of his preaching the *Lotus Sūtra*. [The same applies to] the *Liu-li*...
The King’s slaughter of the Śākyas also occurred after King Śuddhodana had passed away; this is as stated in the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*.
Furthermore, prior to his *parinirvāṇa*, while the Buddha was at the Mahāvana-vihāra in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Three months from now, I shall enter *parinirvāṇa*. He then expounded for them the practice of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
The *Sūtra* (namely, the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra*) and the *Sūtra on Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother* (both of which are recorded in the *Fozu tongji*).
Furthermore, within the Canon there are the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* and the *Catur-mahārājika-samādhi-sūtra*, which are likewise included within the *Nirvāṇa* section.
This is because those who categorized the teachings omitted them, mentioning only the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as the fifth period. Let us examine this in detail once more.
Regarding *nirvāṇa*, one should not say it occurs on the first day at midnight; rather, it should be understood as concluding after three months.

As for the period prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, it was taught according to the capacities of beings, which is logically inevitable. Now, having examined the *Vajrasamādhi* in detail:
Within this [text], the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle is thoroughly investigated, and the principle of "discussing permanence by means of a provisional extinction" is revealed;

it must therefore have been composed after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and before the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Formerly, Master Changshui judged the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* to belong to the period after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and before the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
However, many masters of later generations have largely refuted his error, asserting instead that it belongs to the period after the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras* and before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

It is prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Master Xiancheng of Shengchen judged this *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra* to also belong to the period after the *Prajñāpāramitā* and before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
thus, the two periods are not fixed as distinct teaching phases (*jiaoxiang*).

Now, based on this scripture, although it shares the same profound meaning as the *Avataṃsaka*, it was preached at Gṛdhrakūṭa Parvata alongside the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Furthermore, Śāriputra, at its outset—

At the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he himself had not yet attained full realization; it was only upon hearing the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma that his doubts and regrets were finally severed.
Now, within this present assembly, he ultimately assumes responsibility for the entire world; thus, this sutra must have been composed after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Vimukta poses questions as if they were from after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, and within the *Tathāgataguṇasaṃcayadhāraṇī*, there is again mention of *nirvāṇa*.
The teaching that speaks of permanence while relying on extinction must have occurred at the very moment the World-Honored One proclaimed his parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is combined with the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* as the fifth period, the present *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra* may likewise follow the same precedent as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and be combined with the *Nirvāṇa*.
Indeed, this sutra is most concise and essential; it was likely because the World-Honored One [saw]... [the necessity of this].

Forty-nine years have passed, and much has already been spoken. Now, desiring to encompass the extensive within the concise, [the Buddha] specifically, prior to his *nirvāṇa*, summarized the essential meanings of over three hundred assemblies.
This allows those with perfect capacities to suddenly transcend the forty-one stages.
Thus, at one time, together with the great Bodhisattvas of the Great Vehicle, he preached this *Vajrasamādhi*, which directly accords with the Dharma of the *Avataṃsaka*.

Flower. From beginning to end, it is identical in its Perfect and Sudden nature (to "encompass all dharmas" is called Perfect; to "enter directly into the stage of Buddhahood" is called Sudden). Extending this broadly, one attains sudden vision.

Sudden awakening, sudden transcendence, and sudden entry; reaching the perfection of principle, the perfection of practice, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of stages, the perfection of cause, and the perfection of fruit—every single thing and every phenomenon is perfect.
This is what is called "perfect-perfection. If one practices according to this, one is truly a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
As stated in the *Catalogue of the Precious Dharma of the Great Canon of Holy Teachings*: *The Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*.
Then the bodhisattvas questioned the Buddha regarding the non-arising of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the single-flavored true Dharma.

After the Buddha had preached this sutra, he entrusted it to them, saying: "This sutra can enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. Those who uphold this sutra shall have no further aspirations among all other sutras;
they will encompass the essentials of all sutras—the principles of infinite meanings and the various stages of the mind-ground."

Regarding these various Dharma gates, we have now fortunately encountered them; this is truly a cause for self-congratulation. We should apply ourselves with a hidden, focused mind to our studies, vowing to transcend directly and enter [the path] immediately.
You may do so without harboring doubts concerning the distinctions between earlier and later times. This is appropriate.
Seventh, regarding the periods of translation: Having already clarified the time when the Dharma was preached, it is necessary to examine in detail during which era the translations were made.
Now, "translation" (yi) carries the meaning of exchange; it refers to turning the language of the Brahmā-heaven (Sanskrit) and transforming it into the speech of the land of Han.
Initially, Buddhist scriptures came from the Five Indias of India. India is situated precisely in the center of Jambudvīpa. During the kalpa...
Originally, beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended here; therefore, their speech and written characters were all identical to those of the Brahmā Heaven.

Since these were transmitted to this land, they necessarily required translation before they could become clear. According to the *Liji* (Book of Rites), in the "Wangzhi" (Institutions of the King) chapter, it states: "One must master the languages of the four quarters."
Each had its respective official: in the east was the *ji*; in the south, the *xiang*; in the west, the *diti*; and in the north, the *yi*. The commentator states:
"The *ji* refers to entrusting one's meaning to objects and phenomena to communicate it.
The *xiang* refers to using the mind to imitate and resemble forms to communicate it. *Di* is the same as *di*, meaning 'remote. *Di* is simply footwear; the term implies..."
One who travels afar to observe their practices understands where the meaning of their words lies and thus communicates with them.
A translator conveys and explains the languages of both lands to facilitate mutual understanding. In antiquity, these were collectively called *xiangxu*; "xu" means to assist.
Today, they are popularly referred to as "interpreters. At that time, when the Semblance Dharma first arrived in the land of Han, it coincided with the era of northern translators.

The official was also proficient in Western languages and was thus appointed as the translator (among the various masters of translation during the Six Dynasties period, none were men of shallow learning; within the translation hall, there were those specifically assigned to interpret the language).

There was one who translated the meaning, one who polished the phrasing, one who verified the Sanskrit terminology, one who verified the meaning, and one who compared the Chinese and Sanskrit versions. This scripture has lost the name of its translator.

Appended to the Northern Liang Record. According to Sengyou’s *Chu sanzang jiji*, Daoan’s biography compiled by Huijiao of the Liang dynasty states: "From the Han and Wei dynasties down to the Jin, the number of sūtras that arrived was indeed great;
yet the masters who transmitted and translated them did not record their names, and later students, in tracing their origins, could not determine their dates.

Daoan therefore compiled a catalog of titles to distinguish the contemporaries involved, and categorized the texts as new or old, compiling them into a *Zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures)."

Record. That the various scriptures have authoritative sources is truly due to his merit. Furthermore, Fei Changfang of the Sui dynasty (formerly there was also a Fei Changfang of the Han, who was an earth-bound immortal) had previously been a śramaṇa.

During the persecution of Buddhism by Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, he returned to lay life. When the Sui rose, Emperor Wen issued an edict appointing him as a scholar for the translation of scriptures.
In the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, he presented the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through the Successive Dynasties) in fifteen fascicles. Within it...
The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* was included by Sengyou of the Liang dynasty in his *New Collection of Dharma Master Dao’an’s Heterodox Scriptures from the Liangtu Region*.
However, within that catalog, its source of translation was lost. It is now reattached to the period of the Liang dynasty. This is similar to the case of the *Triprajñā Sūtra* and other such texts.
All [these works] are listed by Sengyou in his catalog as scriptures of unusual provenance from the Liang region according to Master Daoan; they are now appended to the Northern Liang catalog.
Upon examination, Master Daoan passed away in the tenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty, the *wuyou* year (485 CE).

The following year, the *bingxu* year (486 CE), Lü Guang established the Later Liang. Furthermore, fifteen years later, in the *xinchou* year (501 CE), Juqu Mengxun first proclaimed the Northern Liang.

Now, judging by its inclusion among the records of the Liang dynasty, it should be categorized as belonging to the period when the Zhang clan ruled as a state in Liangzhou; it certainly does not refer to Northern Liang.
Furthermore, the *Sanbao ji* records that Dao’an of the Fu Qin dynasty also once translated twenty-four scriptures.

Moreover, since Sengyou’s *Xinji daojian liangtu yi jing* (Newly Compiled Extraordinary Scriptures of Dao’an from the Liang Region) specifically mentions him, these must indeed have been the works of the Dharma Master Dao’an.
Translated.

Regarding the eight commentaries on the *Gantong* (Manifestation and Response): once the transmission and translation of this sutra were clarified, the traces of its "manifestation and response" (*gantong*) were further revealed.
Examining Zeng Ning’s *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song*, it records that Dharma Master Wonhyo was a native of Silla. Initially, together with Uisang... [text continues]
The Master resolved to sail across the ocean in search of the Dharma. Upon reaching Tangzhou, he encountered rain at dusk and took shelter in an earthen grotto.

When he looked there at dawn, he found it was beside the skeletal remains of an ancient tomb. Thereupon, his doubts were dispelled, and he attained a sudden awakening to the principle that the three realms are mind-only.
He immediately returned to his country, where he composed commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and extensively propagated the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden Vehicle.
One day, the King of Silla suffered from a tumor on his consort’s head that no physician could cure.
He offered prayers at a sacred shrine, where a medium declared, "You must go to a great kingdom to seek medicine. The King immediately dispatched an envoy across the sea.
When the vessel had traveled halfway, he suddenly beheld a man emerging from amidst the massive waves, who invited him into the Dragon Palace. In a brief moment, he saw a dragon.
The King said to him, "The Queen of your country is the third daughter of the Blue Emperor.
In my palace, there is already the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, which reveals the bodhisattva practices through the perfect penetration of the two types of awakening.
Now, relying on the illness of the Queen as a superior condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), you may take this sūtra and propagate it in that country. Thereupon, he brought forth the sūtra.
The messenger was instructed further: "This scripture emerged from the ocean; there may be demonic interference, so wrap it securely with waxed paper.
Cut open your calf muscles to insert it within, then apply medicinal ointment to heal them as they were before. The Dragon King spoke again:
"Go and report this to the King, requesting that Master Wonhyo be invited to compose a commentary and deliver a lecture. As for the Queen's illness—"

He recovered on his own. The messenger returned and reported the matter in full detail. The King was greatly delighted and immediately provided offerings for the Dharma Master to compose a commentary (*śāstra*).
Tanyao then realized the meaning of this sutra, taking the two types of awakening—the fundamental and the initial—as its central tenet. He informed the King, who prepared a carriage with horns;

a small table was placed between the two horns, and his brush and inkstone were set upon it. Beginning and ending at the ox-cart, he composed the commentary, which consisted of five fascicles. Indeed...
The man’s illness was indeed cured. The King set a date and invited [the Master] to expound the *Yanyi* at Huanglong Temple.
Furthermore, because his disciples had stolen the commentary and departed, he recorded it again, completing three fascicles titled the *Lüeshu* (Abridged Commentary).
Later, both the extensive and abridged versions circulated in the land; the abridged version was transmitted into the kingdom. Subsequently, a Tripiṭaka Master who translated scriptures revised it.
The treatise states: The *Linjian Lu* (Record from the Forest) by the Song dynasty Chan Master Juefan also records this previous matter.
At the end of the Ming Wanli era, Chan Master Xiansheng Cheng provided a commentary on it; subsequently, Dharma Master Huikai Lang further annotated and expounded upon it.
I have personally examined the *Huayan Xuantan*, the *Zongjing Lu*, and the *Zhizheng Zhuan*, all of which cite the *Jin*.
The *Gāṅ-sam-mae-gyǒng* (Kongō-zammai-kyō) contains the terminology [of this text]. There is also a brief commentary on the *Yuánjué* (Complete Enlightenment).

Furthermore, I have seen a mere glimpse of the commentary by the scholar from the East Sea (Haidong), though it remains a regret that I was unable to obtain the complete work. Moreover, in the *Fányì míngyì jí* (Collection of Translated Names and Meanings), it is recorded that there was a commentary by Sengdùn (a successor of Fǎyǎn);
however, I likewise have not been able to see it.
