At the initial stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), one awakens to the fact that the afflictions of the fundamental ground of ignorance (*mūlāvidyāvāsabhūmi*) are themselves the immovable wisdom (*acalajñāna*) of all Buddhas.

This is because, through one’s own original enlightenment (*prakṛtistha-awakening*), one realizes one’s own fundamental mind; thus, the nature and characteristics of one’s body and mind are no different from those of the Buddha.
As the treatise states: "The provisional teachings and limited views delight in seeking the extraordinary; for Bodhisattvas, [the teaching] is applied coarsely according to their faculties."

One should provide guidance and lead others forward, causing them to develop a joyful inclination toward study before imparting the gateway of reality (*bhūtadvāra*). However, one must not cling to these provisional manifestations as being ultimate truth, for this would perpetually obscure the eye of wisdom.
One should recognize the provisional and proceed toward the real, migrating into the gateway of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Conditioned dharmas are difficult to accomplish;

effortless action in accordance with conditions (*anabhisaṃskāra-anuvartana*) is easily achieved. Those who act laboriously find no merit, whereas non-action in accordance with conditions spontaneously succeeds—this is meritless merit.

The merit [of these practices] is not in vain; yet the merit of such achievements is all impermanent. Though cultivated through the accumulation of many kalpas, it ultimately returns to decay and ruin.
It is better to realize in a single thought that conditioned arising is non-arising, thereby transcending the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles.
This is the clear instruction of the Tathāgata’s true dharma-gate. The Tiantai teachings divide the canon into the four teachings of *zàng*, *tōng*, *bié*, and *yuán*. By means of...
The Complete Teaching (Yuanjiao) is the most supreme. The bodhisattvas in this assembly do not linger in the three provisional [teachings], but have ascended solely to the one reality.
Furthermore, there were eighty thousand elders present together, whose names were: Elder Brahmā-conduct, Elder Mahābrahmā, and Elder Tree...
Regarding the Elder Ti (Ti-jia-zhe):

such elders as these are called *brahman* in Sanskrit, meaning "one who has left desire" (*vītarāga*), because they cultivate pure conduct by being free from desire. By this same principle, Mahābrahmā may be understood.
Regarding Shuti (Shu-ti): this means "fire. His mother died after eating poisonous fruit; fire was used to cremate her corpse, and her abdomen split open.
He was born there. His father requested the Buddha to name him. The Buddha said, "Because this child possesses great merit and virtue, he was born amidst fierce flames;
therefore, he may be named accordingly. This account is recorded in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Furthermore, the term "brahmacarya" (pure conduct) signifies liberation.
The Great Brahmā represents the Dharma-body; fire represents Prajñā; and the elder represents the non-duality of the ultimate and conventional truths.
Just as Vimalakīrti, though appearing as a layman, maintained the pure monastic discipline of a śramaṇa; though dwelling at home, he was unattached to the triple world;
and though proficient in worldly classics, he always delighted in the Buddha-dharma—such a person is a Bodhisattva of the stages who manifests as an elder.
They assist in propagating the Dharma transformation.
Furthermore, there were sixty trillion devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
The above constitutes the general, standard introductory formula. *Deva* (Heaven) is the Sanskrit term for "deva. *Nāga* (Dragon) is the Sanskrit term for *nāga*. *Yakṣa* contains three meanings:

valorous and robust, violent and malevolent, and light and swift; it refers to the deities who announce the proclamations of the heavens. *Gandharva* is translated as "Fragrant Aggregate" (*xiāng yīn*);
fragrance issues from their bodies, and they sustain their aggregates (*skandha*) with fragrance; these are the musical deities of the Lord of Heaven. *Asura*... [text truncated]
Asuras: this is translated as "those bound by fetters," so called because they were once defeated in battle with the devas and captured.
Garuḍas: these are the Golden-Winged Bird deities. Kiṃnaras: this is translated as "doubtful deities"; they resemble humans and have horns on their heads;

they are the deities of the Dharma-music of the Heavenly Sovereign. Mahoragas: these are the great serpent deities, human-headed and snake-bodied. These include humans, non-humans, and so forth, in total.
This concludes the assembly of the eight classes of beings. Among these eight classes, the devas alone are the most supreme;

the others are those whose practice is swift but whose precepts are lax, and thus they fall back into their respective categories. The above is traditionally called the "General Preface," and is also known as the "Sixfold Accomplishment":

first, the accomplishment of faith; second, the accomplishment of hearing; third, the accomplishment of time; fourth, the accomplishment of the principal [teacher]; fifth, the accomplishment of place; and sixth—
There are these six kinds of accomplishment. The Buddha then preached the Dharma.

Furthermore, because he had the assembly present at that time verify the Dharma heard by Ānanda, so as to inspire faith in future generations, it is called the "Introduction of Verified Faith" (*samyaktva-nidāna*).
When the time for his parinirvāṇa approached, Ānanda asked: "At the beginning of all sūtras, what words should be placed? The Buddha said: "It should say: 'Thus' (*evam*)."
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was at a certain place together with a great assembly, preaching a certain sutra and teaching.

After his parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa addressed the assembly, saying: "The disciples of the Tathāgata who have attained supernatural powers (abhijñā) should assemble for the compilation [of the teachings].
Thereupon, they all went together to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, to the Kukkuṭapāda Cave (Kukkuṭapāda being the name of a tree).
The Buddha attained the Way of Bodhi beneath this tree; thus it received its name. (However, because there was a tree within a mountain cave, the cave itself was subsequently named after it.
When the Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata was being compiled, Ānanda alone had not yet exhausted his outflows through practice and was initially unable to enter [the state of realization].

Stimulated by this, as the final watch of the night was passing, he was so utterly exhausted that he lay down to rest. As he turned over and reached for his pillow, before his head even touched it, he attained sudden, vast enlightenment.
Like a flash of lightning appearing in the darkness, he saw the path (as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*). At that very moment, he realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Kāśyapa then addressed the assembly, saying: "This bhikṣu Ānanda possesses great wisdom; regarding the Buddha-dharma he has heard..."
It was like water being poured from one vessel into another, with nothing remaining behind. He requested that the assembly perform the compilation [of the Dharma]. The great assembly remained silent.
Kāśyapa addressed Ānanda, saying, "You should now proclaim the Eye of the Dharma. Ānanda, having received this command, prostrated at the feet of the monks and ascended the Dharma-seat.
Suddenly, he manifested the marks and signs of excellence just like the Buddha. At that time, the entire assembly gave rise to three kinds of doubt. First—
They had three doubts: first, that the Buddha had been born again; second, that a Buddha from another world-system had come; and third, that Ānanda had attained Buddhahood.
When Ānanda proclaimed, "Thus have I heard," the assembly's doubts were instantly dispelled. Thereupon, the multitude rejoiced, prostrated themselves, and practiced accordingly.
Kāśyapa again asked the great assembly: "Is what Ānanda has said free from error? They all replied:
"Truly, it does not differ from what the Tathāgata has taught. Formerly, the Buddha also said: "At the beginning of the sūtras of all Buddhas, this same formula is established;

this is what is meant by 'the Way of the Buddhas is the same for each. Furthermore, within the introduction, there is the significance of teacher and disciple, principal and attendant, and internal and external protectors."
Furthermore, it clarifies that regarding both the mundane and supramundane realms, there is none who would not believe and accept this.

Moreover, one must understand that the various types of natures within and without the three realms are all, in their entirety, merely manifestations of the single mind. When this mind accords with the Buddha-mind, one immediately becomes a Buddha;

when this mind accords with the Bodhisattva-mind, one immediately becomes a Bodhisattva; and this extends even to the superior and inferior states of the eight classes of beings, such as devas and nāgas.

There is nothing that is not manifested through the transformation of the single mind. Therefore, this sutra takes the two types of awakening—original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*)—as its central tenet.
Original awakening refers to the awakened nature of sentient beings, which is inherently and spontaneously complete from the beginning.

Initial awakening refers to the Buddhas’ initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, wherein they are able to awaken themselves and awaken others, such that their practice of awakening is perfected. Furthermore, "self-awakening" means to be aware of and know oneself.
The mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. To awaken others is to realize that all phenomena are none other than suchness (*tathatā*).

To awaken to all sentient beings is to realize they are all identical to the Buddha. To awaken to fulfillment is to realize that self and others are without distinction, such that principle and phenomenon are perfectly interfused, and mind and object penetrate one another, each and every one pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.
It is further said: "When the Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment, they exhaustively [realize] the ten thousand..."
The source of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is thus able to penetrate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The dharma-realm is itself the dharma-nature; it is the one true *tathatā*-mind.
Even bodhisattvas of the ten stages according to the provisional teachings still remain seated within the measure of the dharma-realm, for they have not yet exhausted its depths.

However, now, by means of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) accords with original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), one realizes the non-duality of the original and the initial; therefore, this is taught.

The teaching of the One Vehicle’s true doctrine, the method of Perfect and Sudden Enlightenment, directly enables ordinary people of vast capacity on the mundane ground to suddenly perceive their Buddha-nature.
It is truly the winged support for the school that transmits outside the scriptures, which points directly to the human mind and realizes Buddhahood through seeing one's nature.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly. For the sake of the great multitude, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled "The Single Flavor of Reality," which concerns the signless, the non-arising, the definitive limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the practice of primordial awakening.
This is the general purport of the introductory section of this sutra; it first describes the benefits of the wisdom and function of the Vajrasamādhi.
The Buddha is titled "World-Honored One" because his Way is uniquely honored throughout the three realms and his virtue is endowed with the ten auspicious epithets.

These two characters alone are insufficient to fully express the designation of the ultimate. However, the Buddha constantly observes the capacities of sentient beings and adapts his teachings accordingly;
now, he shall first expound the Mahāyāna to initiate the Dharma of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), just as before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he first taught the *Anantamukha-sūtra*.
Among the Mahāyāna sūtras within the Tripiṭaka, there are some forty or more sections, all intended to instruct bodhisattvas.
Safā. This sutra alone is the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of the Buddha.

By means of the Buddha’s heart-seal, he seals the hearts of all sentient beings, enabling all sentient beings to attain realization in accord with the Buddha’s mind. Furthermore, its meaning is complete and without deficiency.
The language is concise and not prolix; it may be called the ultimate expression. The Sanskrit term *mahāyāna* is translated here as "Great Vehicle" (*dàchéng*).
"Great" (*dà*) is a name established based on its essential nature. "Vehicle" (*chéng*) carries the meaning of transporting or conveying.

As stated in the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed by relying upon the one mind. Therefore, it says: "The aspect of the true suchness of this mind is precisely what reveals the Mahāyāna."

Because it is the essence, it is the characteristic of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of this mind. It is able to demonstrate the self-nature, characteristics, and functions of the Mahāyāna.

Its essence is the *tathāgatagarbha* nature; its characteristics are the characteristics of the eight consciousnesses; and its functions are the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the eight consciousnesses.
Regarding the establishment of the Mahāyāna doctrine, it is said that, for example, if a single atom were broken into a hundred parts—nine... [text fragment].
If nineteen parts are non-existent and one part remains existent, the Mahāyāna cannot excel;
for as long as this one part still persists, it cannot surpass [the Hinayana]. Only when there is a total absence of all hundred parts can the Mahāyāna truly excel.
It is only by being able to extinguish all subtle marks within the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) of all sentient beings that one may be called Mahāyāna.
[The previous section] was concluded. Now, when it says "one flavor," this refers directly to the Dharma of the One Mind.
All the teachings spoken by the Buddha are solely intended to cause sentient beings to clarify this One Mind.

Therefore, from the Small Vehicle entering the Great Vehicle, through the distinction of beginning and end, the provisional and the real, and the sudden and the perfect—just as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where the *ghṛta* (clarified butter) is taken as the single flavor.
It is said that from a cow comes milk; from milk, curd; from curd, fresh butter; from fresh butter, clarified butter (*ghṛta*);
and thereafter, the ultimate essence (*sarpis*) is produced. This *sarpis* is used as a metaphor for the meaning of *nirvāṇa* and the Buddha-nature.

It signifies that [the Buddha-nature] emerges from the twelvefold teachings of the three vehicles, representing the ultimate discourse of the scriptural vehicles. However, *nirvāṇa* is intended solely for those of dull faculties belonging to the two vehicles.
This was taught for those at the root stage and those whose faculties have matured at the very end; yet it still could not fully express the Buddha’s original intent.
Now, this [teaching] is for the sake of great bodhisattvas who are especially those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom in future ages. What is spoken here is again different:
the sutras repeatedly refer to the "single flavor" (*ekarasa*) and also say there are no various mixed flavors. This is truly the single flavor of *amṛta* (the finest essence).
It is a mental phenomenon (*citta-dharma*). However, as a mental phenomenon it is formless and beyond the reach of speech; therefore, it is said:

"In my school there are no words or phrases," and "in truth, not a single dharma is given to anyone. If one were to claim that there is a dharma that can be taught, such a view belongs entirely to falsehood and delusion, and does not constitute the singular, true reality.
Thus, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa with this verse: "The Dharma is fundamentally without dharma; there is no dharma..."

The Dharma is also the Dharma. Now, at the time when the "Dharma-less" is entrusted, how has the Dharma ever been a dharma? For this reason, the venerable masters of the Chan school do not establish written words;
they directly point to that which is above. As soon as one enters the gate, there is a blow; as soon as one steps forward, there is a shout.

They receive people solely through the application of their spiritual pivot (jīyòng). This traces back from Śākyamuni Buddha’s initial sighting of the morning star to his final holding up of the flower.
Addressing the assembly: This was attained at the moment Kāśyapa broke into a smile. It is the true marrow and bone within this Great Canon of the Tripitaka.
Throughout forty-nine years and over three hundred assemblies, [the Buddha] could not fully express it; only this sutra approximates it slightly. The sutra says:
"The Real" refers to True Suchness and the Reality-mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). All Buddhas employ both provisional and ultimate wisdom.
Regarding the establishment of the teaching: this scripture, as a single example, reveals the ultimate reality (*tattva*). For the mind of *tathatā* is fundamentally without marks;

that which is the mark of being without marks is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Thus, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "When the mind of faith is pure, one gives rise to the true mark;
know that this is the foremost rare merit. Now, as for the purity of the mind of faith:
This means that through faith one attains the purity of this mind, which immediately gives rise to the merit of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, one must know that the characteristic of the true mark is the basis upon which all manifold characteristics depend, and that these manifold characteristics take the absence of characteristics (*animitta*) as their root.

One must know that the essence of the absence of characteristics is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and that the mind of non-characteristic is itself non-arising (*anutpāda*). Moreover, all phenomena are empty.
This is precisely signlessness (*animitta*). The emptiness of all mind is precisely non-arising (*anutpāda*); non-arising is the meaning of liberation (*vimukti*). "Decisive" means unchanging.
Regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), none can be apprehended; this mind cannot be shifted or altered, and this is the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This is the meaning of *prajñā*. The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), *prajñā*, and liberation constitute the secret of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) of *nirvāṇa*.

Treasury. Furthermore, these three virtues arise from reversing the three types of defilement (*saṃkleśa*). By reversing the fetters and karma, they become liberation; yet bondage and liberation are non-dual.
By reversing afflictions (*kleśa*), they become awakening (*bodhi*); yet afflictions and awakening are non-dual. By reversing illusory manifestations, they become the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
yet the essence of mind is free from thought, being fundamentally the Dharma-body itself. If one attains this liberation of the Dharma-body...
Prajñā is identical to the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) of all Buddhas. Now, fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is the primary cause for sentient beings;
where there is a cause, there must be a fruit. It is like obtaining profit from a capital investment, or as when a person plants rice, it ripens and is then harvested with a sickle.
This is that which must necessarily be obtained; hence it is called "profit" (*li*). It takes the meaning of reaping grain with a sword.

Since sentient beings already possess the cause of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), they will necessarily obtain the fruit of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*), namely the Dharmakāya, liberation, and prajñā.
All proceed by means of the benefits arising from original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
Therefore, this constitutes the function of the Vajra-samādhi, clarifying the sphere of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
If one hears this sutra, or even receives and upholds a single four-line verse, that person shall enter the ground of the Buddha’s wisdom.
They will be able to teach and transform sentient beings through skillful means, acting as a great spiritual friend to all sentient beings.
This explains the benefit of *siddhānta*. *Siddha* means "universal" (*prabhūta*). *Ānta*, in its full Sanskrit form, is *dāna*; this means "giving" (*tyāga*).
Since both the Chinese and the Sanskrit terms are employed together, it is called *siddhānta*. There are four kinds: first, the *loka-siddhānta*, which brings the benefit of joy to sentient beings.
For instance, all distinct designations such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) are termed "the world."

First is the *prajñapti-siddhānta* (provisional teaching), wherein the Buddha explains things through differentiation according to the inclinations of sentient beings, enabling them to attain right view.

Second is the *pudgala-siddhānta* (teaching for persons), which enables sentient beings to obtain the benefit of generating wholesome roots; as the Buddha teaches the Dharma, he first observes the mental activities of sentient beings and then speaks for their sake, causing them to develop faith and joy and generate wholesomeness.
Third is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (remedial teaching), which enables sentient beings to attain cessation.

It is for the benefit of those who would otherwise suffer harm. Just as the Dharma taught by the Buddha is like prescribing medicine according to the specific ailment to cause the destruction of evil, the four *paramārtha-siddhāntas* enable sentient beings to attain the Way.
Thus, the Buddha, knowing when the faculties of the assembly have matured, preaches the Dharma for their sake.
They immediately attain awakening. Because the Buddha universally bestows these four dharmas upon all sentient beings, they are called the Four *Siddhāntas*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Four *Siddhāntas* fully encompass the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma and the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Therefore, the Tiantai teachings employ them to explain the *Lotus Sūtra*. Now, this scripture is like the signless (*animitta*), the non-arising (*anutpāda*), and awakening.

Benefit (*artha*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), the *tathāgatagarbha*, and so forth—each of these names being distinct—is the meaning of the world (*loka*).
To hear, retain, awaken to, and enter [these teachings], and to transform others through them, is the meaning of the person (*pudgala*).

To shatter the three vehicles with the Dharma of the One Vehicle, and to eliminate the differences between various flavors with a single flavor, is the meaning of the remedy (*pratipakṣa*). If one hears the Dharma of the One Mind, it is vast and open...

However, sudden enlightenment is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). Within this primary meaning, there is no dharma that can be heard by the listener, no dharma that can be received by the recipient, and no dharma that can be maintained by the upholder.
Even what is called a single four-line verse is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) for the sake of others;
ultimately, not a single character can be grasped. This is the true intent of the Fourfold Accomplishment (*catus-sampad*). If...

If one loses this intention, one becomes attached to phenomena and cannot be called a follower of the Mahāyāna. If one attains this intention, then for the sake of sentient beings alone, one preaches the Dharma according to the occasion;
when both self and others are free from attachment, only then does one enter the ground of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Yet, in truth, there is no ground of the Buddha’s wisdom to be entered—this is what constitutes true entry. It is in this way that one can finally employ skillful means.

This refers to the transformation and edification of sentient beings. That which is the locus of righteousness is called the "direction" (fang). To look downward and accord with the capacities and circumstances of others is called "expediency" (bian).

To instruct people through the Right Path is called "teaching" (jiao). To personally practice it above so that it moves like the wind below is called "transformation" (hua). As for "sentient beings" (zhongsheng):...
The five aggregates (skandhas) and the four great elements (mahābhūtas) receive their names through the arising of various phenomena based on three conditions.
Furthermore, it is said that they are called "sentient beings" (sattva) because they arise together in the world. Moreover, the Buddha’s skillful means (upāya) generally do not exceed three types:

the direct means, which teaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles; the ingenious means, which teaches the Mahayana Dharma; and the diverse means, which reveals the ultimate truth (paramārtha). If there were no...
As for expedient means (*upāya*), there is absolutely no opening through which words can be uttered.

Thus, the picking up of the flower and the smile, as well as the actions of the ancestral patriarchs of yore—such as brandishing the mallet, raising the whisk, administering blows, and using shouts—are all likewise categorized as extraordinary expedient means. Furthermore, regarding these expedient means:

after the Buddha had practiced walking meditation from beneath the tree, he realized the ritual protocols for expounding the Dharma used by the Buddhas of the past; he then took what he himself had realized upon beholding the stars...
The Way begins by following the Real to open up the Provisional; it concludes by abolishing the Provisional to manifest the Real.

In the interim, it produces the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. Just as a tree is originally one, yet through the branching of limbs and the development of trunks it attains greatness, only to ultimately return to oneness, so too the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings are all branches and twigs—all are merely expedient means.
Furthermore, one must know the proper time and recognize what is appropriate; one must distinguish the true from the false, and identify the ailment to recognize the remedy.

Only then may one employ these skillful means for the sake of others. As a sutra says: "One who well understands the methods of teaching and transforming, well understands the person practicing the path, well understands the faults in teaching and transforming, and well understands the faults in practicing the path—one who knows these four dharmas is called a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend)."

Furthermore, a sutra states: "One who skillfully understands emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); who thoroughly penetrates all phenomena (*dharma*) as ultimately equal;

whose nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*); who abides in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); and who, within ultimate emptiness, vigorously establishes [the teachings]—this is called a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Therefore, one is titled a 'good friend' and a Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*); this is no small matter. Thus, [it was said of] Huang...
National Teacher Huairang said, "Everywhere else are people who merely consume dregs of wine; do you know that within the Great Tang there are no Chan masters?
At that time, a monk asked, "What about those elsewhere who guide disciples and lead assemblies?
Huairang replied, "I do not say there are no Chan [practitioners], but only that there are no teachers."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, he sat in the full lotus posture and immediately entered the Vajrasamādhi. His body and mind remained unmoving;

this demonstrates the essence of samādhi. This is precisely the place where the World-Honored One correctly expounds the Dharma, and from this point, the great body and fundamental purport of the entire sutra are established.
Indeed, this Vajrasamādhi is the [foundation] of all samādhis.

The Mother has already been elucidated previously. This [teaching] is established based upon the essence (*tattva*). That essence is the *dharmatā-kāya*, which is what is meant by "the true mark is markless.

Its function is the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), which is what is meant by the "penetration of the principle" (*mūla-praveśa*) and the "penetration of the teaching" (*deśanā-praveśa*).

Furthermore, a metaphor is established based on the essence: it is like a great round mirror. When its function is manifested from the essence, it responds to phenomena according to their specific circumstances.
Furthermore, these two characters "Vajra" (Diamond) are established as its name; it is not taken as a metaphor.

Because the body of the Dharma-nature is fundamentally solid and dense, it is called "Vajra. Moreover, because emotions have perished and wisdom has manifested, both the ordinary and the sage are completely exhausted.

The mind is without agitation or distraction; there is nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized; there is neither arising nor ceasing—this is precisely the adamantine right view (*vajrasamyag-dṛṣṭi*).
If the mind accords with this principle, it is called the adamantine right concentration (*vajrasamyak-samādhi*). The objective realm within this samādhi cannot be described by words;
one must simply allow the mind to merge with the principle and wisdom to dissolve into the object, only then [can they be realized].
It is so. Thus, the *Qingliang shu* (Commentary by Qingliang) states: "Because principle is manifest, one sees the Dharma-nature body; because wisdom is luminous, one sees the Buddha-wisdom body;

and because principle and wisdom are darkly unified, one sees the unimpeded body. These three bodies are truly what is meant by 'when a person drinks water, they know its coldness or warmth for themselves.
If it were expressed through words, it would all be a provisional means (*upāya*) for opening the gate of expediency; yet this very state is beyond words."
This discourse on the locus is truly a manifestation of reality; it is exactly like the "closing the door" [teaching] of the Kingdom of Magadha.

It is what is called the time when the full command is brought forth. At that time, there were only the Great Being Mañjuśrī and the ascetic Kāśyapa who recognized the workings of the Old Man with the Yellow Face.
Thus, one day, as soon as the World-Honored One ascended the seat, the great assembly—
The assembly was gathered for meditation. Mañjuśrī then struck the gavel and said: "Contemplate the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from his seat. On another day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat. Kāśyapa struck the gavel and said:

"The World-Honored One has finished preaching the Dharma. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from his seat. In this way, one is able to decisively cut off words, letters, and verbal expressions, thereby attaining the true meaning.
Thus it is first revealed. Now, phenomena do not have a single fixed direction. What was previously revealed was the secret of speech;
now, this *paryaṅka-bandha* (cross-legged posture) is the secret of the body; entering the Vajra-samādhi is the secret of the mind. This is the secret of both body and mind.

Therefore it is said, "immovable. If people today can recognize the face of the Yellow-Faced Old Man—his entire body revealed in its nakedness—at this very point, they will see that the assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly present, as if never having dispersed.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly named Agada. Rising from his seat, he joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke these verses:

This is a request for the Buddha to proclaim his transformative teachings. First, the origin of this initiative is recounted: although the Tathāgata had already silently indicated the purport of the Dharma, the entire assembly remained ignorant of it.
Now, requesting the Buddha to once again turn the wheel of Dharma constitutes both skillful means and the propagation [of the teaching].
The bhikṣu takes the emptiness of all phenomena as his seat; this arises from the emptiness of dharmas. This is the union.

The palms joined together signify single-minded reverence and obedience. Kneeling on the right knee signifies bowing one’s will and humble acceptance. Within the teachings, the left and right are used to represent the heterodox and the orthodox;

the right, being compliant, represents the orthodox, while the left, being contrary, represents the heterodox. As it is said: "When a Bodhisattva pays homage to the Buddhas, they should make this vow:
'I now prostrate with my five wheels at the feet of the Buddha, in order to sever the five paths and abandon the five hindrances. May [all beings]..."
May all sentient beings dwell securely in the five supernormal powers and be endowed with the five eyes.
When my right knee touches the ground, may all sentient beings attain perfect enlightenment. When my left knee touches the ground, may all sentient beings be freed from false views.
When my right hand touches the ground, may it be as when the Buddha sat upon the Vajra Seat, his right hand pointing—
The earth shook, and all at once they swiftly realized great Bodhi. "When my left hand touches the ground, may I gather all non-Buddhists and lead them into the Right Path.
When the crown of my head touches the ground, may I cause all sentient beings to abandon arrogance and achieve the Tathāgata’s invisible crown.
These verses on the meaning [of this] are from the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* among the gāthās of various sūtras.
There are two [types], as found among the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*): *geya* and *gāthā*. *Geya* is translated here as "repeated verse" (*chóng-sòng*).
It consists of verses that repeat the preceding prose (*gadya*) in order to further clarify its meaning;

alternatively, it is spoken again for those of dull faculties, or because those who arrived later had not heard it previously, it is proclaimed once more. This assembly lacks these three types [of conditions], and therefore there are no repeated verses. *Gāthā*...
*Gāthā*. This is translated as "recited verse" (*fèngsòng*). Its meaning is condensed and its phrasing is concise so that it may be easily recited.
It is also called "independent verse" (*gūqǐ sòng*), so named because its meaning does not repeat; this refers to the *gāthā* itself.

Now, the term *bhikṣu* (monk) is used here precisely for this reason, as it likewise signifies this [quality]. Furthermore, the *Fanyì míngyì* (Explanations of Translated Terms) states: *Agada*, medicine.

The name [Avalokiteśvara] means "Universal Gait" (Pǔqù) in this language, signifying the ability to remove all illnesses. It is also said that "A" signifies the meaning of entering non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Furthermore, it is translated as "neither coming nor going. Again, it is called "bottomless. Because it possesses these many meanings, it is not translated [into Chinese]. As for the verse he spoke:
Having deeply realized the meaning of the Tathāgata’s samādhi, he gave rise to the function of compassionate salvation and uttered verses of exhortation and inquiry,
thereby initiating the benefit of the *ekayāna-siddhānta* Dharma.

The Honored One whose Great Compassion is Perfected possesses unimpeded penetration of wisdom; for the sake of extensively delivering all sentient beings, he has taught the meaning of the Single Truth.
This praises the Buddha’s virtues, stating that the Tathāgata’s Great Compassion is truly the Most Honored One, perfected in ten thousand virtues.

That wisdom is able to penetrate all things without obstruction; now, for the sake of extensively delivering sentient beings within the three realms of existence, I have merely spoken of the meaning of the reality of the single mind.

All are brought to the single flavor of the Way; never by means of the Lesser Vehicle. The meanings and flavors of what is taught are entirely free from unreality, entering the ground of the Buddhas' wisdom and the definitive realm of true reality.
All who hear it transcend the world; there is none who does not attain liberation.
This praises the Mahāyāna. It states that the Tathāgata is now different from other times;
he reveals exclusively the unsurpassed path of the single flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter), and never employs the teachings of the Hīnayāna for the sake of transformation and deliverance.
Furthermore, the meaning of the one reality and the path of the single flavor now being taught are entirely free from falsehood and unreality, and they directly cause—
Sentient beings enter the stage of the Buddhas’ self-realized noble wisdom; they proceed until they reach the state of certainty and immutability, culminating in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Whether in this life or in future lives, all who hear this Dharma shall transcend the world;
there is not a single sentient being among them who will not attain liberation.

Immeasurable bodhisattvas all deliver sentient beings; for the sake of the multitude, they pose vast and profound questions, knowing the quiescent nature of phenomena and entering the state of certainty.
This is an exhortation for the assembly to inquire extensively. It says that Bodhisattvas take the liberation of sentient beings as their primary concern;

though they themselves may have no doubts, why do they not, for the sake of future generations, inquire about the supramundane path? Furthermore, this inquiry must be exhaustive, far-reaching, and profoundly deep, rather than being merely superficial or limited.
One must certainly cause all sentient beings to know that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is [originally...]
One may then attain the mark of quiescent extinction and enter the definitive reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The Tathāgata’s wisdom and skillful means shall be explained for the sake of entering this reality; all that accords with it is the One Vehicle, devoid of any diverse flavors.
It is just as when a single rain moistens all the various grasses, causing them all to flourish; yet each grows according to its own distinct nature.

This request is for the Buddha to bestow his instruction, saying that the Tathāgata is fully endowed with great wisdom and, in accordance with what is appropriate for all, skillfully employs expedient means.
Should there be any questions, he will surely, for the sake of sentient beings of future generations, analyze and explain the way they enter [the path].

Regarding the teaching on the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it causes all phenomena to be in accord without exception, so that they all return to the single flavor of the *amṛta* (clarified butter) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Thus, there are no various mixed flavors interspersed therein.

Nevertheless, the previous establishment of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and the fivefold classification of natures (*pañcagotra*) were collectively provisional teachings; now, by speaking of the single flavor and the One Vehicle, the true meaning is revealed.
In fact, this present rain that provides moisture— referring to how there is neither great nor small,
yet all obtain the Dharma-rain of the One Vehicle—
is the moisture of the single flavor of the Dharma that universally suffuses all things. Just as that single rain moistens them all, it causes the sprouts of Bodhi to grow.
Entering the Vajra-samādhi, one realizes the samādhi of the reality of dharmas; decisively severing doubt and regret, the seal of the single dharma is perfected.
This clarifies that upon attaining this dharma, its benefits become transformative.

It is said that if a Bodhisattva receives the moistening of this rain of the single flavor of Dharma, it will universally suffuse all sentient beings, just as a single rain moistens all the various grasses, whereby they will necessarily attain the same realization.
Flourishing and radiating in splendor, the current rain of Dharma moistens sentient beings, enabling them all to grow the sprouts of bodhi-wisdom.
Furthermore, it allows them to enter together into the Vajra-samādhi and realize the samādhi of the Dharmakāya, True Suchness, and the Ultimate Reality (bhūtakoṭi).
If this is so, then for sentient beings of future generations, [the two obstacles] will certainly be severed forever.
To ride upon it is doubt; to regret it is to fail. When one attains the seal of the single dharma, this principle is identical to the myriad phenomena and the ten thousand images.
All are sealed by the single dharma. In the teachings, this is called the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*). The "ten thousand images" are a metaphor for the characteristics of all dharmas;
the "sea" is a metaphor for the one true suchness-mind (*tathatā-citta*). Thus, the bhikṣu exhorted the assembly to inquire extensively, desiring to establish them in the correct [view].
The Dharma transforms sentient beings; this is precisely the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint).
In the past, when the Buddha preached the Dharma, he always employed all four *siddhāntas*, as explained by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Although the Chan school is said to be a "separate transmission outside the teachings," it likewise employs these [four standpoints] to preach the Dharma according to the capacities of those present. Furthermore, the reason for distinguishing the four *siddhāntas* is due to the conditions of the assembly.
Sentient beings possess differing faculties and dispositions; yet when they hear the Buddha’s single voice expounding the Dharma, each attains understanding according to their own kind.
Therefore, it is divided into four. However, the first three are called the "three benefits"; they belong to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and are the domain of mental activity.
The last is the "one ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*); it is the true truth (*paramārtha-satya*), wherein the path of speech is cut off and the domain of mental activity ceases.

If one possesses superior faculties and sharp wisdom, attaining deep realization from even a brief hearing and directly perceiving the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), then it is not necessary to employ the first three *siddhāntas*.
However, for those of middling or inferior capacity who cannot grasp the meaning, the teacher’s compassionate heart is so sincere that they must "enter the mud and the water" with them;
thus, the first three *siddhāntas* cannot be avoided. This is the case within the present Chan school.
To cause people to awaken to the Way, one first exhorts them with the illusory nature of human existence, and later stirs them with the two characters "birth" and "death.

This is the *loka-prasiddha-tīrtha* (worldly standpoint). Since there are differences in the sharpness or dullness of people's faculties, one observes their specific capacities and may employ either the staff and shout or spoken words and phrases;
this is the *pudgala-prasiddha-tīrtha* (personal standpoint). Thereafter, one applies the tongs with great severity.
The hammer strikes the bone to extract the marrow; it discriminates demons from the authentic, seizes the food, and drives the plow. This is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic standpoint).
To encounter this single pivot face-to-face, with arrow-points meeting, and to awaken with a sudden breakthrough—this is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth).
However, the first three *siddhāntas* are merely established for those of dull faculties.

Furthermore, one must understand that within the worldly (*loka*) there is the provisional (*pauruṣeya*), within the provisional there is the remedial (*prātipakṣika*), and within the remedial there is the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Within the ultimate, however, the first three *siddhāntas* do not exist. If one extends this principle further, it applies to all words, phrases, staff-blows, and shouts.

All [teachings] possess the four *siddhāntas*. To speak of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence—this is the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint).

To analyze and debate these four propositions is the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals); using "existence" to refute the view of nihilism and using "non-existence" to refute the view of eternalism is the *pratikāra-siddhānta* (the therapeutic standpoint).
To transcend the four propositions and the hundred negations and awaken directly is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint).
Furthermore, it is like the dialogue concerning the raising of the bamboo staff: to call out [the student] is "contact" (touch); not to call out is "aversion" (back). This is the world.
To cause a person to speak a single phrase from a place where there is neither contact nor aversion is for the sake of others (human teaching).

When nothing at all can be grasped and all various conceptual understandings are swept away, this is the remedial teaching (counteractive). If one awakens, then as soon as the mouth opens, one strikes; this is the primary meaning (ultimate truth). Moreover—
All verbal expressions, staff-blows, and shouts constitute the *dharmadhātu* (the world). To preach the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of beings constitutes "for the person" (*jinen*).

To sever all people's reliance on textual interpretations constitutes "remedial teaching" (*taishō*). To cause people to realize awakening beneath the catalyst constitutes the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*).
As for the essential tenets and purports of the Five Houses, each remains distinct and unconfused; this is the world.
The realms mutually elucidate one another; this is for the sake of people. It shatters the superficiality regarding Buddha-nature and the vague conceptualization of True Suchness.

This is the remedy: within a single phrase, the profound and the essential are complete; guest and host are distinguished; the provisional and the real are discerned; the illumination and the function are clarified;
there is simultaneous release and simultaneous gathering; birth and death are shared; all is one, and one is all—directly beneath, every dharma penetrates through.
It transcends all things; this non-obstruction in every matter is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Is this not, moreover, the very method by which the Gate of the Patriarchs (*zongmen*) preaches the Dharma according to the capacity of beings through the four *siddhāntas*?

If, when a teacher refines and trains others, there are those who cannot be awakened as beginners, then he has failed to employ the *loka-siddhānta*. Or if there are those of middling or inferior capacities whom he cannot uplift and encourage...
As for those of superior capacity, one cannot employ the *puruṣasāntānika-siddhānta* (the teaching according to the individual).

Or, if there are those who cannot dissolve their adhesions, loosen their bonds, remove the wedges, or extract the nails, then one cannot employ the *pratipakṣika-siddhānta* (the teaching of remedial counteraction).

Or, if there are those who cannot manifest the great potential, give rise to the great function, or open the true eye of humans and devas, then one cannot employ the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate teaching).

This refers to the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint). It is like striking someone with a staff as soon as they enter the gate, or shouting "Kun! as soon as they step inside; it employs the *paramārtha-siddhānta* directly.

Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states that for those on the path, the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are taught, so that they may enter the correct path upon seeing the shadow of the whip, just as a swift horse does.
This is precisely that meaning. Furthermore, the first three *siddhāntas* are teachings intended to guide and lead skillfully and indirectly.

As it is said, there are teachings on existence and teachings on emptiness; teachings on the gradual and teachings on the sudden; teachings on the beginning and teachings on the end; and teachings on the provisional and teachings on the real.

Finally, the ultimate truth directly reveals the Dharma of the One Mind. Therefore, apart from the "Plucking of the Flower" which points directly to the essence, this sutra alone is in perfect accord with that.

The Second Chapter on the Dharma of Signlessness (Part One), belonging to the Section on Prajñā.
Now, Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas and the sovereign among all dharmas.
All Buddhas are born from her; all phenomena are established through her. Although she is thus capable of giving birth and...
It stands that the Dharma of Prajñā is fundamentally without marks; therefore, it is called the "Dharma of No-Marks.
Yet this Dharma of No-Marks is precisely the Dharma of True Suchness and one's own mind, capable of encompassing all things.
For this reason, within this Chapter on the Dharma of No-Marks, there are first set forth: non-arising, awakening-benefit, the limit of reality, the emptiness of nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha.
The *Dhāraṇī*: At the conclusion of each of the six chapters, the six *pāramitās* are explained individually;

furthermore, they collectively subsume the teachings of the preceding six stages (*bhūmis*), while specifically manifesting the presence of *prajñā* to elucidate the characteristics of practice in the sixth stage.
Moreover, from the first through the fifth stages, one is unable to dwell for long within the signless (*animitta*) dharma; in the sixth stage, one exclusively cultivates the signless dharma.

On the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), one first realizes the signless (*animitta*) and attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), thereby entering the eighth stage.
Therein, one attains the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) and only then fulfills the stage; only then does one attain full awakening.

For this reason, the Chapter on the Signless Dharma subsumes the preceding six stages, while also initiating the subsequent four stages as well as the two types of awakening—the Equal (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and the Sublime (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Thus, it extends all the way to the stage of Sublime Awakening (*anuttara-bodhi*).
Nor does it transcend this dharma of signlessness (*animitta*). Furthermore, signlessness is the very meaning of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Now, by subsuming [all] under Prajñā and returning them to liberation (*vimukti*), one realizes the secret treasury of the three virtues of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-nirvāṇa*).
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and spoke these words: "The ground of the wisdom of all Buddhas enters into the true nature of phenomena because it is of a definitive nature.
The skillful means and supernormal powers are all benefits devoid of marks. This meaning of singular awakening and realization is difficult to understand and difficult to enter."
This is not known or seen by those of the two vehicles; only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can know it. To deliver sentient beings, [the Buddha] preaches a single flavor.
This is a self-description from within samādhi, representing the beginning of the Tathāgata’s skillful means for transforming and enlightening others. Indeed, samādhi is the fundamental principle.
Words constitute the teaching. Without a fundamental principle (zong), the teaching is not manifested; without a fundamental principle, the teaching cannot be established.

Therefore, we now separately open a second thematic gate to use words to manifest the wordless. This begins from the "Introductory Chapter" (Xupin) and proceeds by entering the ground of the Buddha’s wisdom to expound.
What is called the stage of Buddha-wisdom clarifies only nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*).

Generally, characteristics constitute the tenet that all phenomena are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), while nature constitutes the principle that all phenomena are mind-only (*cittamātra*). Consciousness-only refutes the deluded attachments of non-Buddhists and the followers of the Lesser Vehicle;
mind-only reveals the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha and the self-nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Nevertheless, one must necessarily [understand] both nature and characteristics.
When they are mutually integrated and both mind and consciousness are extinguished, one finally attains ultimate awakening.

Furthermore, other sutras do not clarify both nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*), yet their meaning remains accessible; this sutra does not clarify nature and characteristics, and thus its meaning is not manifest.

Nevertheless, both schools of nature and characteristics compose their treatises based on the meaning of Mahayana sutras. This was indeed after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Based on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* was composed by Vasubandhu (親勝), Siṃhabhadra (師子覺), and Sthiramati (安慧). At the same time, commentaries were also composed.

More than a thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there appeared Dharmapāla, Dignāga, and others, who, based on the preceding verse-treatises (*kārikā*), composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
This is known as the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiang Zong). The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa was prophesied by the Tathāgata; regarding the Buddha...
Born six hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa, he composed the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* based on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.

In it, he extensively explains the three subtle consciousnesses and the six coarse characteristics within the *ālayavijñāna* (alternatively written as *ālīya*), as well as the two gates of the one mind: True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Arising-and-Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).
This is what is called the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-nikāya*). Later, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, citing...

One hundred Mahāyāna sūtras were used to verify the subtle meanings of the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*), as well as their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

This was the beginning of these two schools: the Nature School (*Xingzong*) and the Characteristics School (*Xiangzong*). However, since each school established its own treatises based on a single primary sūtra, they could not reach a common consensus.

If one refers to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun), it [explains] the harmony between the manifesting consciousness (*xiànshí*) and the consciousness of discriminating phenomena (*fēnbié shìshí*).

These are combined to form the central tenet. If one follows the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*, the central tenet consists of the combination of the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*), and the discriminating consciousness of phenomena (*vyañjana-vijñāna*).
The true consciousness is the Tathāgatagarbha, the single mind of quiescence.

The manifesting consciousness is the eighth ālayavijñāna, so called because it manifests immediately upon encountering the five sense objects. The discriminating consciousness of phenomena is the sixth [consciousness].
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to follow after objects and apprehend them as conditions, thereby discriminating the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

However, the seventh *manas* consciousness is not explicitly mentioned here because, given the presence of both the eighth and the sixth consciousnesses, the *manas* must necessarily exist; for the *manas* takes the eighth consciousness as its object.
Furthermore, it evolves based on the eighth consciousness; moreover, the sixth [consciousness] takes the seventh as its root.

Thus, the subtle aspect of *manas* (the seventh consciousness) pervades the manifesting consciousnesses (*darśana-vijñāna*), while its coarse aspect pervades the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). Ancient masters used the metaphor of placing a water vessel in the sun:
the water vessel is like the eighth consciousness, and the sun is like the six consciousnesses. However, the sun uses the water within the vessel as...

Due to conditions, there arises a shadow floating on the wall; this shadow is like the *manas*. Furthermore, according to the tenets established by the *lakṣaṇa-vāda* (Dharmalakṣaṇa) school, it is said that the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are composed of four parts:
the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), and the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

The *svasaṃvittivijñāna* (self-cognizing aspect). Just as the *svasaṃvittivijñāna* is the non-deluded *tathatā* (suchness), the *svasaṃvittivijñāna* is a portion of *tathatā* that is the Buddha-nature within delusion;
it is the very essence of the fundamentally enlightened mind (*mūlajñāna*).

Because sentient beings, despite being deluded, possess the self-substance of *tathatā* that can be realized, it is called "self-realization" (*svasaṃvitti*). Within the substance of *tathatā*, there are two kinds of functions. First, the capacity to...
The function of perceiving is called the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-portion). The function of being perceived is called the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-portion).

When these functions are subsumed back into their essence, there remains only the single *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying portion). Thus, mountains, rivers, and the great earth are the image-portions of the mind;

since there is no phenomenon outside the mind, it is said that "all is consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). This is truly the fundamental principle of the school of names and characteristics (*nāmākāra*). However, later students merely follow the names and characteristics...

when moved by ignorance (*avidyā*), it transforms into the seer within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); when moved by objects (*viṣaya*), it transforms into the seer within the phenomenal consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
These three characteristics are the root of the characteristics of all dharmas and furthermore pervade the eight consciousnesses.

Whenever a thought arises, it is a transformation; thus, all eight consciousnesses arise, and all possess birth and cessation. Furthermore, the movement of the mind is karma; thus, all eight consciousnesses move.
Moreover, the true nature of these eight is collectively termed the "true characteristic"; therefore, it is said that they pervade the eight.
Consciousness. Furthermore, the "karmic" aspect (karma-lakṣaṇa) governs the six coarse states, while the "evolving" aspect (pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa) pervades the three subtle states.
These two aspects—karmic and evolving—possess the two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing; however, the "true" aspect (tattva-lakṣaṇa) is devoid of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Moreover, all consciousnesses evolve in dependence upon these aspects, acting as causes for one another in succession. Specifically, the karmic aspect evolves in dependence upon the true aspect. This is the first...

The eight consciousnesses evolve based on the characteristic of activity (*karmalakṣaṇa*); this is the seventh consciousness. Based on the characteristic of evolution (*vivartalakṣaṇa*), they evolve into the characteristic of manifestation (*nirbhāsalakṣaṇa*);
this refers to the first five consciousnesses. Furthermore, the characteristic of manifestation evolves to form the six coarse characteristics;

this is the *vastuprativikalpavijñāna*. This is the meaning according to the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*. If one clarifies the root of these dharmic characteristics, all faults and afflictions [will be eliminated].
It does not arise; its very substance is empty and quiescent. Therefore it is said: "All mental phenomena are fundamentally non-existent and have no basis that can be apprehended.
Even this 'basis' has no location. In this way, the mind is empty and quiescent, and thus there is no arising.
If the mind has no arising, one enters into emptiness and quiescence; having entered into emptiness and quiescence—
Within the ground of one’s mind, one spontaneously attains the wondrous emptiness of that very mind. This emptiness of mind is the essence of the signless mind;
in reality, there is no mind to be grasped, nor is there a self to be clung to. Therefore, the Chan school says:
"If the mind is not empty, one does not awaken. It is further said: "Once the mind is realized as empty, the environment naturally becomes empty. Wisdom—
This means that one eliminates the mind but does not eliminate objects. It further says:

"If you enter my gate, you must simply cast aside all lifelong views concerning right and wrong, gain and loss, good and evil, acceptance and rejection, as well as seeing, perceiving, hearing, and knowing, along with existence and non-existence, birth and cessation."
Relinquish everything to the very bottom; relinquish directly until there is nothing left to relinquish. Then, naturally and suddenly, you will realize the essence of the mind of all Buddhas.

This is precisely what is called "passing with an empty heart at the imperial examination in the Field for Selecting Buddhas. This first section explains the category of those with sharp faculties regarding original enlightenment.
Bodhisattva Wuzhu, I have come from the originless and now arrive at the place of no-origin, and thus I have set this forth for you.
This is the fundamental [teaching].

The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "Venerable One, if all sentient beings possess a self or possess a mind, by what dharma should they be awakened so that those sentient beings may emerge from these bonds?"
This question concerns the dharma of liberation from bondage and initiates the meaning of entering the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Whereas the previous question regarding cultivation was established from the perspective of the *tathatā* gate of all Buddhas, this question regarding liberation from bondage arises from the perspective of the gate of birth-and-death of sentient beings.

As for what is called "self," it is as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*: the seventh consciousness internally grasps the eighth consciousness as self; furthermore, it is due to the conformity of *tathatā*.
Conditioned by this, the eighth consciousness is established. Based on the eighth, the seventh consciousness arises as the "seer.
Based on the seventh, the first five consciousnesses are produced; based on these five, the sixth consciousness is further induced.

According to the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only), the seventh consciousness clings to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as a real self and real dharmas, while the sixth consciousness clings to the eighth [consciousness].

Because the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the perceiving aspect (*darśanabhāga*) are [erroneously taken to be] a real self and real dharmas, it is said that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses give rise to deep clinging.

Furthermore, because the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) necessarily arises based on the grasping at dharmas (*dharma-grāha*), it is said that the two graspings arise simultaneously in the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
Because one previously grasped at phenomena as being truly existent, there arises the clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*), whereby one designates a self and its phenomena.
For example, taking the four great elements—which are not the self—to be the self, and taking the objects of thought that arise and perish to be the mind; these two constitute the clinging to a self.

The four great elements are like an illusion: they are fundamentally non-existent yet appear as if they were existent. One clings to the characteristics of arising and perishing as objects of thought as if they were real shadows.
These two constitute the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which are the four inverted views of sentient beings; they thereby result in the bondage of birth and death within the three realms.

This is simply because one is deluded regarding the inherent existence of the true self, claiming it to be non-existent, while falsely grasping at the fundamental emptiness of the false self as being existent.
Within the teachings, great effort is expended to eliminate these two attachments for the sake of sentient beings.
This is dry discourse. Alas, the medicine is much while the illness is grave.
If someone were to ask today, "I do not yet know by what dharma one may attain liberation," you should simply reply to them: "Quickly, before your parents were born, speak a single phrase!"
If his eyes flicker or move, strike him across the spine; later, he will naturally attain liberation. The Buddha said:

"Good son, if there is a self, have him contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). The twelve links of dependent origination fundamentally arise from cause and effect.
Cause and effect are produced by mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*). If even the mind does not exist, how much less can there be a body?"
This demonstrates the meaning that causes and conditions are fundamentally empty. It is said that the self and dharmas are originally non-existent;

they all arise from a single thought of ignorance, whereby one is deluded and turns away from one's own mind, falsely grasping at them as existent. Taking internal consciousness as the cause and external objects as the condition, they arise together through their conjunction.
Within a single thought-moment alone, the twelve links of dependent origination are fully contained. First, there is the seeing by means of the eye.

From form, craving arises; this is the mind of ignorance (*avidyā*). Because of craving, one creates karma, which is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). This mind’s focused attention is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Consciousness together with form and formations is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The arising of greed for the six sense bases is the sense bases (*āyatana*). Seeking craving through the sense bases is contact (*sparśa*).
The mind of attachment is feeling (*vedanā*). Clinging and not relinquishing is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Seeking the dharmas that have been felt is...

Grasping. Phenomena arising from the mind are called "existence. The uninterrupted succession [of moments] is birth; the interruption of that succession is death. Furthermore, they are established through succession as a continuity across the three times.

For example, ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are the causes of the past. Consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are the effects of the present.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are the causes of the present. Birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are... [the effects of the future].
The future fruits—namely, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, birth, old age, and death—are the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

Ignorance, volitional formations, craving, grasping, and becoming are the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*); these consist of the two delusions of views and mental afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), also known as the four abodes of affliction (*catur-vāsa-bhūmi*).

Regarding the four abodes (where mental afflictions are divided and views are combined): the delusion of views constitutes one, while the delusion of mental afflictions is divided into three. As for the delusion of views being one: [it refers to the five views].
This refers to seeing the ground that abides in all places; that is, seeing the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the three realms.

These eighty-eight proclivities arise solely from the ten proclivities (by expanding the view-proclivities and combining the thought-proclivities: there are eighty-eight view-proclivities and ten thought-proclivities, totaling ninety-eight proclivities).

To falsely reckon [the aggregates] as a self is the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); to cling to annihilation or permanence is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); and to regard [wrong views] as being correct is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Grasping at wrong precepts constitutes the clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); clinging to oneself as being correct constitutes wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

These are the five sharp fetters (*tīkṣṇakleśa*). Sentient beings falsely identify the four great elements as their body; this is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Knowing that the body is an illusion, the view of a self-identity is severed.

Once the view of a self-identity is severed, the two types of clinging—clinging to extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)—are naturally eliminated, for all four arise from the view of a self-identity.
Furthermore, attachment to that which is identical to one's own nature is craving (*rāga*). Aversion toward that which is not one's own nature is anger (*pratigha*).

Not knowing or seeing delusion (*moha*) as it truly is constitutes the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). That which can summon and accumulate the cycle of birth and death is ignorance (*avidyā*). To claim for oneself "I understand" while asserting "others do not understand" is pride (*māna*).

To be hesitant and indecisive is doubt (*vicikitsā*). These are the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*). However, if the sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*) are eliminated, the dull afflictions...
They are also extinguished because they are driven by the ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) which cause further birth.

Due to these ten latent tendencies, sentient beings enslave their own minds and spirits, thereby resulting in transmigration through the six realms. Furthermore, as these ten latent tendencies pass through the three realms and the four noble truths, they increase and decrease, totaling eighty-eight latent tendencies.
These are not enumerated here in full; one must know that these delusions of view arise from—

The mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*) arises and is able to obstruct the true nature. If one perceives the luminosity of the nature of mind, one can then sever the faculty of thought (*manas*), so that one is no longer driven by it.
Therefore, upon seeing the Path (*darśanamārga*), the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are severed. Furthermore, the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) are divided into three:

first, the ground of attachment to desire (*kāmarāgasthānīya*), which is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); this consists of the nine grades of thought-delusions of greed, hatred, ignorance, and pride. Second, the ground of attachment to form (*rūparāgasthānīya*).
These consist of the four stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the three stages of abiding in craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which are the four stages of the formless realm.

Each possesses nine grades of afflictions consisting of greed, delusion, and pride; since the habituation of anger has already been severed, there are nine grades—namely, superior, middle, and inferior—with each grade containing three sub-grades, thus forming nine grades.
Together, these constitute eighty-one grades. These include both the views and the mental afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). (The views are eight...)

There are eighteen *anuśayas* (eighty-one categories of *cetanā*). These are all contained within the nine stages of the three realms. However, these afflictions of volition (*cetanā-kleśa*) arise from the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

Sentient beings, due to these afflictions of volition, are bound by the cycle of birth and death within the three realms. If one first realizes the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and subsequently cultivates the Path of Meditation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one will forever be free from the binding volitions regarding form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
Therefore, the Path of Meditation severs the afflictions of volition. These are the two types of afflictions.

Both take ignorance as their root, moistening tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*). If one takes the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*) as one's task, then although one does not seek its cessation, the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *kleśa*) fall away of their own accord.
If one contemplates the extinction of ignorance and so forth, this is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

The skillful means that counteract the causal conditions are the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). Suffering and its Accumulation are the causes and effects of the mundane world; the Path and Cessation are supramundane.

The intermediate causes and effects are explained separately as the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). When explained collectively, they are simply the four noble truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*); the difference lies only in their expansion and contraction.
For example, when Śrāvakas hear the Buddha’s oral teachings, they rely on the four truths, taking the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as the primary gateway for contemplation.

Pratyekabuddhas awaken by relying on the twelve links of dependent origination, taking the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) as the primary gateway for contemplation. Bodhisattvas, however, [rely] upon both the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) and the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

The Truths are the primary gateway. Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Regarding this Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, those who contemplate it with inferior wisdom attain the enlightenment of the śrāvaka;
those who contemplate it with middling wisdom attain the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddha; and those who contemplate it with superior wisdom [attain the supreme enlightenment]."
One attains the bodhi of a bodhisattva; through the contemplation of the highest wisdom, one attains the bodhi of a Buddha. All of these are attained according to the magnitude of one's faculties.
However, when one contemplates this dharma of causes and conditions, it is seen that they all arise from the deluded mind of ignorance and non-awakening.
If the deluded mind is extinguished, the view of self is also extinguished; therefore, it is said that even the mind does not exist.
There is. How much more so for this body? But in the School of the Patriarchs, it is not so. This body of yours now: the four great elements are fundamentally empty;
the five aggregates do not exist. The nature of the mind is a mere provisional name. With what, then, would you call "self"?
A single question such as this will naturally cause [delusions] to melt away like ice and crumble like a fortress.
If there is a self, cause the view of existence to cease; if there is no self, cause the view of non-existence to cease. If the mind arises, cause the nature of arising to cease;
if the mind ceases, cause the nature of cessation to cease. By extinguishing this nature of views, one enters the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
These words clarify the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) through the skillful means of counteraction: when "self" ceases, "existence" ceases; when "non-self" ceases, "non-existence" ceases.
Thus, both the dualistic views of existence and non-existence are not established. Nevertheless, although the view of self has been eliminated, the mental phenomena have not yet subsided.
If the mind arises, phenomena also arise; if the mind ceases, phenomena also cease. Therefore, if the mind arises, it must immediately cease.
The nature of arising: if the mind ceases, then the nature of cessation likewise ceases. In this way, the two natures of annihilation and extinction are both severed and no longer exist.

If one eliminates these two views of existence and non-existence, as well as the two natures of arising and ceasing, then the mind becomes identical to empty space and the body equal to the Dharma-realm, thereby entering the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This serves as the foundation for the "Chapter on Entering the Limit of Reality."
Why is this? That which has fundamentally arisen does not cease; that which has fundamentally ceased does not arise. What does not cease does not arise; what does not arise does not cease.
The characteristics of all phenomena are likewise thus.
This inquiry clarifies the meaning of the *tathatā* (actual reality). "That which is fundamentally unborn does not perish" means that its nature is truly eternal;
there is no perishing to be undergone. "That which is fundamentally extinguished does not arise" means that its nature is empty and quiescent;
there is no arising to be undergone. If this is so, then all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are likewise without exception. Since they do not perish, they also do not exist.
As for arising: since there is no arising, there is likewise no cessation. Such is the inherent nature of the body of *tathatā* (suchness).

[Phonetic Explanations: *Cui* (upper tone): to break or suppress. *Ju* (pronounced *jí*): extreme; excessive. *Tzǐ* (pronounced *zǐ*): turbid. *Běi* (pronounced *huì*): anger. *Shèn* (upper tone): a large clam; [a phenomenon occurring when] a pheasant enters...

Transformed by the sea; able to exhale breath, which transforms into towers and terraces). *Dìe* (to judge or decree). *Yù* (pronounced yù; the name of a beast of prey characterized by much doubt). *Yǔn* (pronounced yǔn; to perish or to fall).
*General Record of the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, Fascicle Two.
*General Record of the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, Fascicle Three.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Jizhen, Successor to the Patriarchs at Huading Peak on Mount Tiantai.

In the second part of the "Chapter on the Dharma of Signlessness," the Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "Venerable One, if there are sentient beings who, when seeing a dharma arise, are caused to extinguish what view?
And when seeing a dharma cease, are caused to extinguish what view?"
This question addresses the cessation of views and initiates the meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Its intent is as the Buddha said:

"If there is the arising and ceasing of the mind, one should cause that deluded mind to cease; if one perceives the arising of phenomena, all phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) arise moment by moment."

When seeing that phenomena perish, they do not abide for even a single moment; rather, they shift and cease from moment to moment. Furthermore, when causing them to perish, what kind of view should one cause to perish?
