The Buddha said: "Bodhisattva, if there are sentient beings who, when seeing phenomena arise, cause the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*) to perish; and when seeing phenomena perish..."
This causes the view of existence to cease. If this view is extinguished, one attains the true source of the Dharma. There is no entry into a determinate nature; it is determinately non-arising.
This demonstrates its fundamental source: namely, that at the very moment phenomena arise, one should skillfully recognize their original state.

Regarding the nature of existence: if those of the Two Vehicles hold that phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, one can cause them to eliminate this view of non-existence by knowing that they are ultimately not non-existent.
Furthermore, at the very moment one perceives the transience and cessation of phenomena, it is precisely then that one should recognize their nature as fundamentally non-existent.
If ordinary beings hold that phenomena are fundamentally existent, one [should know] that they are ultimately not existent. Thus...

One may cause these views of existence to cease. If one extinguishes these two kinds of deluded views—existence and non-existence—then one will know that the self-characteristics of external objects, whether existent or non-existent, have nothing to do with me.
In this way, one attains the true source of the dharma-nature and realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally empty.
One understands that the mind is characterized by false conceptualization; by extinguishing the mind’s deluded views, how could there be any fixed attachment to either existence or non-existence?
If one claims that what exists should not be non-existent, how can it be momentary and non-abiding?

If one claims that what does not exist should not be existent, how can it arise in every thought-moment? Viewed from this perspective, there is likewise nothing that enters into a state of fixed nature.
This is for the sake of abiding decisively in non-arising. This serves as the introduction to the "Chapter on True Nature Emptiness.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "Venerable One, causing those sentient beings to abide in non-arising—this is non-..."
"Is it born? (The Northern Canon reads "yes").
This is a mistaken interpretation of the question.
The Buddha said: "To abide in non-arising is itself arising."
This accords with the refutation of that which is erroneous. Why is this?
That which is neither abiding nor arising is precisely non-arising. A bodhisattva, if they give rise to non-arising, uses arising to extinguish arising;

when both arising and extinction are extinguished, original arising is non-arising. The mind is eternally empty and quiescent; being empty and quiescent, it has no abiding; the mind has nothing [to grasp].
Abiding is itself non-arising;
this inquiry clarifies its meaning. It states that one should naturally have no abiding even in non-arising—this is what non-arising is.
If one gives rise to a mind that abides in non-arising, one uses the producer to extinguish the produced, which is utterly improper. Directly...
Both the two kinds of deluded minds—arising and ceasing—must be simultaneously extinguished, so that the delusion of original arising shall never arise again.
In this way, the substance of the mind is eternally empty and tranquil. Having attained this emptiness and tranquility, there is nothing upon which to dwell.
If the mind has nothing upon which to dwell, it is truly non-arising.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "Venerable One, since the mind has no abiding place, what is there to be cultivated or studied?
Is it one who is still in training (śaikṣa), or is it one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa)?"
This question concerns the merit of cultivation and study, which gives rise to the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*. "Cultivation" (*xiū*) refers to cultivating virtuous deeds;

"study" (*xué*) refers to studying the path and its teachings. In ancient times, when there were no written records or symbols, if one wished to accomplish a great undertaking, one would first make incisions on wood with a knife to count the number [of tasks], naming this "deeds" (*yè*). Every single unit of effort was thus recorded.
When it is completed, one simply refines away a single mark. Therefore, the sages all speak of "cultivating practice" (*xiuyè*);
when the marks on the wood have been refined away, it is called "the completion of study. The meaning is thus. Furthermore, regarding the character *xué* (to learn):

it refers to when children first receive their books, holding them with both hands as if playing with the lines and hexagrams of the *I Ching*. This is the meaning of "learning. Furthermore, "learning not yet complete" means...

Those who are in training (śaikṣa) reach the stage of no-more-training (aśaikṣa) and thus become those beyond training. Furthermore, investigating the truth and severing delusions is called "training";
when truth is fully realized and delusions are exhausted, it is called "beyond training. Liberation means that the mind has no dwelling place; it is identical to emptiness and stillness.
Since it is empty and still, what is there to cultivate? What is there to learn? Again, he asked: "Having attained this mind of non-arising..."
"Is this one who is still in training (*śaikṣa*) with studies yet incomplete? Or is this one who has reached the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)?
The Buddha said: "Bodhisattva, the mind of non-arising has neither entry nor exit; it is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, by nature quiescent and immovable."
This demonstrates the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. It is called the mind of non-arising; it has no place of abiding, nor does it have coming or going.
This is the inherently pure Tathāgata-garbha, the original self-nature of sentient beings. Its essential nature is fundamentally empty, quiescent, and immovable.
There are two aspects: being outside the entanglements and being within the entanglements. When realized by all Buddhas, it is "outside the entanglements."

The Tathāgatagarbha is not understood by sentient beings; when it is within the bonds [of afflictions], it is called the "Tathāgatagarbha within the bonds," and when it has emerged from the bonds, it is designated as the "Pure Dharmakāya.
This serves as the foundational basis for the "Chapter on the Tathāgatagarbha";
its meaning will be elucidated in a subsequent chapter.

It is neither that which is in training (*śaikṣa*), nor that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). There is no "training" or "non-training"; this is itself being beyond training. It is not that there is no training;
this is what constitutes that which is to be trained in.

This clarifies that there is neither training (*śaikṣa*) nor non-training (*aśaikṣa*). It states that this is not comparable to the categories of those in training and those beyond training among the four fruits of the two vehicles.
When you ask, "What is there to be cultivated and learned here? you fail to realize that within this state there is neither training nor non-training;
it is precisely non-training (*aśaikṣa*), yet it is not the case that there is no training. This is precisely what constitutes that which is to be learned.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, why is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha quiescent and immovable?
This question concerns its name and meaning.

The Buddha said, "As for the Tathāgatagarbha, when the characteristics of arising and ceasing and the consciousness of deliberation obscure it, its principle is not manifest; this is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha."
"Quiescent and immovable.
This indicates the characteristics [of the Tathāgatagarbha] and eliminates errors. Indeed, the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; it is inherently empty and quiescent.

It is entirely due to the perfuming of the three kinds of falsehoods—the beginningless linguistic designations, the links of existence, and karma—by the seven evolving consciousnesses and their evil habitual tendencies.

It functions as the ignorance of the birth-characteristic (*jāti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*), transforming into the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). It contains all seeds and serves as the cause for both the wholesome and the unwholesome.

Furthermore, based upon this storehouse consciousness, the ignorance of the abiding ground (*sthiti-bhūmy-avidyā*) arises again, giving rise to the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the preceding seven [consciousnesses].
This ignorance of the abiding ground then merges with the preceding seven; through this, the mutual production of the manifest and the seeds occurs, and by virtue of their arising...
There is cessation. Because of the cessation of arising, there is deliberative cognition. Due to these four characteristics, the true reality is obscured and cannot manifest.
However, the root source of this arising and cessation truly derives from the *tathāgatagarbha*, which transforms into the *ālayavijñāna*.

Thus the seven consciousnesses arise. Now, sentient beings are merely obscured by the four marks [of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing], and thus do not know that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally without birth or extinction, and is inherently empty and quiescent; therefore, they are not moved by them.
The Bodhisattva Jie-tuo addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what are the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of deliberative cognition?
This question was intended to examine the nature of conceptual error.

The Buddha said, "For a Bodhisattva, there should be neither 'yes' nor 'no. If there were 'yes' or 'no,' then various thoughts would arise, leading to a thousand reflections and ten thousand deliberations."

This is the characteristic of arising and ceasing. When a bodhisattva contemplates the characteristic of the fundamental nature, the principle is naturally complete. A thousand reflections and ten thousand deliberations do not benefit the Way;
they merely cause agitation, leading one to lose the sovereign mind-king.
This demonstrates four kinds of errors. It is said that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the principle of true nature is fundamentally devoid of affirmation and negation.
If there were affirmation or negation, there would be right and wrong; if there were right and wrong, then all manner of discursive thoughts would arise and fly about in confusion.
Consequently, there arise a thousand kinds of thoughts and ten thousand kinds of anxieties. From this, both awakening and affliction emerge, mutually encroaching upon one another.

One fails to realize that all these are merely the characteristics of arising and ceasing. If one turns back to contemplate the characteristic of the original nature, its principle is fundamentally complete in itself.
If one follows the deliberations of the conscious mind, one will be unable to benefit from the principle of the ultimate Way.
They are merely stirred into disorder by these [objects], causing the King of the Mind to lose its proper guard.

If there were no discursive thought, there would be no arising or ceasing. If things do not arise according to reality, the various consciousnesses will be peacefully stilled; their continuous flow will not be produced.
Attaining the purity of the five dharmas constitutes the Mahāyāna;
this clarifies the efficacy of the preceding cultivation and study. It is said that if the mind is free from discursive thought:
Thus, there is neither arising nor ceasing, and one immediately attains entry into the ground of the reality-limit (*tathatā-bhūtakoṭi*).
Erroneous thoughts certainly do not arise; all consciousnesses abide in empty stillness. When the flowing consciousnesses no longer arise, the five dharmas are all purified.
This is what is called the Mahāyāna. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing:
namely, the arising of the flow and the arising of the marks; the abiding of the flow and the abiding of the marks; and the cessation of the flow and the cessation of the marks."

In the *Awakening of Faith*, it is said that within the eighth consciousness, the manifesting consciousness (*xiànshí*), its three characteristics are subtle and hidden; this is the most subtle among the subtle and is termed "streaming-forth" (*liúzhù*).
This streaming-forth is entirely the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is neither born nor extinguished.

Due to the non-awakening of ignorance (*avidyā*), it suddenly becomes conjoined with birth and extinction, transforming into consciousness; this is called the "birth of the streaming-forth. It continues in succession throughout long kalpas.

This is called "abiding as a continuous flow. Upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) following the Vajra Path, one attains the wisdom of instantaneous correspondence (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*) and suddenly severs the ignorance of the characteristic of arising (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*).
This is the movement of thought within the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), the most subtle among all thoughts.

Once severed, the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), and the first five consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*); only then is [the obstacle] extinguished.
The eighth is the characteristic of the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), called the cessation of the flow. This limit of the flow is extremely subtle;

it can be truly severed only by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwelling in the stages (*bhūmi*) who have realized the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*) through the complete abandonment of the dual grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).

Only then can one truly know it. During the remaining stages of the Mahāyāna path—the paths of accumulation and preparation—one employs skillful means to investigate and remain far removed from the dualistic grasping at a self and phenomena.
Thus, the sixth consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation.
The seventh consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality. One contemplates the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa and attains realization of the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body.
Those who have first obtained non-conceptual wisdom also know this; having known this, [they proceed].
By means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one observes the subtle flow [of consciousness]. If cultivated with superior intensity, one suddenly transcends the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

If cultivated with middling intensity, one suddenly transcends the eight stages. If cultivated with inferior intensity, one proceeds from stage to stage, gradually severing [afflictions] and gradually realizing [the fruits].
Only upon reaching the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) can one begin to perceive the subtle flow of the deluded thoughts of one’s own mind.
This refers to the three types of flow—arising, abiding, and ceasing—within this eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*.

As for these three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, they are actually characteristics belonging to the preceding seven consciousnesses; however, within the state of their continuous abiding, they are divided into three, which include the subtle and the intermediate.

The coarse among these is that which is cognized by the first five [consciousnesses] and the seventh; the subtle within the coarse and the coarse within the coarse is that which is cognized by the sixth.
These three aspects constitute the coarse and manifest. For example, when the seventh consciousness first arises, it grasps the eighth as a self.
The arising of names and marks is their conjunction with the preceding objects; their continuous, uninterrupted succession is called the abiding of names and marks.
In the Mahāyāna, from the initial stage of the ground corresponding to the arousal of right faith, one severs the grasping of marks; this is the cessation of the coarsest among the coarse marks.

This is precisely the severing of the sixth [consciousness’s] discriminative attachment to a self, because the sixth consciousness—the discerning consciousness of objects—arises with grasping due to its conceptualization based upon the eighth manifesting consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Furthermore, from the first stage (*bhūmi*), one realizes the universally pervasive suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*), severs the characteristic of continuity, and attains partial awakening as the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*);
that is, awakening to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and realizing that mindfulness has no abiding characteristic.
Because one is free from the characteristics of coarse conceptualization, this is precisely the severing of the sixth [consciousness’s] discrimination of dharma-attachment (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*).

This, too, arises as a continuous stream by means of the sixth [consciousness] calculating the manifested images of the eighth [consciousness]. Upon reaching the seventh stage, the characteristic of wisdom (*jñānalakṣaṇa*) is severed;

this, too, is the sixth [consciousness], for it is because of the manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsavijñāna*) that the characteristic of wisdom is established. This severs the sixth dharma[-attachment].
This is the grasping that arises simultaneously (*sahaja*). This dharma-grasping arises spontaneously along with the body;
therefore, it is the subtle aspect within the coarse [grasping] that functions as the sixth consciousness’s general apprehension of objects.

From the eighth stage onward, the manifest aspect is severed, because the seventh consciousness only grasps the internal eighth consciousness as a self and lacks dharma-grasping. Furthermore, this is the empty seventh-consciousness simultaneous self-grasping. Moreover—

Because the first five consciousnesses evolve based on the evolving aspect (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*) of the eighth [consciousness] as their manifesting aspect (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*), one cuts off the evolving aspect in the nine stages.

This is because the seventh [consciousness] evolves based on the karmic aspect (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) of the eighth, and thus evolves as its evolving aspect. These two—the first five and the seventh—are that which cognize objects;
they are the cessation of the subtle, medium, and coarse aspects. This is called the cessation of the aspects (*lakṣaṇa-nirodha*). Furthermore, these aspects are the continuous flow (*pravṛtti*).

The middle characteristic is the continuous flow; that is, the flow within the characteristics. If the consciousness of this continuous flow ceases, one immediately attains the samādhi of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
However, if even subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not extinguished, the consciousness of the continuous flow cannot be extinguished either.
Now, observing the minds of sentient beings, they arise and perish moment by moment, thought after thought. How should one treat this? One must necessarily observe their arising.
To contemplate abiding is like a barren woman conceiving a child. To contemplate difference is like the waves surging upon a mirage.
To contemplate cessation is like the myriad transformations of floating clouds. To contemplate the momentary is like withered blossoms vanishing into the sky.
Within the mind of True Suchness (Tathatā), not even a single hair’s breadth of conceptual thought has ever stirred. Thus, as for the continuous flow...

All characteristics are completely exhausted. Therefore, in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva is able to enter and emerge from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in every thought-moment.
This [absorption] extinguishes the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) within the two characteristics of manifestation and transformation;

however, among the three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, there remains a portion of the beginningless ignorance of karmic activity (*karmalakṣaṇa*) that has not yet been severed. Consequently, full realization occurs at the tenth stage.
The subtle secret delusion is the perfectly awakened vajra-mind. It severs the subtle cognitive and afflictive obscurations;
these cognitions and afflictions are termed the "two obscurations," which fundamentally arise from the two types of grasping: to a self and to phenomena.
The afflictive hindrances [obstruct] Great Nirvāṇa, while the cognitive hindrances [obstruct] Great Bodhi.

Within the context of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), it is said that defiled phenomena obstruct the objects of knowledge, preventing wisdom from knowing them; thus they are called "cognitive hindrances.

Therefore, it is not that the object of knowledge itself is the hindrance, but rather that the hindrance obstructs the object of knowledge. One reaches the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) before finally severing these two hindrances. Furthermore, regarding the objects, there still remains a subtle...

There is the delusion of subtle attachment and the delusion of subtle obstruction. Therefore it is said: "Even Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) still sit within the cave of ignorance.
Upon reaching the Path of Liberation of Wondrous Enlightenment (Miaojue), the eighth stage, one transforms the aspect of karma based upon the aspect of true reality (zhenxiang).
Furthermore, the eighth consciousness—emptiness—and the five preceding consciousnesses, along with their dependent evolving aspects and manifesting aspects, are simultaneously extinguished.
This is the entry into the Buddha-ground by means of the dharma-attachment within the aforementioned eight and five consciousnesses; that is, the so-called "cessation of the flowing consciousness.
This is the cessation of one portion of the beginningless ignorance and karmic aspect within the eighth consciousness. When this karmic aspect is extinguished, [the Buddha-ground is attained].

The continuous flow [of afflictions] is extinguished. When this flow is extinguished, the true nature of the eighth consciousness is finally revealed. This true nature is the characteristic of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind;
it pervades from antiquity to the present, neither interrupted nor extinguished. Although it arises in accordance with conditions, it has never truly arisen;
although it ceases in accordance with conditions, it has never truly ceased. This is the essence of the originally enlightened mind (*mūla-bodhi-citta*), which has existed from time immemorial.
Now, that which flows on without changing or decaying is such that its cessation consists only in the extinction of mental characteristics, while the substance of the mind remains eternally present;
for this reason, it is called the "eternally flowing true nature. Because sentient beings are deluded regarding this, they transmigrate through the three realms;

because the Buddhas realize this, they attain equal and perfect enlightenment. However, in the School of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇavāda*), one discusses the two attachments to self and phenomena, which are of coarse and [subtle] degrees.

Subtle. The coarse refers to discriminative [ignorance], while the subtle refers to innate [ignorance]. Furthermore, among the one hundred dharmas of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the first ninety-four types pertain to the sphere of sentient beings and consist of the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).
The latter six types of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas pertain to the two vehicles and bodhisattvas and consist of the two attachments to self and phenomena.
Moreover, among the eight consciousnesses, since the sixth and seventh both possess the two attachments, the fifth...

In eight [of the consciousnesses], both are absent. According to the Nature School (Xingzong), there are five and eight: the fifth has only the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*); the seventh has only the attachment to self (*ātman-grāha*);
and the sixth possesses both the attachments to self and phenomena. That which is signless, non-apprehending, non-conceptual, and devoid of the two attachments is True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, the five dharmas are those mentioned in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*: appearance (*nimitta*), name (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).
It is further said: "The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness—these entirely encompass the Mahāyāna.
Now, all the myriad phenomena of the world are subsumed under names and marks;
therefore, wherever there is a mark, there is necessarily a name, and these are all merely established by our own conceptual imputation. Nevertheless, all that possesses form and color is a mark.
Based on characteristics, one designates them as "names. From names and characteristics, conceptual discrimination arises; this is false imagination (*vikalpa*).

To know that these names and characteristics are by nature originally empty—such that not a single dharma can be established and not a single dharma can be negated—and to know that the essence of all dharmas is empty and quiescent, transcending all conditioned activity: this is Suchness (*tathatā*). From the essence of Suchness...
When one turns back to examine all names, marks, and delusive thoughts, they are seen to be like passing travelers, coming and going without ceasing;

yet when one seeks their actual nature, it is utterly unobtainable—this is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* specifically presents the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*), and the two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*), which are likewise fully subsumed within these five dharmas.
Specifically, among the three self-natures, the first is the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is "name."

Characteristics (lakṣaṇa). Second, the nature of false conceptualization (parikalpita-svabhāva), which corresponds to its name. Third, the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), which is suchness (tathatā) and correct wisdom (samyag-jñāna).
Furthermore, the eight consciousnesses are termed characteristics and false conceptualization; if the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms, this is suchness and correct wisdom.

Moreover, there are two kinds of selflessness (anātman): namely, the selflessness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya) and the selflessness of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya). "Self" and "phenomena" are the names for these.

Characteristics (*nimitta*). Clinging to a self and clinging to phenomena are false conceptualizations (*parikalpita*). To realize the two kinds of emptiness and non-self is precisely suchness (*tathatā*) and correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).
For this reason, all Buddha-dharmas do not, in total, transcend these five dharmas. Furthermore, names originally have no names; characteristics originally have no characteristics;
all arise from false discrimination (*vikalpa*). One says that this name is not that, and that characteristic is not this. If one knows...

That which is unreal has no thought, deliberation, or the characteristics of arising and ceasing; even "suchness" and "wisdom" are merely provisional names—how could there be any characteristic to be apprehended?
If one claims that suchness and wisdom exist as realities, this too belongs to deluded imagination.
In this way, the five dharmas are all purified and exhausted without remainder.
When a bodhisattva enters the purity of the five dharmas, the mind is immediately free from delusion. If there is no delusion, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata’s (self-realized noble wisdom).
One who enters this stage of wisdom thoroughly knows that all things are fundamentally unarisen; knowing they are fundamentally unarisen, one is immediately free from false conceptualization.

This clarifies the entry into the stage of the Buddha’s wisdom. Indeed, from the state of ordinary sentient beings up to the stage of Buddhahood, there is nothing that does not seek to empty these five dharmas.

It is simply because sentient beings transmigrate through the six realms due to their attachment to names and marks (*nāma-rūpa*) and deluded thoughts, giving rise to praise and blame, love and hatred, and various kinds of conceptualizations based on mental discourse.
If one can realize the emptiness of "names," then [praise and blame]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*
When praise does not move one and signs are empty, then hatred and love do not arise. When names are extinguished, the path of speech is cut off.
When signs are extinguished, the sphere of mental activity ceases. If deluded thoughts are extinguished, the single mind alone manifests.
If one attains the essence of suchness, then while functioning vigorously, one remains eternally in quiescent extinction. If one attains right gnosis, one dwells within afflictions themselves.
This is bodhi. Abiding in birth-and-death is no different from nirvana. Thus, it cannot be taken as an object by any mind or consciousness;
it is called "the nameless" because names are fundamentally non-existent, and "the signless" because signs are fundamentally non-existent.

Since names and signs are both absent, deluded thoughts do not exist, nor is there correct wisdom, nor is there suchness. There is neither Buddha nor sentient being. This is what is meant by "entering the five dharmas."
When the mind is purified, it is free from delusion. If there is no delusion, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata’s noble self-realized wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
This noble self-realized wisdom is the realm realized by sublime awakening (*vibuddha*). As the Buddha said: "Contemplating that nothing exists, the Buddha-ground is non-arising;
one reaches the destination of noble self-realization. Furthermore, he said: "This is my own ground; it is sovereign."
This is the most supreme state; therefore, know that this is precisely the ground of the Buddha’s wisdom (*buddhajñānabhūmi*).
Entering this ground of wisdom, one thoroughly understands that all mundane and supramundane phenomena have never been self-arisen from the very beginning.

Since one knows they are not self-arisen from the beginning, how could there be any deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*)? This chapter summarizes the meanings of the "Absence of Marks," "Non-arising," "Awakening Benefit," "Reality-limit," "Nature-emptiness," and the "Tathāgatagarbha" within the "Dhāraṇī Chapter."

In the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the Buddha once taught seven kinds of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which are precisely these seven categories of dharma. The first is called the ultimate truth of the mind’s objective sphere;
it is the self-nature of the mind itself, free from further conceptual differentiation, and is thus signless (*animitta*). The second is called the ultimate truth of the wisdom’s objective sphere.
One contemplates all phenomena; there is nothing that is not thoroughly understood, yet in reality, nothing exists—this is precisely non-arising.
Third is the ultimate truth of the sphere of wisdom (*jñāna-viṣaya-paramārtha*). It is called "mind" because it accumulates karma, but when it does not accumulate, it is wisdom;

this is the benefit of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). Fourth is the ultimate truth of the sphere of vision (*darśana-viṣaya-paramārtha*). One attains the Buddha’s correct knowledge and vision, knowing all forms.
All forms are the Buddha’s form; all sounds are the Buddha’s sound. This is precisely the entry into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Fifth, it means transcending the two views.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of the objective realm is free from existence and non-existence, identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, and all other dualistic oppositions;

this is the emptiness of true nature. Sixth, it means transcending the stage of the "only son" (*ekaputraka-bhūmi*) to reach the ultimate truth of the objective realm. It refers to the initial teaching of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

Abiding in the stage of the "only son" (*ekaputraka-bhūmi*), one now speaks of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and the single nature (*eka-dhātu*); thus, one transcends the stage of the only son. This is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The seventh refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of the Tathāgata’s own-attained realm, which is the noble wisdom of self-realization (*svapratyātma-āryajñāna*).

It is not realized through another; it is the thorough penetration of the Buddha-dharma. This is the subtle excellence known well by all Buddhas. It is only that sentient beings are deluded regarding their own fundamental nature.
It is precisely through this knowing that it transforms into deluded thought. Therefore it is said: "The single word 'knowing' is the gate to all wonders, yet it is also the gate to all calamities.
Later, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva first inquired whether dharmas arise from conditions, thereby encompassing the meaning within this context.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "Venerable One, one who is free from delusive conceptualization should have no cessation.

This question concerning being without delusion and without cessation is derived from the two characters "non-arising" (abhinirvṛtti) from the preceding chapter, which here emerge as this phrase "no cessation."
The Buddha said: "Bodhisattva, delusion is fundamentally unarisen; there is no delusion to be extinguished. Know that the mind is no-mind; there is no mind to be stilled.
Without division and without distinction, the manifesting consciousness does not arise; there is no arising to be stilled. This is then neither 'stilling' nor 'not stilling.'"
Why is this? Because cessation itself is without cessation.
This clarifies the meaning of cessation being without cessation, precisely revealing entry into the realm of the Tathāgata’s own realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
Indeed, all sentient beings, by means of the seven preceding consciousnesses, grasp at the specific and general characteristics of the five aggregates; it is from this that causes arise.
It is merely that one falsely conceptualizes and becomes attached to phenomena arising and ceasing, such that they continue in an uninterrupted succession.

What is called "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) refers to what is personally realized through direct perception (pratyakṣa), such as touching fire and feeling heat, or entering water and feeling cold;

it is that which cannot be reached by verbal expression. "General characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), on the other hand, is the domain of inference (anumāna); it is that which can be reached by verbal expression, as for example...

To speak of "one dharma" is to penetrate through many dharmas, for they all share this characteristic. It is like how all fires possess the same nature of heat, and all waters possess the same nature of moisture.

Furthermore, even a conceptual cognition that employs a name to express its own intrinsic nature belongs to verbal expression and is likewise subsumed within the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, all characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the mind are, in total, merely...
It is merely due to the two characteristics of self and other that there is the continuity of conceptualization and attachment.
Furthermore, when examining this within the context of the five dharmas, it is not only the characteristics of names, marks, and conceptualization that constitute the continuity of attachment;
even if one clings to suchness (*tathatā*) and correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) as being substantially existent, these too become the continuity of conceptualization. Why is this so? Because...
Just as with right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), it is established solely as an antidote to the deluded conceptualizations of names and forms.

Ultimately, what "suchness" (*tathatā*) or "right wisdom" could there be to be attained? This is what is called the one true dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*), wherein not even a speck of dust can be established.

It is not something known by ordinary, ignorant people; it is only when a Bodhisattva dwelling on the stages (*bhūmi*) realizes the equal nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) that they are able to know it. For...
Within the state of equal dharmatā, there is neither ordinary delusion nor sagely understanding.

By observing the realm of the self-manifesting direct perception of one's own mind, one knows that both specific and general characteristics—the mind and its mental factors, and all phenomena—are from the very beginning empty and quiescent.
Although they manifest from one's own mind, they are like forms appearing in a mirror; fundamentally, they leave no trace.

They arise in their very place and are extinguished in that same place. Within the continuity of deluded conceptual attachment, there is originally no arising, nor is there any continuity of deluded conceptual attachment to be ceased.
One should firmly know that the mind is fundamentally non-existent as a mind; it neither arises nor ceases.
Movement. Furthermore, there is no characteristic of mind that can be ceased. Thus, there is neither division nor distinction;

one immediately attains the eighth consciousness, the *ālayavijñāna*, wherein the continuous flow ceases to arise. Its very substance is empty and quiescent, such that there is no further arising to be ceased.
This is called "non-ceasing. Yet, it is not that there is no cessation, for it ceases within non-ceasing. (Seal script)
To take "zhì" (止) as the character for "step" (bù): it is like first lifting the left foot and then advancing the right foot; this is what is called a step.

If the left foot has already come to rest while the right foot does not yet rise, this is called "stopping" (zhi). Previously, I discussed the meaning of "stopping at ultimate goodness" (*zhìyú zhìshàn*) from the *Great Learning*.
It is like the preceding and succeeding thoughts of an ordinary person: delusions and distractions arise in competition;
one pursues evil and becomes defiled by it, unaware of when to stop. If one knows the numinous and luminous nature-virtue within oneself, one stops at ultimate goodness.
"Good. This means that no second thought can be admitted; this is what is called "stopping" (*zhi*). "To arrive at" (*zhì*) is a term for reaching the ultimate limit.
"Good" (*shàn*) refers to the subtle and refined. Thus, one must certainly stop at the profound depths of the brilliant virtue that reaches the ultimate limit and the subtle refinement.
I have always said: once this mind comes to rest, it immediately attains its rectitude; how, then, could there be any sprouting of private desires?
This is precisely where the disciples of Confucius applied their efforts. Furthermore, our own school takes the "first thought" as its starting point.

Because it is the objective realm of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), Huangbo Xiyun said: "To suddenly transcend both Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment, and to definitely not flow into a second thought—only then can one be said to have entered the gate of our school.

This is because the Gate of the School fully manifests the Great Function, directly cutting off the conceptual discrimination of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is true *śamatha*. It is like Linji establishing the [first] stage...
A single phrase is a cloud of Dharma; the seal of the three essentials opens, and the vermilion dot is narrow. There is no room for deliberation, for host and guest are distinguished.
How could there be any room for the mind and consciousness to calculate within this? If you can, before it is even raised, lift yourself up and go.

This is merely a slight comparison. As soon as a second thought arises, one immediately falls into the discrimination of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), thereby forming deluded conceptualization and attachment that continues without ceasing; this constitutes inference (*anumāna*).

This occurs because one uses external conditions—the five sense objects—to infer characteristics such as long or short, good or bad; therefore, it is censured by all the Sages above, who say it is "tied by a hair's breadth."
Reflect: when the karmic causes for the three miserable realms arise from a fleeting emotion, one is bound in shackles for ten thousand kalpas.
If, however, one’s estimation does not cling to them, they are like scenes in a dream or what is seen during the delirium of illness; these are termed "non-valid cognition" (apramāṇa).

These three types of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are the cognizing mind as it manifests in opposition to the objects of the five sensory realms; regarding these objects, there is that which is favorable...
Evil grows whether in length or brevity, yet the mind relies upon it, giving rise to hatred and love, acceptance and rejection, until one reaches the point of deep attachment.
Through habituation, the two natures of good and evil are formed, which evoke the two retributions of suffering and pleasure; thus, one wanders incessantly through the three realms.
Alas, sentient beings are deluded by this, failing to realize that it all arises from the mental consciousness. Were one to thoroughly investigate and penetrate this delusive mind—
Regarding delusory objects: when, right here and now, both subject and object vanish together and no further discrimination arises, this is truly attaining the cessation of the unarisen (*anutpāda*).
This immediately enables one to transform fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) into the light of prajñā-wisdom.

Amidst the defilements of saṃsāra, one manifests great capacity and great function, remaining everywhere sovereign and unimpeded, moving freely and spontaneously in every direction. Attaining it in this way is true attainment.
This refers to those who have entered the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
A liberated Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "Venerable One, if cessation is itself non-cessation, then cessation is birth.
What, then, is meant by 'non-birth'?"
This interrogates the meaning of ceasing birth. It says that if birth ceases within a mind that is itself unceasing, it cannot be called "cessation.
For if one generates a mind seeking cessation, that very cessation is itself birth. As the Third Patriarch’s *Inscription on Faith* says:
"Ceasing movement returns to cessation; yet cessation further intensifies movement. Now, if the mind seeking cessation has already arisen, how can it be called [cessation]?
"Is it non-arising?
The Buddha said, "Bodhisattva, one should bring this arising to rest. Once brought to rest, there is no longer resting;
nor does one abide in non-resting, nor does one abide in non-abiding. What, then, is this arising?"
This demonstrates the meaning of not abiding in non-abiding. However, this merely answers the single phrase, "Cessation itself is arising.
That is to say, at the very moment of cessation, although the mind is indeed arising, it is nonetheless non-abiding in every thought-moment;
thus, this cessation itself has no object of cessation. How much less does it abide in non-abiding, nor does it abide in non-abiding?
"How can you say that cessation is itself arising?
The Bodhisattva Vimokṣa addressed the Buddha, saying, "Venerable One, in a mind that is non-arising, what is there to be grasped or abandoned? In what characteristic of phenomena does it abide?"
This question concerns non-arising and the taking up or discarding [of phenomena]. It inquires: what is the meaning of the single phrase "non-arising" mentioned previously?
The Buddha said: "The mind of non-arising neither takes up nor discards; it abides in no-mind and abides in no-dharma."
This demonstrates the meaning of non-abiding regarding all dharmas: if there were any place of abiding, there would necessarily be grasping and rejecting.

Such grasping and rejecting occur precisely because within the five aggregates, the aggregate of consciousness has not yet been shattered; one internally grasps at the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), calling it "self."
Externally apprehending the five sense objects as differentiated by consciousness and taking them to be "mine" constitutes the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).

If one has already abandoned the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), yet again takes that which abandons it to be the self, and regards that which is realized as "mine," this is termed the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
These two types of grasping are precisely the two kinds of mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). Now, it is said that these do not exist.
The mind of arising does not grasp at nor reject any phenomena; it abides in the mark of non-arising, neither in the mind nor in phenomena.
Thus, both self and phenomena are empty, and subject and object are both extinguished. This is the true meaning of the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "Venerable One, how does one abide in the non-mind and abide in the non-dharma?
This question regarding the non-mind and the non-dharma seeks to clarify the meaning previously indicated.
The Buddha said: "Not giving rise to the mind is dwelling in non-mind; not giving rise to dharmas is dwelling in non-dharma.
Good son, when neither mind nor dharmas arise, there is no basis for reliance and one does not dwell in any conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

The mind is eternally empty and quiescent, free from discursive thoughts, like space, which has neither movement nor stillness, neither arising nor activity, neither 'that' nor 'this. Thus one attains the emptiness of the mind."
(The Northern Canon reads "empty mind" for "eye. The eye attains the empty mind of dharmas; the five aggregates and six sense bases are all entirely empty and quiescent.

This is a reiterated explanation of the non-arising of the mind-dharma. Because the previous question asked about the characteristics of the dharma that is without arising or abiding, the answer was given as "abiding in neither mind nor dharma.
In reality, this is simply the single phrase "non-arising of the mind-dharma. Since it is the non-arising of the mind-dharma, [it is thus].
There is then nothing upon which to rely. Since there is no reliance, one does not abide in any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
The mind is constantly empty and tranquil, devoid of grasping or rejecting, affirmation or negation, right or wrong, and all conceptual distinctions.

It is like space, lacking the characteristics of movement or abiding, lacking the characteristic of arising, lacking the characteristic of action, and likewise lacking the characteristics of "this" and "that."

If one can truly act in this way, one immediately attains the emptiness of mind and realizes that the four great elements are without self; one attains the emptiness of phenomena and realizes that all dharmas are without self.
Therefore, it is said: "One attains the eye of the emptiness of mind; one attains the mind of the emptiness of phenomena.
Indeed, the eye of the emptiness of mind is the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye; the mind of the emptiness of phenomena is the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*. From...
The Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity realized only this mind-eye. As for what are called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): the accumulation of the four great elements is form (*rūpa*);
that which experiences and nourishes craving is sensation (*vedanā*); grasping at signs and pursuing them is perception (*saṃjñā*); subtle and subtle shifting flows are formations (*saṃskāra*);
and burning discrimination is consciousness (*vijñāna*). These five are able to obscure true nature; therefore, they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*). However, regarding birth...
Because consciousness exists, [the world] arises; by eliminating form, it ceases. As for the "six entrances" (*ṣaḍāyatana*):

they are the six internal faculties—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—which grasp and cling to the six external objects—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas. Because there is a sense of mutual interpenetration between them, they are called "entrances.
However, now that one has realized and testified to this mind and these dharmas, the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), entrances, and so forth naturally all [cease].
All are empty and quiescent. Later, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva asked: "How is it that all phenomena are not one?
[The Buddha] used this to encompass the meaning within:
"Good son, one who cultivates the dharma of emptiness does not rely on the triple world, does not abide in the marks of precepts, and is pure and free from thought. No...
It encompasses all without release; its nature is like a vajra; it does not destroy the Three Jewels; the empty mind is unmoving; it is endowed with the six pāramitās.
This clarifies that the dharma of emptiness fully encompasses the six perfections. Now, emptiness is the primary gateway to the Mahāyāna.

However, in cultivating this dharma of emptiness, one does not rely on the triple world, because it transcends the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) of the triple world. One does not abide in the Lesser Vehicle.
Riding upon the characteristics of conditioned precepts, because the three spheres are empty in essence, they are pure by nature.

There is no discursive thought; one is free from distraction. There is no deliberate concentration of the mind; one is free from indolence. There is no laxity of intent; the essential nature is equal to a vajra.
It does not destroy the self-nature, the pure and luminous essence of the Three Jewels. Indeed, the self-nature is eternal.
Awakening without delusion is the Buddha Jewel. The self-nature track and its unwavering adherence are the Dharma Jewel. The self-nature’s purity and harmony are the Sangha Jewel.
Furthermore, when one’s own mind is pure and every thought-moment is untainted, that is the Buddha.
When the light of one’s own mind illuminates everything without exception, that is the Dharma. When the pure light of one’s own mind is unimpeded everywhere, that is the Sangha.
This is precisely the Sangha. There is no need to seek it externally; it resides solely within the single mind of one's own nature.
If you believe in this Three Jewels as a single essence, you will immediately attain the empty mind that is unmoving and be endowed with the six pāramitās.
The Sanskrit term *pāramitā* is translated here as "reaching the other shore" (*dào bǐ'àn*) or "crossing over" (*dù gài*). This means that while worldly conditioned phenomena exist only...
This shore. One cannot reach the other shore. For example, when a person practices giving, they take the giver, the gift, and the recipient as the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*).
When these three wheels are empty and quiescent, it is called signlessness (*animitta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this is reaching the other shore.
If the three wheels are not empty, then cause and effect are not forgotten, revolving like a wheel; this is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) of the mundane world.
It is indeed so. Within the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), each fully possesses the three wheels (trimaṇḍala). If they were not empty, they could not be called the six pāramitās.
Furthermore, while practitioners of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas practice the same six perfections, they differ only in that the former seek their own benefit while the latter benefit others.
Furthermore, in the provisional teaching, one cultivates only the six perfections as the cause. In the ultimate teaching, one first seeks to awaken to and clarify one’s own mind;
once this clarity is attained, one brings all [other practices] to rest and cultivates only the fundamental nature. To desire solely to deliver sentient beings is called "arousing the bodhicitta.
Having already aroused this mind, one should cultivate all practices to accomplish the wondrous fruit of the Dharma-body, adorned with myriad virtues.
Phonetic Explanations: Yù (homophonous with yù; to advance; to exist; to reach). Zú (to finish). Zhì (pronounced zhì; young and small). Wàn (same as wán; to observe leisurely for one's own pleasure).

Kuò (first tone of the Kun rhyme; a cave or burrow). Méng (pronounced méng; the first sprouts of grass). Chóu (pronounced chóu; to calculate). Piè (second tone of the Pian rhyme; a sudden glimpse). Jī (pronounced jī; to tether or bind).

Suǒ (pronounced suǒ; vulgarly written as suǒ). Dān (dū hán qiè; same tone as dá; means "to love and long for"). Nài (pronounced nài). Kàn (kān in the departing tone). Guǐ (pronounced guǐ; means "law" or "to follow").
*The Record for Penetrating the Essential Tenets of the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*,
Scroll Three *The Record for Penetrating the Essential Tenets of the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*,
Scroll Four Composed by the Śramaṇa Jizhen, Successor to the Patriarchs at Huading Peak on Mount Tiantai.
In the second part of the "Chapter on the Dharma of Signlessness," the Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "Venerable One, these six pāramitās all possess signs.
Can a dharma that possesses signs transcend the world?"
This distinguishes [the path] from the conditioned characteristics of the mundane world.
The Buddha said: "Good son, that which I have taught as the six pāramitās is signless and unconditioned.
This clarifies that the dharma of the unconditioned is not identical in meaning to what is taught for the two vehicles.

Why is this? Because they have skillfully entered into the state free from desire, their minds are ever pure, and through truthful speech and skillful means, they benefit others with their fundamental benefit;
this is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
This section clarifies the dharma of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). When a bodhisattva cultivates the six perfections, a profound understanding manifests before them.

They cultivate the dharma of true suchness (*tathatā*) and the single mind by way of detachment from marks (*lakṣaṇa-viveka*), taking the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) as their essence and functioning solely in accordance with that nature.
What is meant by "dharma-nature"? It refers to the fact that the nature belongs to the dharmas; furthermore, it is so named within the context of sentient beings.

Buddha-nature, when existing within non-sentient things, is termed *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). Furthermore, this *dharmatā*, when it pertains to the Buddha, constitutes the *dharmatākāya* (Dharma-nature body);

when it pertains to the Dharma, it constitutes the *dharmatā-kṣetra* (Dharma-nature land). This is because the essence [of the nature] varies according to its manifestations. Now, knowing that the substance of *dharmatā* is devoid of stinginess and greed, one practices the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
That is to say, the mind constantly and skillfully enters the pure Brahma-conduct that is free from desire, and relinquishes...

Regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), one is without grasping or attachment; yet, through words of truth, one accords with others as is appropriate and employs skillful means to teach the primordial awakening (*prakṛti-ādi-bodhi*) of intrinsic nature.
This is able to produce the benefits of the Dharmakāya, liberation, and Prajñā, whereby one attains the fruit of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*).
To benefit others with these Dharma-benefits is the perfection of the Mahāyāna gift of Dharma (*dānapāramitā*).
To have steadfast and firm mindfulness, with a mind that is always non-abiding, pure and untainted, and unattached to the three realms—
this is the perfection of śīla (morality).

In Sanskrit, this is *śīla*; here it is translated as "precepts" (*jie*). Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is unstained and is free from the faults of the five desires, one cultivates pure precepts.
Consequently, through steadfast and focused mindfulness, one is not shaken by worldly appearances. The mind remains constantly non-abiding, cutting off both the paths of good and evil.
Since neither upholding nor violating arises, one is pure and unstained, transcending all worlds and remaining unattached.
The three realms: this is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) of the Mahāyāna.

Cultivating emptiness to sever the fetters, not relying on any forms of existence, bringing the three karmas to stillness, and abiding neither in body nor mind—this is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

In the Sanskrit language it is *kṣānti*; here it is translated as "patience" (*ren'uru*). Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without suffering, one practices patience by remaining free from anger and affliction.

However, one must first cultivate the dharma of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in order to sever the nine types of stubborn fetters of the deluded mind—namely, craving, hatred, pride, ignorance, views, grasping, doubt, envy, and stinginess—and furthermore, to become detached from all forms of existence (*bhava*).
These are called the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*): the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), [the form realm, and the formless realm].
There are the realms of form (*rūpa-bhava*) and the formless realms (*arūpya-bhava*). They are also called the nine realms of existence (*nava-bhava*):

the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the four dhyānas and four concentrations (*samādhi*). Furthermore, there are the twenty-five realms of existence: the four continents and the four destinies (the three paths of suffering together with the asuras making four); the six heavens of the desire realm; the Brahma heavens; the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*);

the realm of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*); and up to the *anāgāmin* (non-returner) realm. Collectively, these are termed the three realms (*tridhātu*) and the six paths of existence (*ṣad-gati*). Moreover—

In the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the path of the immortals (*ṛṣi*) is included among the seven destinies. If, however, the mind does not rely on these, abiding instead in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), such that the three karmas are stilled;

if one externally forgets the objects encountered and does not dwell upon body or mind, and internally severs the thought of a "subject" that endures—this is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) of the Mahāyāna.
To remain far removed from names and numbers, to sever the views of emptiness and existence, and to penetrate deeply into the emptiness of the aggregates (skandhas)—this is the *vīrya-pāramitā*.

In the Sanskrit language, *vīrya* means "diligence" (*jingjin*). Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is devoid of the characteristics of body and mind, one abandons indolence and thus cultivates diligence.
However, one remains far removed from all phenomena, which are merely provisional names and empty numbers, like the number two.

The five types of contemplation—contemplating impurity, compassion, counting the breath, dependent origination, and mindfulness of the Buddha—are the "five stations of the mind" (*pañca-vinodana-citta*).
These serve to eliminate the five obstacles consisting of excessive greed, hatred, distraction, delusion, and doubt.

Furthermore, through various enumerations such as the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, and the five powers, one severs the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
Seeing this, one deeply penetrates the emptiness of the dharmas of the five aggregates; this is the great progress of the Mahāyāna.

Fully possessing detachment from emptiness and quiescence, one does not abide in any forms of emptiness; the mind dwells in non-abiding and does not dwell even in the Great Emptiness—this is the dhyāna-pāramitā.

In the Sanskrit language, it is fully called *dhyāna*; here it is translated as "meditative concentration" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternally settled and its essence is without agitation or disturbance, one cultivates *dhyāna*.
However, this fully involves being free from the two vehicles' stagnation in emptiness and attachment to stillness, while also not dwelling in any forms of emptiness.
As in the initial gateway of the Mahāyāna, the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are taken as "internal emptiness" because they lack intrinsic substance. The six...

The signlessness of sensory dust is external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*). The non-existence of the six consciousnesses is internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*). The absence of the signs of arising and ceasing is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).

The absence even of the characteristic of emptiness itself is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). That the essential nature is fundamentally void is the emptiness of the beginningless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*).

The Dharma is fundamentally and eternally non-existent; its nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). That both [existence and non-existence] are absent is the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).

To speak extensively, there is the emptiness of the ultimate (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-phenomena (*abhāva-dharma-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of phenomena (*bhāva-dharma-śūnyatā*).
The emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of emptiness itself (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).

He does not dwell upon such meanings of emptiness, yet his mind constantly abides in non-abiding. Furthermore, he does not abide in "great emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*), which refers to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) where the body resides;
because the ten directions are immeasurable and boundless, all of them are empty, and thus it is called great emptiness. This is the Great...
This is the practice of the dhyāna-pāramitā.

The mind is devoid of the characteristics of mind; it does not grasp at empty space. All conditioned phenomena do not arise, yet one does not realize a state of extinction. The mind has no entering or exiting.

Its nature is eternally equal; it is the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of all phenomena, characterized by absolute certainty. It does not rely upon the various stages (bhūmi), nor does it abide in wisdom.
This is the Prajñāpāramitā.

In the Sanskrit language it is *prajñā*; here it is translated as "wisdom" (*hui*). This is because when worldly people hear "prajñā," they conceive a sense of reverence, whereas they find the term "wisdom" to be slighted;
therefore, the Sanskrit term is used. It refers to knowing that the essence of the dharma-nature is luminous and is free from ignorance.
Therefore, one cultivates Prajñā. However, ordinary beings cling to the mind as having characteristics; the Buddhas, however, have no such mental characteristics.
Those of the Two Vehicles grasp at the characteristic of emptiness; the Mahāyāna does not grasp even at empty space. In the provisional teaching, one practices various activities;
in the ultimate teaching, all activities do not arise. Those of the Two Vehicles take realization of quiescence as their goal; Bodhisattvas, however, do not realize quiescence.
The minds of those of the two vehicles have entering and exiting; their nature is not equal. The Bodhisattva, however, has a mind without entering or exiting; its nature is eternally equal.
In this way, one thoroughly understands that the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena is of a definitive nature.
This is precisely the true meaning of *prajñā*. Yet, upon attaining this *prajñā*, one does not depend on the gradual cultivation of the various stages (*bhūmi*), nor does one...
To abide in and cling to wisdom—this is the Mahāyāna perfection of prajñā.
In the past, the Tathāgata, in order to sweep away signs and dispel attachments, extensively expounded the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of prajñā for those of the two vehicles;

only thereafter did he preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and bestow predictions of their buddhahood. Indeed, without the subtlety of prajñā, one could never have extinguished the views regarding phenomena.
If one clings to emotional attachments, how could one possibly receive the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*) without the power of *prajñā*?
As for the direct pointing by holding up a flower, all verbal explanations and conceptual snares were completely swept away, revealing only the great function of the present moment.
Only Venerable Kāśyapa transmitted this through a single smile; this was the Dharma-seal of *prajñā* received and bestowed between Buddhas and patriarchs.

Furthermore, as for this single act of holding up a flower: it is something that the World-Honored One could not reach through his words and teachings across more than three hundred assemblies, nor could it be fully elucidated by the five thousand scriptural treatises.
Yet, were it not for this act of holding up the flower, he would have been unable to manifest the Dharma of Prajñā.
Were it not for *prajñā*, one would likewise have no means to fully comprehend the intent behind the "Plucking of the Flower. Subsequently, the successive patriarchs transmitted this mind-seal;
sometimes through witty remarks, sometimes through blows and shouts, they presented the whole directly before one’s face, brooking no deliberation.
These were those who had deeply attained *prajñā*. Thus, the single school of Bodhidharma values nothing more than clarifying the mind and seeing one's nature. As for viewing...
The entire Great Canon of teachings would then be nothing but superfluous words; how could there have been more than twenty years of extensive discourse?
Alas for the wild Chan practitioners of the末代 (final age), who cast aside the scriptural vehicles and recklessly prattle on about Prajñā.
Their conduct is identical to that of ordinary worldlings, yet they presume to be equal to the Buddhas—this is truly pitiable. Indeed, such is the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata’s vocal teachings.
All these are called "phrasing" (*vyañjana*). To be free from all speech, sounds, and written characters, such that the principle cannot be expressed—this is called "meaning" (*artha*).
Therefore, a sutra says: "Whatever is spoken is termed conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); if one knows the characteristic of the signless, this is the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
To penetrate the true characteristic is called the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Thus, the Tathāgata knows conventional truth and knows the ultimate...
There is one ultimate truth: by means of the wisdom corresponding to each moment, one is able to realize the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
All subtle habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*) never arise again; this is called "abandonment without remainder," and one is thus named a Buddha.
What is called "Dharma"? True Dharma is indestructible; this is what is called Dharma. Furthermore, that which has no attachment within the mind is called the true Dharma.
To seek nothing among all dharmas is the true seeking of Dharma.
Regarding all dharmas, there is no grasping or attachment, because the true mark of all dharmas is ungraspable. Thus, one does not grasp at any dharma whatsoever.
One does not contemplate signs, nor does one contemplate signless phenomena, because both signs and the signless are ultimately unapprehendable.
Therefore, when practicing profound *prajñā*, there is nothing seen, nothing attained, and no place of abiding; yet it is also not a case of non-abiding.
Being without change and without discrimination, it is said that one neither abandons the dharmas of ordinary beings nor grasps the dharmas of the Tathāgata.
This is the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Yet, one does not practice for the sake of attaining dharmas, nor does one practice for the sake of not attaining dharmas;
one does not practice for the sake of practicing dharmas, nor does one practice for the sake of not practicing dharmas.
To have faith in *prajñā* is to have no faith in any dharma; to practice *prajñā* is to not practice any dharma. And yet...
If one wishes to establish all phenomena (*dharmas*), one should study Prajñāpāramitā, because Prajñāpāramitā is able to establish all phenomena;
for all phenomena arise from within Prajñāpāramitā. Regarding all phenomena, one neither grasps nor rejects them, because within the reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) there is no grasping or rejecting.
Furthermore, one skillfully penetrates the reality-mark, understanding that within it there is neither defilement nor purity.
Furthermore, one should not observe all phenomena as either obtainable or unobtainable, yet be able to abide in all phenomena, cultivate all practices, and achieve all-knowledge.
Therefore it is said: "If one lacks skillful means, one cannot practice Prajñā.
Nevertheless, among all forms of correspondence, [it is] with the empty characteristic of all phenomena...

One should be foremost. As the Sūtra says: "Whether one encounters a person with an evil mind who cuts the Buddha’s left shoulder with a blade, or encounters one with a reverent mind who anoints the Buddha’s right shoulder with incense, the Tathāgata harbors no resentment toward the one who cuts him."
One who applies ointment does not regard it as a favor. Thus, Master Yongjia said: "When the mind corresponds with emptiness, what worry or joy can there be in censure or praise?
When the body corresponds with emptiness, what suffering or pleasure can there be in being cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance?"
When one's conditioned environment corresponds with emptiness, what is gained and what is lost in giving or plundering?
This is truly one who can correspond with emptiness. Furthermore, to correspond with the emptiness of all dharmas is to correspond with *prajñā*.
To correspond with *prajñā* is to be most honored, most supreme, and foremost; for *prajñā* is—
It is associated; that is, it is associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), associated with signlessness (*animitta*), and associated with wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Ultimately, there is neither association nor non-association.

Therefore, a bodhisattva training in *prajñā* regards all dharma-doors as like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like the moon in water, like a flower in the sky, and like a transformation.
Regarding transformative activities: they are like a city of Gandharvas; although they are all devoid of reality, they appear as if they exist.

Therefore, with respect to all phenomena (*dharmas*), one does not grasp at existence, nor does one grasp at non-existence, nor does one grasp at both existence and non-existence, nor does one grasp at neither existence nor non-existence.
Even to the point of not grasping at "not grasping," there is thus no grasping whatsoever toward any phenomenon. By means of this...
All phenomena have an unapprehendable intrinsic nature, because their intrinsic nature is the absence of intrinsic nature.
Since this is the case for all phenomena, one does not apprehend practice even regarding *prajñā*, nor non-practice, nor both practice and non-practice, nor neither practice nor non-practice;
even the non-apprehension of non-apprehension is not apprehended. Therefore, regarding *prajñā*—
If there is nothing whatsoever to be grasped, because the intrinsic nature of prajñā is unattainable— since its very nature is the absence of self-nature—
the Tathāgata knows that all phenomena are empty, all phenomena are without self, and all phenomena are unattainable.
All that exists within the three realms is but the single mind. Sentient beings cling to a self and give rise to deluded actions;
failing to understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are confused regarding their own nature, whereby all manner of suffering increases. The various sense faculties are unreal.
If one can clearly comprehend the ultimate truth, then one will know there is no self, no "mine," and no agent.
There is no experiencer. Since there is neither self nor what belongs to a self, there is no agent and no experiencer, and likewise no ignorance.
When ignorance is absent, the remaining eleven links follow suit and cease. All sentient beings coexist with the twelve links of dependent origination without perceiving or knowing them;
for this reason, they revolve in saṃsāra and cannot see its beginning or end. The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes...
Śāriputra, one sees only the end but does not see the beginning. The Buddhas see both the beginning and the end; therefore, they clearly perceive the Buddha-nature.

It is merely when conditions conjoin that we speak of "birth," yet birth is not a real birth. It is merely when conditions disperse that we speak of "extinction," yet extinction is not a real extinction.
To cling to emptiness is the view of annihilationism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi); to cling to existence is the view of eternalism (śāśvata-dṛṣṭi). These two—

Both are wrong views; they are not right views. Furthermore, because sentient beings are covered by the true nature due to the dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they neither know nor see it, falling among the class of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and being unable to escape.
For this reason, a bodhisattva contemplates form within the five aggregates of the body as like a mass of foam, feeling as like a floating bubble, and perception as like a mirage.
[He contemplates] the flames. He contemplates formations as being like a plantain tree. He contemplates consciousness as being like an illusion.
Having performed this contemplation, all consciousnesses are empty, lacking the characteristic of discrimination. All formations are empty, lacking the characteristic of volitional construction.

All perceptions are empty, lacking the characteristic of grasping images. All sensations are empty, lacking the characteristic of experiencing. All forms are empty, lacking the characteristic of obstruction and change. In this way, he does not perceive form.
Feeling is conjoined with feeling; perception is conjoined with perception; formations are conjoined with formations; consciousness is conjoined with consciousness.
There is not even the slightest dharma that is conjoined with another dharma, because their intrinsic nature is empty. Furthermore, one contemplates the four great elements within the body:

the earth element exists because it arises from the grasping of views; the water element exists because it is produced by craving and views; the fire element exists because it is triggered by conditions and views.
Because they are stirred by false views, there is the wind element. These four great elements arise through mutual resonance caused by the four views of sentient beings.
When the physical form returns to earth, the vital essence returns to water, the warmth returns to fire, and the movement returns to wind, the four great elements each disperse;
not even the slightest phenomenon can be found, for their fundamental nature is empty. Regarding the five aggregates, the Śrāvakas of the Two Vehicles—

Within [this state], one perceives that the body is subject to suffering and constantly harbors a sense of weary detachment. Desiring to sever all accumulations (*saṃudaya*), one remains ever fearful of rebirth.
Realizing *nirvāṇa*, the mind accords with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Diligently practicing the Dharma of the Path to seek one's own deliverance, one’s resolve is directed toward *nirvāṇa*.
Although the Bodhisattva’s mind inclines toward *nirvāṇa*, they do not grasp at *nirvāṇa*; although their body dwells in the world, they do not [become attached to it].
They are defiled by worldly dharmas because they take pleasure in dwelling within birth and death, rather than taking pleasure in nirvana.
Furthermore, those heterodox practitioners with false views, seeking liberation, merely desire to sever death without realizing that they must sever birth.
If a phenomenon is not produced, it cannot cease. The Bodhisattva merely cuts off its production, and death ceases of its own accord.
Therefore, regarding the Four Noble Truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, the Bodhisattva does not apprehend even the slightest phenomenon.
He does not perceive that the body possesses suffering, nor is there an origin to be abandoned, a cessation to be realized, or a path-dharma to be cultivated. By means of this...
Possessing sublime wisdom associated with mindfulness, one knows that all phenomena are by nature fundamentally empty. Practicing *prajñā*, one attains skillful means;
thus, regarding giving, the mind has no attachment. Since the three spheres are empty in essence, there is neither giver nor recipient.

Abiding in *śīla*, one perceives neither the characteristics of the precepts nor the one who maintains or violates them. Practicing patience both internally and externally, one perceives neither the one who endures nor...
Being able to endure, one practices diligence without perceiving either the agent who practices or the phenomena being practiced.

With right mindfulness, one practices meditative concentration without perceiving either distraction or tranquility. One practices profound *prajñā*, observing with correct wisdom that all phenomena are empty because they are ungraspable.
Because they are ungraspable, one practices the six perfections and fully cultivates the myriad practices for oneself.
They have no regard for or attachment to their own bodies or lives; their minds take no pleasure in worldly enjoyments;

they know that the nature of all phenomena is entirely equal; they never retreat from or abandon the vow for omniscience; and knowing that phenomena are like space, their minds have no point of reliance.
There is no attachment; in reality, not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended, because its intrinsic nature is empty.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices profound prajñā, they contemplate the secret treasury of all dharmas taught by the Tathāgata: it is cut off from the path of speech, and the nature of words is empty.
The twelve links of existence of sentient beings arise through causes and conditions; there is no one who assembles them, nor is there anyone who extinguishes them.

Therefore, the nature of dependent origination is emptiness. Regarding the five aggregates of the body, they exist due to false conceptualization; therefore, the nature of the five aggregates is emptiness.
All four great elements arise from the emotional perceptions of sentient beings and are externally manifested as formations; being hollow and unreal, the nature of the four great elements is empty.
This extends to the six sense bases, the twelve spheres, the eighteen constituents, and so forth, which all depend upon the five aggregates and the four great elements.
