Thus, the six sense faculties arise. By means of these internal six faculties, one grasps the external six objects; this is called the "entrances" (*āyatana*). The mutual production of the faculties and their objects constitutes the "bases" (*dhātu*).

The faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are established through their mutual causality; these are called the "elements" (*dhātu*). Since all phenomena arise through mutual dependence, none possess substantial reality.
Therefore, the natures of all phenomena—such as the entrances, bases, and elements—are empty. In this way, one comes to know the multitude [of phenomena].
The non-existence of arising is called the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Knowing that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Since both persons and phenomena are empty, one does not perceive the Four Noble Truths; extending thus to the Six Perfections and the myriad practices, there is not even the slightest dharma to be attained.
Not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended; therefore, the mind has no object of thought. Because the mind has no object of thought, there is no attachment.

Because there is no attachment, it is called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Since the dharmas of the emptiness of intrinsic nature are truly without outflows, one does not fall into the three realms.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "All dharmas that fall within the three realms are called 'with outflows' (*sāsrava*); supramundane dharmas are called 'without outflows' (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, if all dharma-gates are subject to arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, they are called 'conditioned' (*saṃskṛta*);
if a dharma is such that arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing cannot be apprehended, it is called 'unconditioned' (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding all dharmas, to be attached to 'self' and 'mine'..."
This is not bodhi. To realize the equality of all phenomena (*dharma*), being free from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," is called bodhi.
If one does not contravene the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and accords with the Dharma, one can enter into equality and manifest its underlying meaning and principle;
this is the teaching of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). I shall now briefly explain this within the six hundred fascicles of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Such is its meaning. Furthermore, our Chan school is known as the gate of Bodhisattvas who study Prajñā.
As for the teachings of great spiritual friends (mahā-kalyāṇamitra) such as Baizhang, Huangbo, and Linji, all of them expound the Mahāyāna meaning of Prajñā;
yet later students conversely claim these are fragmented and discard them without regard, seizing only upon [the superficial] questions.
Answering according to the capacity of the interlocutor is called "true cutting and holding.

Yet, there are those who take the wielding of staffs, shouts, and words as the actual Dharma, or who identify the "original host" or the "original face" as the true understanding; such people are far removed from Prajñā.
Nevertheless, this single phrase, "non-abiding wisdom," may serve as the medicinal tonic for the Chan school.
Good son, these six pāramitās all attain their fundamental benefit, enter the nature of certainty, transcendently emerge from the world,
and achieve unimpeded liberation.

This section clarifies the dharma of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). In the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna, the first five perfections are like the blind, while Prajñā (wisdom) is like a guide;

this is because it is able to lead them all back to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Furthermore, from Prajñā, the four perfections of skillful means (*upāya*), vows (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) are initiated.
Moreover, giving (*dāna*) and patience (*kṣānti*) assist morality (*śīla*), while diligence (*vīrya*) assists meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). [The subsequent...]

The four perfections all assist *prajñā* (wisdom), collectively constituting the three trainings of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). These serve as the provisions for bodhi.
This is the ultimate teaching of *nirvāṇa*, which likewise takes the clear vision of the Buddha-nature as its final goal.

The definitive teaching takes the awakening to the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena as the perfect and sudden One Vehicle. In all these cases, *prajñā* is honored as the primary guide. Furthermore,
These six perfections all obtain the benefits arising from original enlightenment and enter into the nature of certainty;
thus, one transcends the mundane world and attains unimpeded liberation.

Now, this liberation is not what is meant by the Two Vehicles’ cultivation of the Truth of Cessation to sever the bonds of suffering. Rather, within the Mahāyāna, it is the realization that all phenomena are empty.

Characteristics—the habitual tendencies of beginningless false and delusive conceptualization—are all completely extinguished. Furthermore, one realizes that external natures are all manifestations of one's own mind;
thus, one does not give rise to the active functioning of discrimination. With ignorance and afflictions already subdued, one attains liberation even within the midst of birth and death.
Apart from birth and death, there is no separate liberation. However, the practitioners of the Two Vehicles cultivate the dharma of emptiness.

They are still obstructed by empty phenomena (*śūnyadharma*). Not knowing the true benefit of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), their minds are nevertheless able to transcend all things and penetrate all things without hindrance regarding all phenomena of affliction and birth-and-death;
thus, they attain unobstructed liberation. They know that *prajñā* is like space, and that liberation is also like space. They know *prajñā*...
It is boundless; liberation, too, is boundless. This is the sphere of unimpeded liberation in this Mahāyāna.
Good son, such characteristics of the dharma of liberation are all conduct without marks (*animitta*), and there is neither liberation nor non-liberation;
this is called liberation. Why is this? The characteristic of liberation is markless and without conduct; it is unmoving and undisturbed—quiescent nirvāṇa.
...nor does one grasp at the mark of *nirvāṇa*.
This passage clarifies the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*. As it is said in the teachings: "That which is quiescent yet illuminating is *prajñā*;
that which is illuminating yet quiescent is *vimukti*; the essence in which quiescence and illumination are non-dual is the *dharmakāya*. However, as for *prajñā*, by means of non-...
The *lakṣaṇa* (marks) constitute the essence; liberation takes the signless (*animitta*) as its practice; and the *dharmakāya* takes the signless as its substance.
All are produced from within this single reality of the signless. Furthermore, *nirvāṇa* is fully called *mahāparinirvāṇa*, which here means "Great Extinction.
"Great" (*mahā*) signifies the *dharmakāya*; "extinction" (*nirodha*) signifies liberation; and "passing beyond" (*pāra*) signifies...
This is precisely the meaning of *prajñā*. Therefore, the *dharmakāya*, liberation (*vimukti*), and *prajñā* constitute the secret treasury of the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*.
Three are one, and one is three; thus they are likened to the three dots of the syllable *oṃ*.
Now, among these six *pāramitās*, liberation is the ultimate goal; therefore, it is said that the characteristics of the dharma of liberation are all practices of signlessness (*animitta*).
If one were to grasp at liberation, one would instead be bound by that very liberation. Therefore, it is further said:
"There is neither liberation nor non-liberation; this is called liberation. Subsequently, to further clarify the characteristics and meaning of liberation, it is said:
"It has no marks, no activity, no movement, and no disorder. Body and mind, internally and externally, are fundamentally quiescent from the beginning. This...
This is precisely the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure; this is *nirvāṇa*.
If one dwells in *nirvāṇa*, that is the bondage of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is said that one should not even grasp at the mark of *nirvāṇa*.
Within the vehicles of the teachings, the investigation has reached this point, and the exposition is complete. Even were it the Buddhas of the three periods of time...
It must also be hung upon the wall; not another word can be added.
Only the special transmission of the Dharma by Bodhidharma requires that one seek clarity right here. Thus, the ancient masters said:
"The matter of the School of the Patriarchs is like having confiscated a family's property and then demanding that they pay a fine. It is simply this: ask now.
Who is the person that does not grasp at the mark of nirvana? Only when one can utter a decisive word here that is precise and clear may they be permitted to discuss Chan and expound the teachings.
Upon hearing these words, the Bodhisattva Vimukta was filled with great joy and delight, experiencing what he had never known before.
Desiring to proclaim the meaning of his realization, he spoke in verse.

This passage describes the joy and delight felt upon hearing the Dharma; "joy" (欣) refers to exultant joy, while "delight" (懌) refers to pleasurable satisfaction. The subsequent verses provide a general summary.
Thus, the meaning of the Dharma is concluded through the method of question and answer.
The Greatly Awakened One, the Perfected Honored One, expounds the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes; he teaches all as the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), for there is no path of two vehicles.
The single flavor of signless benefit is like the great void; there is nothing it does not accommodate.
This praises the virtue of the transformation through the Dharma. In the preceding Preface Chapter, Great Compassion was praised in order to seek the compassionate transformation of sentient beings.
This praises the Great Awakened One, who, through hearing, has realized the Dharma of self-awakening and awakening others, wherein the practice of awakening is perfected.
According to their diverse natures, all attain [realization] within their own ground; just as that which is free from mind and self is accomplished by means of a single dharma.

All those who possess various concordant and divergent practices shall fully attain the fundamental benefit. Having extinguished the dualistic views of subject and object, they enter the quiescent nirvana;
yet they do not abide in the realization of attainment, entering instead the state of certainty.

This clarifies the benefit obtained equally by all. It is said that the Buddha, according to the differing natures of sentient beings, causes them all to enter the state of the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Just as those sentient beings are able to abandon the deluded mind of self, they attain the accomplishment of the One Dharma. As for all sentient beings, although their practices may differ, they are all...

It enables one to attain the benefit of the original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) of one's own mind, thereby extinguishing the false views of the dualistic marks of existence and non-existence, and attaining the quiescent nirvāṇa;
yet, one does not abide in the grasping of such realization. If one were to grasp at the realization of nirvāṇa...
This refers to the bondage of the fruits of the two vehicles, whereby one fails to achieve further progress and does not act for the sake of the Mahāyāna;
because one does not abide in or grasp at realization, one is able to enter the stage of certainty.

Signless and without activity, the mind is empty and the ground is quiescent; with a quiescent mind there is no arising, identical to that vajra-nature, indestructible regarding the Three Jewels, and endowed with the six pāramitās.
These words describe the subtlety of signlessness (*animitta*). As the Buddha taught, within signlessness and non-action, one attains a mind of empty stillness and abides in the ground of cessation.
With every thought in a state of cessation, one suddenly flows into the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
This cessation is non-arising within the mind; it is identical to the adamantine essence (*vajra-svabhāva*) and does not destroy the self-nature of the Triple Gem.
They are endowed with the six pāramitās; these are all dharmas never before heard.
They deliver all living beings and transcend the triple world, doing so entirely without recourse to the Hīnayāna, but through the seal of the single flavor of the Dharma.
This is the accomplishment of the One Vehicle.

This describes the vow of transformation: "I now know for the first time that in delivering all sentient beings and causing them to transcend the triple world, it is by no means possible through the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle;
rather, I shall preach only this single-flavored, true Dharma to seal them."
Nevertheless, sentient beings will surely achieve realization within this One Vehicle of Perfect Suddenness.
At that time, the great assembly, hearing this teaching, felt profound joy and satisfaction; they attained liberation from the mind and the self, entering into emptiness and signlessness.
Vast, expansive, and boundlessly open, all have attained certainty, severing the fetters and exhausting the outflows.

This summarizes the benefits of the joy derived from the *siddhānta*. What is described as "vast, expansive, and boundlessly open" is a depiction of the mental state and objective realm of entering emptiness and signlessness (*animitta*).
As for "exhausting the outflows," in the desire realm, craving arises based on internal mind and external objects.
The outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) consists of all afflictions produced within the realms of form and formlessness through the causal conditions of internal and external unwholesome phenomena.

Furthermore, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) arises from ignorance (*avidyā*) within the three realms conjoined with the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), whereby one fails to clearly understand "self" and "what belongs to self," and cannot distinguish between the internal and the external.
This is the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). These three outflows cause the mind to flow on in continuous succession.

It is scattered; therefore, it is identical to the two delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), as well as the afflictions of the five stages of abiding (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*).

However, once one is detached from the false mind and self, those outflows (*āsrava*) will naturally be exhausted. This verse [addresses] the Bodhisattva Vimukta, who extensively inquires about the supramundane methods of practice.
The final five sections specifically clarify the meaning within this signless (*animitta*) Dharma, and finally—

This is the first chapter. It further collects the doctrines and meanings from within the preceding six chapters. However, the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*), in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:

"All that exists within the three realms is but the one mind. The Tathāgata, in this regard, analytically explains the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), all of which are established based upon the one mind.
Thus, by contemplating the characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in both reverse and direct order, one comes to know for oneself...
The nature is empty; there is no agent and no recipient. Thus, the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) manifests before one.
Knowing that self-nature is extinguished and that not even the slightest dharma arises, the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) manifests before one.

Entering into emptiness and signlessness, being without aspiration or seeking, the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) manifests before one. Furthermore, one desires to fulfill the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*).
One contemplates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) proceed when there is conjunction and do not proceed when there is no conjunction;
they proceed when conditions assemble and do not proceed when conditions do not assemble. One must certainly sever these causes and conditions of conjunction.

Nevertheless, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to fulfillment, one does not ultimately extinguish all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). Thus, giving rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one does not abandon anything. That is to say:
One attains the manifestation of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is called the "Light of Unobstructed Wisdom.
Because it is able to contemplate the equality and purity of all intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), one enters the profound gateway of the Dharma.

Although one cultivates the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) through causes and conditions, one does not dwell in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Although one contemplates the conditioned, its intrinsic nature is quiescent; and furthermore—
Not dwelling in the state of quiescent extinction, one attains hundreds of thousands of gateways to the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, all of which manifest before one.
Regarding the true mark of all phenomena, one accords with them without contradiction and attains the sharp and penetrating patience of accord.
This "Chapter on the Dharma of Signlessness" is identical in meaning to the "One Dharma.
