The Fifth Chapter on Entering the Reality-Limit (Bhūtakoṭi), Part One:
This constitutes the section on Eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Now, one who wishes to attain great eloquence and wisdom—if they do not enter the reality-limit, how could they possibly achieve it?
Therefore, within the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī*), for the sake of delivering sentient beings, one cultivates unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). First...

First, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*); second, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*); third, the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*); and fourth, the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
Among the śrāvakas, these are obtained only in part, because they are unable to know language and meaning, and furthermore lack the three types of skillfulness (*kauśalya*).

This is because they are unable to employ gentle speech, harsh speech, or speech that is neither gentle nor harsh according to the capacities and natures of sentient beings, yet must preach the Dharma through skillful means for their sake.
If one were among the pratyekabuddhas, they would delight in cultivating quiescence (*śamatha*), and their guidance of others would consist solely in manifesting supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Therefore, when a bodhisattva dwells in this ninth stage, they attain immeasurable virtues.
They possess skillful, unimpeded wisdom that knows all Buddha-dharmas—their names, natures, characteristics, distinctions, and equality—without grasping or attachment;

this is the unimpededness of dharmas (*dharmapratisaṃvid*). Furthermore, they know the meanings of the dharmas and the meanings of the names of all Buddhas, as well as the meanings of their natures, characteristics, distinctions, and equality.
They thoroughly understand how the Tathāgata accords with the mental activities, faculties, and inclinations of the eighty-four thousand classes of sentient beings.
To distinguish various sounds without grasping or attachment to them is the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).

Furthermore, to know all phenomena according to their verbal expressions, to determine their characters, to skillfully recognize the forms of syllables, and to understand their true meaning—while extensively explaining the non-differentiated characteristics of the stages and paths without grasping or attachment—is the unimpededness of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
Moreover, to be able to [expound] by means of the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*)...
Through skillful means, according to the faith and understanding of sentient beings, he expounds with the wisdom of the Tathāgata and pure conduct in its full perfection.
Although he delights in such supreme eloquence, he remains unattached to it; this is the unhindered eloquence (*pratibhāna-asaṅga*).
Because he has no grasping or attachment toward any phenomena, he attains non-obstruction. Furthermore, he thoroughly realizes that all phenomena are without obstruction.
Thus, one attains unimpededness regarding meaning; because of knowing meaning without impediment, one attains unimpededness regarding expression.
Knowing expression, knowing phenomena, and knowing meaning, one attains inconceivable teaching—this is the unimpededness of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

In this way, the duties within the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*) are completed. Furthermore, while dwelling in this stage, the Bodhisattva exerts himself day and night, single-mindedly seeking wisdom.
[It is] clear. There are no further conceptualizations; one enters solely the realm of the Buddha and draws near to the Tathāgata.

Therefore, all Buddhas provide dharma-gates according to the dispositions and inclinations [of beings]. Now, this Tathāgata speaks of his own accord without being questioned, thereby inciting the inquiry;
it is just like that. Furthermore, in this stage, the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) is preeminent; for this reason, it is called "Great Power."
The Bodhisattva responds to the occasion; however, this discourse generally serves only to elucidate the meaning of entering the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality).
As for what is called the *bhūtakoṭi*: it is that wherein all phenomena (*dharma*) are equally unobtainable, and even this "unobtainability" is itself unobtainable.
Although they are unobtainable, one nevertheless cultivates wisdom and eloquence to benefit sentient beings. Furthermore, regarding the three characters for "entering the *bhūtakoṭi*," first—
Emerging from the dharma of signlessness, this serves as the foundation for this chapter.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata spoke these words: "The bodhisattvas, through their fundamental benefit, have entered deeply; they are able to deliver sentient beings."

If it is later and not the proper time, one should preach the Dharma accordingly. When the [proper] time and benefit do not coincide, whether the teaching is compliant or non-compliant, identical or different, it should correspond to what has been taught.
This draws forth all faculties and wisdom, causing them to flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). One must not allow the assembly to merely skim the surface like a hollow wind;
rather, one should cause all those present to partake of the divine milk of a single flavor.
This is the transmission of the Dharma for the sake of broad propagation, clarifying the practice of benefiting sentient beings.
It is said that a Bodhisattva must first attain the benefit of original enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya*) and enter deeply into *amala-vijñāna* before they can truly benefit sentient beings.

Even after my parinirvāṇa, during the time when the True Dharma no longer remains in the world, you should all preach the Dharma in this manner. Even if sentient beings are unable to believe or understand it, or even if—

The assembly is not uniform. Furthermore, for those whose faculties and dispositions are dull, one may skillfully transform them through teaching that accords with their nature, or subdue them through teaching that opposes it.
This is truly not a matter of treating everyone as identical, nor is it necessary to insist upon their differences;
rather, one should take what is appropriate and teach according to the Dharma, thereby leading the hearts of all sentient beings of wrong views and dull faculties.
Consciousness and the mental wisdom of sentient beings with sharp faculties both flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (translated here as "all-encompassing wisdom").
Now, *prajñā* is the cause and *sarvajñā* is the fruit; this is for the purpose of causing one to attain this fruit of wisdom.
Do not allow those sentient beings who are capable of being transformed to merely draw in the empty wind.
"To draw" (yì) means to ladle out. To ladle out that wind is like the common expression "inhaling the wind.
However, you must certainly cause all those multitudes to consume the single-flavored, divine, and wondrous milk of the Dharma; only then will it be so.
The world is not the world; it abides, yet is not a place of abiding. It enters and exits the five emptinesses, without grasping or rejecting. Why is this?

Because the characteristic of all phenomena is emptiness; their nature is neither existent nor non-existent, neither non-non-existent nor non-existent, neither non-non-existent nor non-existent, and they possess no determinate nature.
Not abiding in existence or non-existence, and not being within the realm of existence or non-existence, ordinary or holy, one is nonetheless able to fathom their hidden depths.

This demonstrates the dharma of the five emptinesses. Whether it be the mundane or the supramundane, whether abiding in the characteristics of the mundane or not abiding in the characteristics of the mundane—within this state of abiding and non-abiding, one contemplates the five emptinesses. If...

Whether emerging or entering, no signs of grasping or rejecting arise in his mind. Because these dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness, their nature belongs neither to existence nor to non-existence;
it is neither non-existent, nor is it not non-existent. Since it is neither non-existent nor existent, [it is beyond conceptualization].
Thus, there is no determinate nature; therefore, one does not abide in existence or non-existence.
Yet, this is not something that can be fathomed by the wisdom of ordinary beings or sages regarding the reality of existence and non-existence, for they cannot grasp its subtle and hidden intent.
If all bodhisattvas know this benefit, they immediately attain bodhi; this clarifies the benefit of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the essence of the characteristic of the emptiness of this Dharma is itself the benefit of primordial awakening (mūla-bodhi).
If one knows this to be the benefit of original enlightenment, one shall immediately attain bodhi.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Mahābala, who rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:

"Venerable One, as the Buddha has taught, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing in the entry into and exit from the five emptinesses. How is it that in these five emptinesses there is no grasping or relinquishing?
This is my request concerning the meaning of emptiness according to the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said: "Bodhisattva, as for the five emptinesses: the three realms of existence are empty; the shadows of the six destinies are empty;

the characteristics of phenomena are empty; names and appearances are empty; and the meaning of mind and consciousness is empty. When a Bodhisattva [realizes] such emptinesses, they do not dwell in emptiness, for emptiness has no characteristic of emptiness.
In a dharma that is without characteristics, what is there to be grasped or abandoned? Upon entering the stage of non-grasping, one enters the three emptinesses."

This answer is called "indicating the meaning," clarifying that the characteristic of emptiness is without grasping. However, when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he may refer to someone as a Bodhisattva or as a "good son" (kulaputra), each term having its own symbolic significance.
Whenever the matter is urgent, essential, and critical—when one desires to cause [the practitioner] to directly accord with principle and exercise resolute decisiveness—he must say "good son.
If it is for the sake of proclaiming [the teaching] for sentient beings of future generations...
One who clarifies this meaning is called a Bodhisattva. In this sutra, the Buddha and the two great Bodhisattvas Mahāsthāmaprāpta and Kṣitigarbha engage in a dialogue of questions and answers;
there is no mention of "good sons" (kulaputra). The three realms of existence—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm—all belong to the outflowing and conditioned.
The six paths of rebirth—devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—are likewise included therein.

All are produced by the deluded mind and are unreal, like shadows. Whether they be the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) or names of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*), encompassing both the mundane and the supramundane, they all arise from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) through false discrimination.
Both "mind" (*citta*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are merely provisional designations; fundamentally, they possess no real meaning.

The meaning of these five kinds of emptiness is likewise for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; they are expressed as "emptiness" to convey this, yet one must know that even emptiness does not abide in emptiness.
Emptiness itself lacks the characteristic of emptiness, such that they collectively constitute the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).
How, then, could there be any room for acceptance or rejection within them? If one can enter the ground of non-grasping, then one advances further still.
"With a single step, one enters the three emptinesses.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva asked, "What are the three emptinesses?
This was another inquiry regarding the meaning of the three emptinesses.
The Buddha said: "Regarding the three emptinesses: the characteristic of emptiness is also empty; the emptiness of emptiness is also empty; that which is emptied is also empty.
Such emptinesses as these do not abide in the three characteristics, yet they are not non-existent in their reality. The path of words and letters is severed; it is inconceivable."

This indicates that names reveal meanings. These three kinds of emptiness are known only by those in the ninth and tenth stages, as well as by the two types of Perfectly Awakened Ones (Samyaksaṃbuddhas) of the Equal and Sublime [stages];

others cannot understand them. This refers to the fact that the characteristics of the five kinds of emptiness mentioned above are themselves empty, and furthermore, the emptiness of emptiness is empty, and that which is emptied is also empty.
Entering into these three kinds of emptiness, one does not dwell even in them.
Regarding these three kinds of emptiness, within that interval, is there not the principle of ultimate reality?
Reaching this point, words and expressions are cut off; it is truly inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said: "It is not that there is no reality; it is that which exists in accordance with suchness.
This was intended to distinguish [reality] from the erroneous understanding of it as having characteristics.

The Buddha said: "Non-existence does not abide in non-existence; existence does not abide in existence. That which is the dharma of neither existence nor non-existence does not abide in non-existence, yet it is not non-existent."

This characteristic does not abide in existence; nor can the principle be expressed through existence or non-existence. For the Bodhisattva, there is no characteristic of name or meaning, which is inconceivable.
Why is this? Although it is a name without a name, it is not that names do not exist; although it is a meaning without a meaning, it is not that meanings do not exist.
This demonstrates the meaning of the true name. It is said that "non-existence" does not abide in non-existence, and "existence" does not abide in existence.
Therefore, any phenomenon that is not existent is "non-existent," yet it does not abide in non-existence;
the characteristic of being not non-existent is "existent," yet it does not abide in existence. Nevertheless, within this non-abiding, the nature of reality is not absent.
This, moreover, cannot be expressed through existence or non-existence so as to fully exhaust its principle.
Since it cannot be expressed, there is fundamentally no characteristic of name or meaning to be apprehended; this is truly inconceivable.

Yet, as for the "name of no-name," the name does not name itself; because the name is expressed by means of meaning, it is not that the "name of having a name" is non-existent, even though the meaning is absent.
The meaning of this is as follows: meaning does not exist inherently; it is manifested through names. Therefore, it is not that meaning does not exist within existence.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said: "Such names and meanings are the true suchness (*tathatā*). The suchness of the Tathāgata is suchness that does not abide in suchness;

it is suchness that lacks the characteristic of suchness, because characteristics lack suchness. Yet, it is not that it is not the Tathāgata. The mental characteristics of sentient beings—those characteristics are also suchness."
"Come! The minds of sentient beings should have no distinct objects.
This Bodhisattva understands that, by virtue of this principle, things are as they are. Since these names and meanings are mutually devoid of intrinsic nature,"
This is precisely the mark of true suchness (*tathatā*), which is immovable; it is also the suchness-mark of the Tathāgata.
Such a suchness-mark is established only as a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) and does not abide even in suchness, because within suchness there is fundamentally no mark of suchness.
If there is no mark of suchness within the [phenomenal] marks, then it is not different from the Tathāgata. As for sentient beings—
The characteristic of the mind is that this characteristic is also identical to that of the Tathāgata. Inferring from this, how could the minds of sentient beings not likewise be such?
They ought naturally to have no separate objects.
The Buddha said: "It is so. The minds of sentient beings truly have no separate objects. Why is this? Because the mind is fundamentally pure; because in principle it is without defilement.
It is because it is stained by dust that it is called the 'Three Realms. The mind within the Three Realms is what is called 'separate objects.
These objects are illusory and are produced through transformation from the mind. If the mind were without delusion, there would be no separate objects."
This seal is like a bright mirror; it refers to the minds of sentient beings. Originally, they are pure by nature. When examined through principle, they are truly free from defilement.
It is only because of the emotional dust of greedy attachment that they turn their backs on the Truth and depart from awakening; thus, they are called the "three realms.
Consequently, they form the deluded mind of the three realms—defiled, outflowing, and subject to birth and death. This is precisely what is called the "mind of sentient beings."
These are the distinct objects of cognition (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*). Although such objects exist, they are fundamentally illusory;
they arise as a magical transformation from within the pure mind. If the mind is free from deluded thoughts, it is inherently *tathatā* (suchness).
When the mind and its objects are one, there is no mind outside of objects, and no objects outside of the mind. In this state, there are no distinct objects of cognition.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said: "If the mind is in a state of purity, no objective realms arise. When this mind is pure, there should be no threefold world.
This clarifies that when the mind is pure, the land is pure."
The Buddha said: "It is so, Bodhisattva. The mind does not give rise to objects, and objects do not give rise to the mind.
Why is this? All objects that are perceived are merely the perceived mind. If the mind is not illusory, then there is nothing to be perceived.

Bodhisattva, when internally there are no sentient beings and the three natures are empty and quiescent, then there is neither one's own assembly nor another's assembly, and even regarding the two entrances, the mind does not arise. Thus one attains [realization]."
Such benefit means that there are no three realms.

This clarifies that the mind and its objects are empty and quiescent, thereby establishing the meaning of purity. It is said that the mind does not falsely give rise to various objects, being like a mirror suspended in space;
likewise, objects do not arise from the mind, for they fundamentally do not reach one another. If one can be thus, then that which is perceived—
All objects are merely the mind that perceives them. When one reaches this point in the teachings of the Chan school, the path of speech is cut off.
One then says: "At this very moment, tell me—where exactly does this mind see? Do not hesitate for a moment;
if you hesitate, you fall into the realm of conceptualization by means of the faculty of thought. Even if there should be someone who does not recognize good from evil, they would [fall into error].
A footnote states: "The environment manifests from the mind; when seeing form, one sees the mind. This merely explains the principle.
You must directly seek it beyond speech and silence, at the point where the essence is nakedly revealed.

If you can pivot upon this single mechanism, you will immediately breathe through the same nostrils as Śākyamuni Buddha. If you do not understand it within the scriptural teachings, you have no choice but to rely on a footnote.

To add further commentary: if the mind does not undergo illusory transformation, then externally there would be no various objects to be perceived, and internally there would be no sentient beings with the three natures of good, evil, or neutral;
all would be fundamentally empty and quiescent. Being thus, there would be no view of self.
Because there is the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span, it is said that there is no self-group and no other-group;
even regarding the two entrances, one does not give rise to a mind. Thus, there is neither the view of phenomena nor the view of non-phenomena.
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "One who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should know thus, and thus..."

One sees thus and resolves with such faith; not giving rise to the marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one attains this very state and thereby realizes the benefit of original enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*).
There being no longer a triple world for oneself, one transcends it and emerges beyond it.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said: "How can the two entrances not arise in the mind? Since the mind is fundamentally unarisen, how can there be any entrance?
This is a question that distinguishes the meaning of the two entrances.
The Buddha said: "As for the two entries: the first is called entry by principle (li-ru), and the second is called entry by practice (xing-ru).
This clarifies the names of the two entries; subsequently, the meanings of these two entries will be shown individually. [O] Formerly, Master Bodhidharma...
A brief exposition of the four practices of the Mahāyāna: It is said that while there are many paths for entering the Way, to summarize them, they do not exceed two types:
first, entry through principle (*lirù*); second, entry through practice (*xingrù*). As for entry through principle, it means awakening to the fundamental tenet by relying on the teachings.
One must have deep faith that all living beings share the same true nature, which is merely obscured by adventitious delusive thoughts and thus cannot manifest clearly.
If one abandons the delusory and returns to the Real, remaining steadfastly in the "wall-contemplation," where there is no self and no other, and all—ordinary people and sages—are equalized as one;
if one dwells firmly without wavering and no longer follows the teachings of others, this is to be in profound accord with the Principle (Li), free from discrimination, tranquil, and non-active.
This is called "Entry through the Principle" (Liru). As for "Entry through Practice" (Xingru), it refers to the four practices; all other practices are entirely included within them.
In this context, what are the four? First is the practice of repaying enmity. This means that when a practitioner of the Way undergoes suffering, they should reflect to themselves:

"Throughout countless kalpas in the past, I abandoned the fundamental for the peripheral and wandered through the various realms of existence, frequently giving rise to resentment and hatred, causing infinite harm and injury.
Although I have committed no offense now, this is the result of my own past calamities and evil karma."
When the fruit ripens, it is neither a god nor a human who can bestow it; one accepts it with a willing heart and endures it, without any resentment or complaint.
As the Sutra says: "Encountering suffering, one does not grieve. Why is this? Because of thorough understanding. When this mind arises, it accords with principle;
by taking resentment as the substance for advancing on the Path, it is called the practice of repaying resentment. Second is the practice of following conditions. Sentient beings have no self.
All things proceed according to karma; suffering and pleasure are experienced equally, for all arise from conditions.

Even if one obtains superior retribution, such as honor and renown, these were fashioned by my past causes and conditions and are now attained; when conditions are exhausted, they vanish again. What cause for joy is there?
Gain and loss follow conditions, yet the mind neither increases nor decreases. Unmoved by the wind of joy, one remains in profound accord with the Way.
Therefore, it is said that one acts in accordance with conditions. Third is the practice of seeking nothing. Ordinary people are constantly deluded;

they crave and cling everywhere, which is called "seeking. The wise awaken to the truth, wherein principle and conventionality diverge. They settle their minds in non-action (*wuwei*), while their physical forms follow the turning of events.
All phenomena are empty; there is nothing to desire or delight in. One knows that the darkness of those [worldly] merits constantly pursues them.
Dwelling long within the three realms is like being in a burning house; having a body entails suffering for all—whom can it ever satisfy?

Having thoroughly realized this state, one abandons all forms of existence, ceasing conceptualization and seeking nothing. As the Sūtra says: "Where there is seeking, there is suffering; where there is no seeking, there is joy."

To fully realize that there is nothing to seek is truly the practice of the Way; therefore, it is called "the practice of seeking nothing. Fourth is the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānusāra-caryā*).
This refers to the principle of intrinsic purity, which is designated as "Dharma. This principle is empty of all characteristics; it is without defilement and without attachment.

There is neither this nor that. As the Sūtra says: "The Dharma has no sentient beings, for it is free from the defilement of sentient beings; the Dharma has no self, for it is free from the defilement of the self.
If a wise person can believe and understand this principle, they should act in accordance with the Dharma.

Since the essence of the Dharma is without stinginess, one should practice the giving of *dāna* through body, life, and wealth, with a mind free of attachment or regret, and attain a thorough understanding of the three kinds of emptiness. Not...
It does not rely on anything, but merely serves to remove defilements. To transform sentient beings according to their needs while not grasping at signs—this constitutes one's own practice.
Furthermore, it can benefit others and also adorn the path to Bodhi. Just as it is with the perfection of giving (*dāna*), so it is with the other five.

To eliminate false conceptualizations, one practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) without anything being practiced; therefore, it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānulomika-caryā*).
These four constitute the practice of entering [the Way]. According to the First Patriarch’s teaching, this is established based on this very sutra. As for the entry through principle (*liru*):
one has deep faith that sentient beings are not different from true nature (*tathatā*), being neither identical nor distinct, but merely [obscured] by adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*).

That which obscures and hinders neither departs nor arrives; it remains steadfastly fixed within contemplation and observation. One clearly contemplates the Buddha-nature as being neither existent nor non-existent, neither self nor other, and where ordinary beings and sages are not two.
This adamantine ground of the mind remains firm and immovable; it is quiescent, unconditioned, and free from discrimination.
This is called "entrance through principle."
This demonstrates entry by means of principle (*li*). It means to accord with the principle of true nature (*dharmatā*) in order to benefit sentient beings. Therefore it is said:
"One must have deep faith that the true nature of sentient beings is fundamentally no different from that of the Buddha.

That the bodies of the present Buddha and sentient beings are distinct and cannot be one, and that the ranks of the ordinary and the sage are divided and cannot be shared, is due solely to the obscuration caused by adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*). However, one must...
Know that the nature of the mind is the host; it is fundamentally pure, like a bright mirror.
Those deluded thoughts are like guests, arising through continuous succession and defiling the nature of the mind, carrying the sense of dust and grime.
This is like the accumulation of dust and grime upon a mirror, which obscures its luminosity. If one can polish it to remove the dust and grime, then...
The essence of luminosity remains ever-present. Nevertheless, one now employs this method of cultivating the nature of mind to benefit sentient beings.
First, one should immediately sever the faculty of the mental organ (*manas*). Let the preceding thought not follow after it, and do not allow the succeeding thought to return.
Directly employ the single thought of the present moment, stabilizing the observation of awareness, and contemplate with clarity this which is primordially possessed.
The Buddha-nature does not exist within phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), yet it is not non-existent within principle (*tattva*). It is without self and without other; its essence is fundamentally one.
It is without sequence and without remainder; ordinary beings and sages are not two.

Being thus, one dwells firmly and immovably within the adamantine ground of the mind, attaining the essence of wisdom that is tranquil and unconditioned, and awakening to the function of wisdom that is non-discriminative. This causes [the practitioner] to...
One enters the emptiness of phenomena through principle.
As for entering through practice: the mind does not lean or depend [on anything]; its reflection is without fluctuation. In all circumstances, one maintains still mindfulness without seeking.
Unmoved by the gales of wind, one is like the great earth. Having abandoned the mind and the self, one brings salvation to sentient beings.
This demonstrates the practice of entry. It means that by abiding in the practice of true mind, one benefits sentient beings.
These characters for "practice" (xing) refer to the mental activities that respond to conditions and encounter objects throughout all daily life;

therefore, it is said that the mind abides in the Middle Way, giving rise to no thoughts of leaning toward or depending upon extremes, and remaining without shifting or changing amidst the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects.
In daily life, amidst all activities and undertakings, one’s thoughts remain tranquil, forever severing all restless seeking.
Even when buffeted by the winds of external circumstances, one remains unmoved, as stable as the great earth.
Although one attains such a state, there is fundamentally no dwelling or attachment; thus, one casts off the deluded mind of self and abides only with...
One exercises compassion through mercy in order to benefit sentient beings.
Being without birth and without marks, one neither grasps nor abandons. For the Bodhisattva, the mind has no entering or exiting;
because there is no mind that enters or exits, and because there is neither entry nor non-entry, it is therefore called "entering."

This clarifies the meaning of the character "entering" (ru). It states that the principle of nature (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally unborn from the beginning, and the activities of the mind (*cittagati*) are fundamentally signless (*animitta*) from the beginning.
Therefore, one neither grasps at a single dharma nor abandons a single dharma. This is because the principle of true nature cannot be grasped, and the activity of the true mind cannot be abandoned.
Furthermore, since the activities of the mind are signless, they fundamentally have no point of emergence; this is the principle.
The nature is unborn; fundamentally, there is nothing that enters. Therefore, the Bodhisattva’s mind that benefits sentient beings fundamentally has no entering or exiting.
Yet, by attaining this mind that neither exits nor enters, one knows that although one enters, one does not enter.
Because one enters while not entering, it is conventionally and forcefully designated as "entering."
The Bodhisattva enters the Dharma in this manner. The characteristics of phenomena are not empty; that which is not empty is a phenomenon that is not discarded in vain.
Why is this? Because that which is not non-existent is replete with merit; it is neither mind nor reflection, but is inherently pure by its very nature.
This concludes the preceding argument, clarifying the merit of entering into the Dharma.
It is said that if one can enter into these two dharmas—principle and practice—one will know that the characteristics of this Dharma are, in truth, fundamentally not empty.
If so, why is it called a "non-empty dharma"? This dharma is now clearly manifest; it must certainly not be treated as something vain or discarded.
Since it is not discarded in vain, one will certainly know for oneself that it is not non-existent.
If one knows this non-non-existence, then one possesses the true merit of the *dharmatā*. This is neither the deluded mind nor a shadow of conditions;
it is truly the inherent purity of the *dharmatā* itself. Yet, from the beginning, it is free from grasping or abandoning, and devoid of entering or exiting.
It emerges as non-empty, not in vain, and not non-existent; only then does it bring forth these four characters: "Endowed with Merit.
Long ago, when the Patriarch Bodhidharma first met Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the Emperor asked, "I have built monasteries and ordained monks;
what merit do I have? The Patriarch replied, "There is no merit at all. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit? The Patriarch said: "This..."
"However, the small fruits of humans and devas are caused by outflows (*sāsrava*); like a shadow following a form, they exist yet are not real.
The Emperor then asked, "What is true merit? The Patriarch replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and still—this is true merit.
The Emperor asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Patriarch replied, "It is vast and open."
"There is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that stands before me? The Patriarch replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not attain awakening.
The Patriarch subsequently crossed the river and entered Wei. At that time, all people throughout the realm hailed Emperor Wu as the "Buddha-Mind Son of Heaven.

He once provided an imperial commentary on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and personally lectured on the *Aṣṭadaśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly; he was truly able to rely upon the teachings.
I practiced the Way merely because I did not yet know its true merit; therefore, I failed to awaken to the words of the First Patriarch.
Later, when I heard that the Dharma-way had become widely renowned, I deeply regretted my former lack of understanding.

Furthermore, after the Patriarch’s passing, I heard that a Wei envoy encountered him atop the Pamir Mountains, who was returning with a single sandal in his hand. My longing and veneration increased all the more, and I subsequently composed an imperial inscription for his memorial stele.
I have recorded this in writing. It is said: "Alas! To see yet not see; to encounter yet not encounter. Whether now or in the past, one can only regret and lament.
Although I am but a single ordinary person, I dare to take him as my teacher hereafter and have further composed a eulogy for him.
If the mind exists, one undergoes sinking and wandering through kalpas; if the mind does not exist, one attains perfect enlightenment in a single instant.
Nevertheless, had Emperor Wu understood the meaning of this sutra on that day, he certainly would not have missed the opportunity to meet the venerable Bodhidharma face-to-face.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said, "What is meant by 'neither mind nor reflection,' being inherently pure?
This is the meaning of the request that I do not yet understand.

The Buddha said, "The dharma of emptiness and suchness is not a dharma of mental consciousness; it is not a dharma produced by the afflictions of the mind; it is not a dharma characterized by the mark of emptiness."

It is not a phenomenon characterized by form; it is not a mental factor associated with conditioned phenomena; it is not a non-associated mental factor; it is not a non-conditioned phenomenon that is associated;
it is not a manifested reflection; it is not something displayed; it is not self-nature; it is not differentiation; it is not name; it is not sign; it is not meaning.

Why is this? Because meanings have no suchness (*tathatā*). There is no dharma that is suchness, nor is there the absence of suchness. There is no non-suchness, nor is it the case that there is not non-suchness.
Why is this? The dharma of the fundamental principle is neither principle nor root; it is free from all disputes and its characteristics are not perceived.
O Bodhisattva, such a pure dharma is not produced by that which produces production, nor is it extinguished by that which causes extinction.
This elucidates the principle that emptiness is suchness (*tathatā*), which is the meaning of the pure Dharma. As it was said previously: "The three realms are mind-only;
all phenomena are consciousness-only. This was solely because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) hold false views and do not believe in their own minds.
Now, this Dharma of emptiness-as-suchness cannot be known by the mind, nor can it be cognized by consciousness. This first destroys the capacity of the mind and consciousness; this very capacity is—
This refers to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*); therefore, it is said that this is not a dharma of mind or consciousness.

Furthermore, because sentient beings possess the capacity of mind and consciousness, there subsequently arise mental factors (*caitta*). These are defined as those that always arise in dependence upon the mind, are associated with the mind, and are subordinate to the mind;
possessing these three characteristics, they are called mental factors. There are fifty-one such mental factor dharmas in total, while as for the dharmas of the mind...

These are all that which is governed by the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*). This is the locus where the mind-consciousness is destroyed; it is the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
All of these arise from the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) characteristic of the Hīnayāna.

If one follows the Mahāyāna’s sudden realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), these attachments no longer exist. Therefore, it is said that these are not dharmas governed by the mind, nor do they belong [to it].
Because it is not the non-existence of the view of annihilationism, it is said that this is not a phenomenon characterized by emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, because it does not belong to the existence of the view of eternalism, it is said that this is not a phenomenon characterized by form (*rūpa*). Moreover, it is not the conditioned mind of the mundane world, nor is it any phenomenon that is dissociated from it;
yet it is not the unconditioned mind of the supramundane world, for it is originally a phenomenon that is associated with it, unlike an illusion.
The reflection manifested through transformation cannot be displayed by words; it is not a self-nature or a true essence, nor is it the function of differentiated wisdom.
It possesses no names, no characteristics, and no underlying principles. For within this pure Dharma, who could bestow a name?
Its meaning is fundamentally empty and quiescent, and since there is not even a "thusness," we now merely employ provisional designations for it.
Yet it is the dharma of "non-as-such" (wu-ru). Furthermore, originally there is no such name as "non-as-such.
Since the name "non-as-such" does not exist, it is not that one makes it "non-as-such," yet this "non-as-such" can nonetheless exist.
If one further investigates the meaning and principle of this root, there is no real principle to be sought, nor is there any real root.
The source can thus be understood. Therefore, one is free from all verbal expressions and contentious debates. In reality, its mark of "non-existence" cannot be seen.
Such a pure dharma is not something that can be produced by production, yet it is produced;

nor is it something that can be extinguished by extinction, yet it is extinguished. The Buddha’s explanations of the names and characteristics of mind and consciousness are all intended to shatter duality.

Riding upon the heterodox views of external paths—as in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, where the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two forms of selflessness are variously analyzed and distinguished—there is nothing that does not serve to reveal the Dharma of the One Mind. Thus the Sūtra says:
"The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence. It also says: "Among the various gates of the Mahāyāna perfections, the mind of the Buddhas is foremost. The Patriarchs of later generations...
The school that establishes nature based on Mind-Only and the school that establishes characteristics based on Consciousness-Only both equally manifest the Dharma of the One Mind.
Later students who follow these traditions either cling to characteristics to challenge nature, or cling to nature to refute characteristics.
As nature and characteristics stand in opposition, the deluded mind of right and wrong and arising and ceasing arises. Master Bodhidharma rejected such characteristics.
This refers to the mind. [Huike] once transmitted the *Laṅkāvatāra* to the Second Patriarch, saying it could serve as a seal for the mind;
this refers to the Buddha’s words on the "Mind as the Doctrine. Furthermore, the biographies record that the Second Patriarch would frequently cite the *Laṅkāvatāra-śāstra* and often lament:
"After four generations, this sutra will degenerate into mere names and characteristics—how tragic! This refers to...

Later generations do not understand that these names and characteristics were established to reveal the single mind. Because they have not clarified the nature of the mind, they know only names and characteristics;
by grasping at names and characteristics as being truly existent, they fall entirely into deluded thought, which is precisely the realm of sentient beings.
If one knows that the characteristics of names are fundamentally empty and that deluded thoughts do not exist, such that only the single mind is revealed, this constitutes right wisdom and suchness;
it is the realm of all Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said: "Inconceivable! Such characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) are neither compounded nor singular;
they are neither bound nor fettered, neither gathered nor dispersed, neither arising nor ceasing. Furthermore, they possess no characteristic of coming or going.
They are inconceivable."
This is a profound comprehension of the meaning of the Dharma. Having first praised its inconceivability, he then spoke, saying:
"Such a dharma-characteristic, I now know, is not composed of a combination of manifold dharmas, nor can it be said to be produced by a single dharma alone.
It is not bound by any existent dharmas, nor by any non-existent..."
Bound by the Dharma, it cannot be said that there is anything accumulated therein, nor can it be said that there is anything lost.
One does not see a single dharma that arises, nor does one see a single dharma that ceases. Furthermore, no characteristic of coming or going can be apprehended;
its essence is fundamentally as it was from the beginning. Having spoken thus, he sighed again and said: "Inconceivable! How profound it is!"
One can understand this by grasping the Buddha’s intention.
The Buddha said: "It is so. It is inconceivable. The inconceivable mind—mind is also like this.

Why? Because it is not different from suchness; the mind is fundamentally suchness. The buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither one nor different. The nature of sentient beings is fundamentally..."
There is no arising or ceasing. The nature of arising and ceasing is, by its very essence, nirvana. The essence and its characteristics are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*).
Because suchness is unmoving, the characteristics of all phenomena do not arise from conditions; the nature of these arising characteristics is suchness, and suchness remains unmoved.
This seal constitutes a further explanation, clarifying the meaning of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind. The Buddha said: "It is so.
This, moreover, is not the same as what preceded it; for it speaks of how that which is praised as inconceivable must indeed be thus.
However, one must further understand that the inconceivable mind of all Buddhas and the minds of all sentient beings are also just as [described] before.

It is inconceivable. For, as previously stated regarding the dharma of emptiness and suchness (*tathatā*), when one follows this principle through reasoning, it is fundamentally no different from the minds of all Buddhas and sentient beings.

Since the essence of mind is inherently identical to suchness, although the Buddha-nature of sentient beings flows and turns in various ways, its return to the source is fundamentally no different. Therefore, sentient beings...
This nature is precisely the nature of emptiness and suchness. Its essence is fundamentally without birth or cessation that can be apprehended.

However, what is currently perceived before one's eyes as having birth and cessation is merely a characteristic (lakṣaṇa). That which is capable of arising and ceasing within these characteristics is the nature (dharmatā).

This nature of arising and ceasing is fundamentally identical in essence to *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is said that this nature and its characteristics are fundamentally identical to *tathatā* (suchness).
This *tathatā* is precisely the nature of quiescent extinction; quiescent extinction is itself *tathatā*. Thus, the nature of *tathatā*—
This is because there is fundamentally no mark of movement characterized by arising and ceasing.

Nevertheless, although all phenomena (*dharma*) in the world arise from conditions, no mark of arising can be apprehended. This is because the nature of the mark of dependent origination is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*);
and the nature of suchness is fundamentally unmoving.
The nature and characteristics of causes and conditions are fundamentally empty and non-existent. Conditions are themselves empty; there is no such thing as dependent origination.
All dharmas of conditionality are the deluded mind’s false perceptions; they appear yet are fundamentally unarisen, for conditions are fundamentally non-existent.
This clarifies the meaning of the emptiness of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

It is said that sentient beings delusively perceive the nature and characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination, yet they do not realize that these characteristics are fundamentally empty and non-existent from the beginning.

Although one currently perceives the nature of the subject that cognizes (*ālambaka*) and the characteristics of the object that is cognized (*ālambana*), one must know that the subject is also empty and the object is also empty; their nature is fundamentally [empty].
There is no characteristic of subject or object within dependent origination.

All phenomena that arise in a continuous succession of causes and conditions are due to sentient beings whose afflictions—arising from the karma they initiate and the moisture of rebirth—delude the mind, causing false perceptions to arise. Although appearances manifest, [they are devoid of inherent nature].
Yet its nature is fundamentally unarisen, for it arises through conditions and is inherently non-existent.
The mind is like the principle of dharmas; its own essence is empty and void. Like that King of Space, it has no place of abiding from the beginning. Such is the mind of ordinary beings.

The views of false discrimination are like the mark of suchness (*tathatā*); fundamentally, neither existence nor non-existence exists. As for the marks of existence and non-existence, one sees that they are merely mind-consciousness.

This clarifies that the mind accords with the principle of the Dharma. When speaking of the mind and the mark of suchness, as well as the phenomena of causes and conditions and the principle of true nature, if one investigates their own essence, all are empty and non-existent.
It is like that "King of Space," which takes the nature of emptiness as its covering.
Vast and sovereign, it is likened to a king; yet its essential nature is perfectly interfused and unimpeded, fundamentally having no place of abiding.
Nevertheless, the minds of ordinary beings give rise to false conceptualizations and views regarding this.
How could they know that the mark of suchness fundamentally belongs neither to existence nor non-existence? Yet now, sentient beings merely employ the dualistic distinction of subject and object.
Regarding the characteristics of existence and non-existence, one does not know the seer and the seen; these are merely mind-only and consciousness-only.
O Bodhisattva, such mental phenomena do not lack intrinsic nature, yet their intrinsic nature does not exist; they are neither existent nor non-existent. O Bodhisattva!

It is neither non-existence nor the markless; it is not a ground accessible through verbal expression. Why is this? The Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) is vast and empty, devoid of marks, and is beyond the reach of those of the Two Vehicles.
It is the realm of empty space, unfathomable from within or without; only those who practice the six perfections can know it.
This section clarifies the meaning of the mind-dharma (*cittadharma*).

It states that such emptiness and the mind-as-it-is, in relation to dependently originated phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna*), ultimately do not lack a self-nature (*svabhāva*) as their substance. Why is this? If one investigates the substance of its self-nature, it is certainly non-existent;
yet, when viewed from the opposite perspective, although it is non-existent, it is also not non-existent, because it arises through dependent origination.
Because it is manifest, one must understand that this teaching is the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the Bodhisattva, which is neither existent nor non-existent;

it is not a realm accessible through verbal expression. For the Dharma of the true suchness (*tathatā*) is void, vast, and expansive, devoid of any characteristics or forms, and is beyond the reach of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). It is like the realm of empty space, having no interior.
External limitations cannot be measured or discerned; only those who practice the six perfections can know them.
Later, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva asked about the fundamental emptiness and non-existence of marks, thereby subsuming the meaning contained herein.

Phonetic Explanations: Ruan (same as yuǎn). Yi (pronounced yì; to draw or pour). Ce (pronounced cè; to measure). Gai (first tone; to encompass exhaustively). Di (pronounced dí; to see face-to-face). Jie (pronounced xiè; to borrow.

Also same as jí, as in "lángjí" [disorderly] which uses the radical for grass, and "diànjí" [classics] which uses the radical for bamboo). Ning (pronounced níng; appearance of being undispersed). Lin (pronounced lìn; stinginess). Gou (pronounced gòu; structure). Ying (rúngxīng dìng)

Qiè (fourth tone): clean. An alternative reading is móyìng (polished); it means bright and clear). Gǔ (pronounced gǔ): to blow and shake. Yī (pronounced xī): not upright. Hàn (first tone of hán): to sway and move. Cōng (pronounced hūn).
Chì (pronounced chī; meaning "to dismiss" or "to exclude"). Zhé (pronounced chū; meaning "suddenly"). Bàn (cut by pǐ juǎn; meaning "near" or "change"). Xiàn (first tone of xián).
*Record of the Penetrating Essence of the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
