To take emptiness and silence as the Way, and to forget emotions and sever wisdom as cultivation, is to cling to the empty and obscure essence of the eight consciousnesses.
Furthermore, to say, "Vague and indistinct—within it there is a thing;

profound and dark—within it there is an essence," is merely to identify with the *vijñāna* (consciousness-spirit) while remaining ignorant of the One Mind. Since this is not identical to the One Mind, [it cannot be the Way].
If one practices the Way in this manner, then the Way is not "mine. If one does not realize that all phenomena are simply the mind, then phenomena will follow after divergent views.
Thus, the ancient masters said: "Those who study the Way do not recognize the Truth, solely because they have long been attached to consciousness.
This has been the root of birth and death for immeasurable eons; the deluded call it the 'original body. Those of today who rely upon consciousness...
"To regard the entry and exit of spirits as the ultimate achievement of cultivation—is this not foolish?
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "The nature of phenomena is thus: both internal and external are empty. Both the objective realm and wisdom are primordially quiescent and extinguished.
This Dharma of the true mark and ultimate emptiness spoken of by the Tathāgata is precisely not an accumulation."
This statement is not without the sense of "gathering" (*saṃgraha*). Within the section on the benefits of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*), the meaning of gathering still persists.

When it says, "The characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) are thus," this refers precisely to the profound essential meaning of the passage concerning entry into the stage of Buddha-wisdom within that section on the benefits of original enlightenment.
In this context, it goes without saying that both internal faculties and external objects are equally empty and quiescent. As for sentient beings...
The sensory objects of this world and the wisdom-ground of all Buddhas—these two kinds of manifold dharmic characteristics are, from the very beginning, inherently quiescent.
This means that both wisdom and its object are simultaneously extinguished; this is precisely the true mark of ultimate emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*) spoken of by the Tathāgata.
Such a dharma is not something that can be gathered or accumulated. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Gathering..."

Karma constitutes consciousness (*vijñāna*); the absence of accumulation constitutes wisdom (*jñāna*). The commentary states: "Accumulation" means gathering and collecting; "gathering" means summoning and assembling.

When the sense faculties encounter their objects, one gives rise to grasping and attachment, producing wholesome and unwholesome karma and thereby summoning and assembling birth and death—this is consciousness.
To be able to discern the faculties and objects as being beyond duality, to forget both self and things, and not to give rise to grasping and attachment—this is wisdom.
The Buddha said: "It is so. The Dharma of reality as it is has no form and no abiding; it is not that which is accumulated, nor that which accumulates;
it is neither meaning nor letter. It is the single principle of the Dharma, a profound mass of merit."
This explains that it is not an accumulation. It is called the dharma of the *tathatā* (suchness) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Because it is primordially pure, it is formless; because it does not cling to a location, it is without abiding. It is not that which is accumulated, because external objects are empty;

it is not that which accumulates, because the mind and consciousness are empty. It is not a meaning, because it cannot be expressed; it is not a word, because it is beyond the reach of speech. This very one—
This fundamental text (*mūla-pāṭha*) truly transcends the world and constitutes a profound accumulation of merit.

The two characters "fundamental text" (*benke*) refer to the section on the "Great Meaning" (*mahārtha*) within the preceding *Tathāgata-garbha* chapter; it takes the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) as its topical heading.
And it comprehensively encompasses the dharmas of the Great Meaning and so forth.
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "It is inconceivable; it is an inconceivable collection. The seventy-six [in the Northern Canon, erroneously recorded as seventy-five] are non-arising."

85 (The Northern Canon erroneously reads 86): Quiescence. Ninth: the emptiness of marks. There is emptiness of existence, and there is non-existence of emptiness; there is non-existence of emptiness, and there is non-existence of non-existence.

As the Venerable One has said: "The meaning of all phenomena is entirely empty. Entering this emptiness, one acts without action, yet does not lose the consequences of karma. There is no self and nothing belonging to a self.
The views of self regarding both subject and object, as well as all internal and external fetters, are entirely stilled; thus, all vows also cease.

Such contemplation of principle consists of wisdom, concentration, and True Suchness (*tathatā*). The Venerable One once said that this reality, like the dharma of emptiness, is indeed a potent medicine.

This clarifies that both phenomena (*dharma*) and their meanings (*artha*) are empty. It also encompasses the meaning of the section on the "non-arising of the seven and six" within the *Prakṛti-parivarta* (Chapter on Entering Reality).
"Inconceivable" and "the mass of the inconceivable"—these two phrases praise the entry into the *Prakṛti-parivarta*.

The mind is as wondrous as the dharma of emptiness. Regarding "the non-arising of the seven and six": the seven consciousnesses and the sixth consciousness are of the same nature of inference (*anumāna*);

they are subsumed within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Since conditioned phenomena are fundamentally characterized by arising and ceasing, when one now abides in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is no arising.
Regarding "the quiescence of the eight and five": the eighth consciousness and the first five consciousnesses are of the same nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). [They are] unconditioned.
It is subsumed within the nature [of reality]. Since the unconditioned is inherently quiescent from the beginning, it is said that "the eighth and fifth are quiescent.

However, in the Northern Canon, this was erroneously rendered as "the seventh and fifth are non-arising; the eighth and sixth are quiescent. This was clearly due to a failure to recognize that these lines belong within the "Chapter on Entering the Reality-Limit" (Bhūtakoṭi-praveśa-parivarta).
Previously, there was the phrase "the seven and six do not arise," which clearly indicates a scribal error. Regarding "the nine marks are empty and non-existent":
the essence of the ninth consciousness-mark is fundamentally empty and non-existent from the start.

However, these two characters, "empty" and "non-existent," are also merely provisional names used for expression. Why? Although the names consist of the two characters "empty" and "non-existent," they both exist because of [linguistic] expression.
It is expressed as "existent," yet in its true nature, there is within this very [reality] no "emptiness" (*śūnya*) or "non-existence" (*abhāva*) that can express such existence.

For example, when the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Venerable One and the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta is entirely empty, one enters into the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of emptiness and non-existence;

thus, while emptiness and non-existence are not themselves empty, the meaning of their non-emptiness remains. Therefore, although they are empty and non-existent, one does not abandon or lose any wholesome dharmas or karmic actions.

Furthermore, one is able to sever all outflows (*āsrava*) as in the case of the seven consciousnesses, yet one clings to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] as one's own internal self (*ātman*).

However, this seeing is not the true self. Since one falsely regards it as the self, the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*) arises. Regarding *Vijñaptimātra* (Cognition-Only), take the analogy of a king and his ministers:
wherever the king goes, the ministers follow. Once there is that which is possessed ("mine"), there is that which possesses ("I"). As for the possessor...

The internal faculties arise as that which is capable of seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving; the external objects arise as the locus to which seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are attached.
Taking that which sees as the self and that which is seen as its characteristic marks, and further, because there is this body of self, there arises the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
With the view of a self-body, there arise the nine fetters, the ten proclivities, and so forth, which delude and obscure the true nature.

Now, by merely shattering this view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), all phenomena (*dharma*) are simultaneously shattered. Therefore, it is said: "There is no self (*ātman*) nor anything belonging to a self (*ātmīya*).

Thus, the views of a body as subject and object, as well as the internal and external fetters (*saṃyojana*), are all utterly stilled. When it is thus, there is nothing above toward which one can look up with longing.

Below, one cuts off the self; there is no path to be realized and no birth to be delivered from. One immediately attains the liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*); hence it is said that "all vows also cease.
Within such contemplation of principle, the dharmas of wisdom, concentration, and *tathatā* (suchness) are perfectly complete without exception.
The Venerable One once said: within the dharma of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the mind is pure according to principle, and all dharmas possess the characteristic of emptiness. Now...
I have reflected deeply upon this, and herein the mind accords with principle; it is precisely what is called the excellent medicine for delivering sentient beings.
The Buddha said: "It is so. Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is empty. Since emptiness is non-arising, the mind is eternally non-arising. Empty.

Nature is without cessation; the mind is likewise always without cessation. Emptiness has no abiding place; the mind also has no abiding place. Emptiness is unconditioned; the mind is also unconditioned.
Emptiness has no entering or exiting and is free from all gain and loss; the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are likewise entirely non-existent.
The non-attachment of the mind is also like this. O Bodhisattva, I speak of all things as empty in order to shatter all forms of existence.
This seal establishes the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Furthermore, it elucidates the principle that the nature of the mind is like space.
Now, the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is identical to empty space; thus, empty space is used as a metaphor.

Therefore, it is said that the nature of empty space is without arising and without ceasing, without abiding and without action, and likewise lacks the characteristics of entering or exiting, or of gain and loss. It is also devoid of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).
However, the nature of space is such that it cannot be grasped or clung to; likewise, the principle that the mind is like it cannot be grasped or clung to.
The fundamental emptiness of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is also not to be grasped or clung to.

Furthermore, it can accord with all phenomena and establish them, just as space—whose essence is not the various forms—is not obstructed by the manifestation of those various forms. This is the nature of emptiness.

The meaning is as follows. Later, he further clarifies the statement regarding the correspondence between medicine and disease, specifically answering the phrase "that which is truly effective medicine.
This is because sentient beings are attached to existence (*bhava*); therefore, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is taught for them. Once that existence has been dismantled...
Then even emptiness would not be established. This is precisely the meaning found in the "Chapter on the Emptiness of True Nature.

The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha said: "O Venerable One, to know that existence is not real, like water in a mirage, yet to know that reality is not non-existent, like the arising of the nature of fire—to observe in this manner is the wisdom of a person."
This statement means that true wisdom is not non-existent; it is the ocean of wisdom of the emptiness of nature at the end of the "Chapter on the Emptiness of True Nature.
It is also the meaning of the four wisdoms within the "Tathāgata-garbha" chapter. As the verse by the householder Brahmacarin says:
"If one says phenomena exist, it is the delusion of mistaking a mirage for water. If one sees phenomena as non-existent, it is the delusion of a blind man who does not see the sun. Now...
This means that sentient beings all cling to delusion as being existent.

If one can know that existence is an illusion and is fundamentally not real—like a mirage appearing on dry land, known to be not water—this is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s teaching of emptiness to shatter existence.
Once existence is shattered, emptiness is truly not empty; for within the self-nature of sentient beings, each possesses [it].
There is the seed of *tathatā*, which is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha*. However, apart from its own nature, there is no *tathatā*;
and apart from *tathatā*, there is no *tathāgatagarbha*. If one were to abandon birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one would likewise be unable to perceive *tathatā*.
Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Depending upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is birth-and-death; therefore, there is *tathatā*. This is because of the *Tathāgata*...
The "Treasury" (garbha) is precisely the *tathatā* of the gateway of birth and death.

If one can awaken to the *tathatā* of one's own nature and enter into the Tathāgatagarbha, then one knows that it is truly not non-existent; it is like the nature of fire arising within wood. This is the analogy.
This was already established previously in the "Chapter on the Practice of Non-arising. However, knowing that existence is not real, one conceals the reality to employ expedient means.
When this knowledge of reality is no longer absent, one then sets aside the expedient to manifest the reality.
One who can contemplate in this manner may indeed be called a wise person.

The Buddha said: "It is so. Why is this? Because these people practice true contemplation, contemplating the single state of quiescence. Whether regarding characteristics or the absence of characteristics, they grasp them equally as empty.
By cultivating emptiness, they do not lose the vision of the Buddha; by seeing the Buddha, they do not follow the three currents [of existence].
Within the Mahāyāna, the three paths of liberation are of one essence and devoid of self-nature. Because they lack self-nature, they are empty; because they are empty, they are non-existent."

Characteristics are non-characteristic; because they are non-characteristic, there is no activity. Because there is no activity, there is no seeking. Because there is no seeking, there is no aspiration.
By means of this karma, the mind is purified. Because the mind is pure, one sees the Buddha. Because one sees the Buddha, one shall be born in the Pure Land.
O Bodhisattva, regarding these profound dharmas, through diligent cultivation in the three transformations, wisdom and concentration are perfected, and one immediately transcends the triple world.
This seal constitutes a further explanation. The Buddha said: "Such a person attains entry into the contemplation of True Suchness (tathatā).
Contemplating the single nature of quiescence, they attain equanimity toward all phenomena before their eyes, as well as those that do not manifest as phenomena."
One takes emptiness as the object of practice. If all marks are empty, that is the universal mind;
awakening to the universal mind is awakening to one's own mind. Because one awakens to one's own mind, one clearly perceives the Buddha-nature. Therefore it is said: "By practicing emptiness."
In the end, one will not fail to gain the benefit of seeing the Buddha; this is the cause within the stages (*bhūmi*).

Thus, by seeking to see the Buddha, one resolutely does not follow the shifting flux of the three realms of existence (*trabhava*) in the world, but is able to accord with and enter the path of the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*) within the Mahāyāna.
This is precisely entering the "Chapter on Entering the Reality Limit" (*bhūtakoṭi-praveśa-parivarta*), the liberation of space and the liberation of the vajra.
Liberation. This is the liberation of *prajñā*. It is also identical to the practice-aspect of the aforementioned sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
As in the sixth stage, by knowing that intrinsic nature is empty, being without action and without reception, one immediately attains the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*).

By knowing that intrinsic nature is extinguished and that no marks of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) can be apprehended, one immediately attains the liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa*). Entering into emptiness and signlessness, there is no further seeking or aspiration; thus one immediately attains...

The liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*). Up to this point, one attains hundreds of thousands of gateways to the samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Furthermore, these—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are themselves the Dharmakāya, liberation (*vimukti*), and prajñā; they constitute the secret treasury of the three virtues of nirvāṇa.
Now, these three paths of liberation precisely elucidate this meaning, as the sutra says: "The single essence is without..."
Nature is empty because it lacks inherent nature; being empty, it is signless; being signless, it is without activity; being without activity, there is no seeking;
and because there is no seeking, there is no aspiration. However, in the previous "Tathāgata-garbha" chapter, [these were discussed] by way of emptiness, signlessness, and lack of activity.
This constitutes the three samādhis. From the sixth bhūmi through the tenth bhūmi, the bodhisattva relies entirely upon the gate of *anabhisaṃskāra* (non-action) to establish all practices.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva relies upon the four truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-catur-āryasatya*): namely, that the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) are all suchness (*tathatā*), so there is no suffering to be abandoned;
that afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves bodhi, so there is no origin of suffering to be severed; and that extremes and deviations are all the middle way.
There is no path to be cultivated; birth and death are themselves nirvāṇa. There is no cessation to be realized.

To contemplate all phenomena as being equal to empty space is precisely the mode of practice on the various stages (*bhūmi*). Nevertheless, the Bodhisattva gives rise to the four great vows and cultivates the practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
If one does not practice the six perfections, those vows will be in vain. Therefore, although one practices, one enters into emptiness and non-existence.
Among these characteristics, one fundamentally does not cling to practice; this is to act through non-action (*anabhisamskāra*).
Thus, there is seeking without seeking and aspiring without aspiration, all of which rely upon non-action.

Therefore, by speaking only of non-action, the meanings of non-seeking and non-aspiring are implicitly contained therein. Nevertheless, it is precisely by means of this practice of non-action that one attains [the goal].
The pure mind: because the mind is pure, one sees the Buddha. Not losing the vision of the Buddha previously was the cause;
this seeing of the Buddha through mental purity is the fruit. Now, awakening to the purity of the mind is truly seeing the Buddha-nature.
Since one has seen the Buddha, one shall be born in the Pure Land; thus, the mind is pure and the land is also pure. Thereupon, in this profound...

The Dharma has three gates of transformation. Diligently practicing these is precisely to cultivate the three doors of liberation: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
By cultivating these three, wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are spontaneously perfected. *Prajñā* is wisdom; liberation (*vimukti*) is concentration.
When wisdom and concentration are equalized, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is perfectly realized, and the three virtues are fully possessed. This is to transcend the triple world. This...
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva who had first attained liberation asked about the means to escape the three realms, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
"That which the Tathāgata describes as neither arising nor ceasing is itself impermanence. Cessation is the cessation of arising;

once the cycle of arising and ceasing has ceased, quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa) is permanence. Because it is permanent, it is uninterrupted; this is the dharma of non-interruption, which is free from all three [realms]."
Regarding the dharmas of the realms, whether moving or unmoving, one should regard conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as avoiding a pit of fire. Based on what dharma does one reproach oneself?
One enters through that single gate;
these words are true, eternal, and uninterrupted. This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the eternal dharma as taught within the *Tathāgata-garbha-parivarta*.
That which is neither arising nor ceasing is spoken of in contrast to arising and ceasing; once it involves such relative opposition, it is no longer truly permanent.

If cessation were merely the cessation of arising and ceasing, one would simply cause the two views of arising and ceasing to be extinguished so that they do not arise again, thereby abiding in quiescent extinction;
this alone constitutes true permanence. Having attained this true permanence and quiescent extinction, then...
This is the dharma of non-interruption and non-extinction. This is the dharma of non-interruption and non-extinction. It is that which enables transcendence from the triple world.
Regarding the dharma of movement and non-movement: "movement" refers to all worldly phenomena; "non-movement" refers to the meditative concentrations of the two vehicles.
All of these abide within the triple world and are subsumed under conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
One should contemplate conditioned phenomena as one would avoid a pit of fire, so as not to be burned or submerged by them. This was said while looking back at the great assembly present;
subsequently, he turned his body toward the Buddha and asked, intending to say: "All worldly sights, cognitions, sounds, and..."
I understand. All that possesses names and characteristics is entirely a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Apart from these, there is nothing to be cultivated.
Now, for the sake of sentient beings in future generations, by what dharma should they reproach themselves and enter that single gate?
This refers to the three gates of transformation; first, one must enter through one gate.
The Buddha said: "Bodhisattvas should reprove their minds regarding three great matters and enter into practice through three great truths.
This first demonstrates the essentials of cultivating and purifying the truth of phenomena."
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "What are the three matters by which one reprimands the mind? What are the three truths by which one enters into the single practice?
This is the formal inquiry into their names and meanings.
The Buddha said: "The three great matters are: first, cause; second, fruit; and third, consciousness.
This indicates the names of these three matters. Indeed, for sentient beings, conditioned karma is the cause and receiving retribution is the fruit.
For example, ignorance conditioning volitional formations is the cause, and birth, old age, sickness, and death are the fruit. These causes and fruits all depend upon [consciousness]."
Consciousness exists [only] through these three things.
Yet these three things have been empty and non-existent from the very beginning; they are neither the self nor the true self. Why, then, do you give rise to attachment and defilement toward them?
Contemplate these three things as the bonds that bind you, causing you to drift through the ocean of suffering. For this reason, one should constantly reproach oneself.
This demonstrates the meaning of reproach. If one examines these three matters in reverse, then the consciousness-mind is not real;
it is empty and non-existent from the very beginning. It all arises from the deluded discrimination of ignorance, which grasps at things as being existent.
This is truly not the true self of the self. Why, then, would one falsely grasp at it with the consciousness-mind?
Attachment arises. Furthermore, one should more deeply observe these three matters with the mind:
one must know that they are all due to the uninterrupted binding of the mind’s recollections, whereby one is fettered and eventually drifts into the ocean of suffering.
One should thus reprimand this consciousness-mind; this is the essential precept for beginners. ○ At the very beginning, the Bodhisattva takes the Unconditioned as his object.
Measuring the Four Noble Truths, one gives rise to the four great vows of wisdom. Contemplating the Truth of Suffering, one perceives its immeasurable aspects;

knowing that the karmic retributions of the ten dharma realms differ, one thus gives rise to the vow to deliver all sentient beings. Contemplating the Truth of the Origin [of Suffering], one perceives its immeasurable aspects;
knowing that the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling differ, one thus gives rise to the vow to sever all afflictions. Contemplating the Truth of the Path, one perceives its immeasurable...

Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): because one knows that the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are diverse, one generates the vow to cultivate all dharma-gates. By contemplating the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), one perceives its immeasurable characteristics;
because one knows that the various *pāramitās* are diverse, one generates the vow to bring the Buddha-way to full completion.

This correctly elucidates the Dharma of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, within the teachings, four types of the Four Noble Truths are distinguished, according to which sentient beings’ faculties and capacities they may practice and progress.
Just as the śrāvakas practice by relying on the four truths of arising and ceasing, the Buddha further advances them with the four truths of non-arising:
he says that suffering has no characteristic of oppression, accumulation has no characteristic of conjunction, the path has no characteristic of duality, and cessation has no characteristic of birth.
The Bodhisattva resolves his mind by taking the four truths as immeasurable objects. The Buddha further advances him toward the four truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

There are two kinds: arising-and-ceasing and non-arising. [In the former] one practices only the six *pāramitās*. There are two kinds of the immeasurable: [the immeasurable of arising-and-ceasing and] the immeasurable of non-action.
This encompasses the ten pāramitās; it is here that their relative superiority and inferiority are distinguished.

Now, the Buddha offers this final instruction, which remains within the meaning of contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination from the "Chapter on the Initial Dharma of Non-characteristics.

This clarifies the non-duality of the beginning and the end, wherein one transcends all stages instantaneously, rather than proceeding through gradual penetration and entry by means of successive levels.
Furthermore, as for the three truths: first, it refers to the path of bodhi; this is the truth of equality, not the truth of inequality. Second, it refers to great awakening;
it is the truth attained through right wisdom, not the truth attained through false wisdom. Third, it refers to wisdom and concentration; it is the truth entered through non-dual practice.
It is not by departing from practice that one enters the Truths.
This further demonstrates the method for entering the Truths through practice. First: it is said that one should know the dharmas of the path to Bodhi;
this is the equal nature of awakening shared by both sentient beings and Buddhas. Therefore, it is called "equality," and not inequality. Second:

This refers to the path of Bodhi, which must inevitably lead to great awakening—just as the Buddha entered right samādhi and, beholding the morning star, attained vast and perfect enlightenment, becoming a Samyak-saṃbuddha. This is the truth of attaining the right wisdom of all Buddhas;
because it uses the correct to discern the false, it is said that this cannot be attained through false wisdom. Third, this refers to the Great...

Awakening and right wisdom do not transcend the two trainings of wisdom (*prajñā*) and concentration (*samādhi*). As is the case with those of the Two Vehicles and non-Buddhists, they all possess concentration but lack wisdom;
because they first attain concentration, wisdom does not function. The Bodhisattva, however, first uses wisdom to purify the mind, and concentration is thereby contained within it.
Possessing both wisdom and concentration, one immediately attains the adamantine essence of the mind-ground precepts (*vīra-citta-bhūmi-śīla-svabhāva*); therefore, although...

Regarding the precepts (*śīla*), the essence of the precepts is fully perfected. Therefore, for the two vehicles and beginners, the Buddha first taught the prevention of wrongdoing, the cessation of transgressions, and the guarding of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Within the Mahāyāna, however, "that which should be done" (*kārya*) is supreme, with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) being secondary.
This is why he does not speak of "concentration and wisdom" (*samādhiprajñā*), but rather "wisdom and concentration. Apart from this wisdom and concentration, there are no other practices.
Therefore it is said that one enters by means of no divergent practices; nor can one enter apart from the two practices of wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
By cultivating the path to Buddhahood through these three truths, there is no one who, within this Dharma, fails to attain right awakening and achieve right [enlightenment].
Awakened wisdom flows forth as great, ultimate compassion; benefiting both oneself and others, one attains the Bodhi of Buddhahood.
This constitutes the perfection of Right Enlightenment. Although these are called the Three Truths, in the final analysis they are but a single Truth.
If one can cultivate the One Buddha-way by means of these Three Truths, I say that such a person, within this Dharma—
There is no one who does not attain their perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). If one attains this wisdom of the perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas, one will flow into the Mahāyāna;
within the three gates of liberation, one will give rise to immeasurable compassion, benefiting both self and others, and thereby accomplish the path to Buddha-bodhi.
There is a version of the text that forms a phrase with the three characters "Dà jí cí" (Great Ultimate Compassion), but in terms of meaning, it is not [correct].
Correct. It is proper to take "manifesting great ultimate compassion" as the phrase. "Ultimate" (ji) means immeasurable.

Phonetic glosses: *cāo* (level tone; meaning to maintain or observe); *yì* (cut with *zhì*; lineage or descendants); *hū* (pronounced *hú*; meaning vague and indeterminate); *tuǒ* (upper tone of *tuò*; meaning to rely on or rest secure).
*The Commentary on the Penetrating Essence of the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*,
Scroll Ten *The Commentary on the Penetrating Essence of the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*,
Scroll Eleven Composed by the Śramaṇa Jizhen, Successor to the Patriarchs at Huading Peak, Mount Tiantai.
The eighth chapter, "Dhāraṇī," Part Two, Lower Section.
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "Venerable One, such a dharma is without causes and conditions.
If there is no dharma of conditions, then causes do not arise. How can the immovable dharma enter the Tathāgata?"
This question concerns the meaning of entering the Tathāgata. It concludes by clarifying the final verse of the *Tathāgatagarbha-parivarta*.
There is that which is eternal, sovereign, and suchness; this is the meaning of entering the *tathāgatagarbha*.

That is to say, regarding the dharmas taught in the *Tathāgatagarbha-parivarta*, there is no arising or ceasing to be found through causes and conditions. Why? Because if there were no dharmas conditioned by causes, [arising and ceasing would not exist].
Thus, there is no arising; conditioned origination does not occur. This is the state of profound stillness and immobility within the true essence of Suchness (tathatā).
One may ask: how can one enter the path of the Tathāgata’s perfect wisdom by means of this dharma of the immovability of Suchness?
At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke these verses: "The characteristics of all phenomena are empty by nature and immovable.
These phenomena do not arise at this time, nor do they arise at any other time."

This refers to the true nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Now, although all phenomena before one’s eyes possess their respective characteristics, their nature is fundamentally empty and non-existent;
their essence is suchness (*tathatā*), unmoving. When observing by way of their characteristics, each phenomenon stands forth distinct and vivid;

when observing by way of their nature, every thought-moment is empty and quiescent. Although they are empty and quiescent, they are nonetheless able to move in accordance with conditions. Therefore, it is called...
Although such phenomena as described above manifest at what is considered the "proper time," they do not abide for even a single moment;
in reality, they cannot be subsumed within the three periods of time. Therefore, they do not arise with any fixed certainty at a so-called "proper time.
What is referred to here as "these phenomena" is precisely the dharma of true-nature dependent origination; it is that very "single phrase before one's eyes" of the Chan school.
"At this time" means precisely at this moment; it refers to the very instant when the preceding thought is just arising.
Once, a monk asked Zen Master Zhiwei, "What is the meaning of 'the dependent origination of true nature'? Zhiwei remained silent for a long while.

At that time, An-guo Xuanting was standing in attendance. [Zhaozhou] suddenly called out to him, saying, "Virtuous One, at the very moment you give rise to a single thought to ask this question, that is precisely the dependent origination within true nature.

Upon these words, the monk had an awakening. Later, Chan Master Juefan Huihong of Mount Jing asked, "When a single thought has not yet arisen, can it be said that there is no dependent origination? Suppose someone were to say, 'When a single thought has not yet..."
Xing asked, "What do you call 'conditioned arising' (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? I simply want you to speak in this way.
Regarding these two statements, Anguo elucidated that "this Dharma arises at this very moment," while Jingshan elucidated that "it does not arise at this very moment.
Furthermore, Master Linji said, "A single thought-moment of conditioned arising is unborn; it transcends the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles. All of these—
One who deeply penetrates this subtle principle cannot fathom it through mere intellectual knowledge.
Phenomena have no distinct times; they do not arise at different times. Phenomena have neither motion nor stillness, for their nature is empty and thus quiescent.
This refers to the essential nature and characteristics of the *dharmatā*. Now, phenomena do not exist at different times;
that which does not arise at a different time refers to this single phenomenon before one's eyes, which manifests in its very essence without any distinction from the present moment of thought.
Therefore, it does not arise at a distinct or separate moment of the present thought. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "dharmas are neither moving nor unmoving;
because their nature is empty, they are quiescent": this refers to the single dharma before one's eyes.

Although its substance is manifest, it is empty and quiescent within the very moment of its perception, possessing neither the characteristic of movement nor the characteristic of non-movement. Moreover, because the essential body of its nature is fundamentally empty, it accordingly...

This refers to abiding in quiescent extinction. Regarding this section of meaning, if one does not clarify the mind and see the nature, failing to awaken to the single stroke of direct presentation, it is just like a tiger watching a water mill.
Therefore, those who read these teachings must not merely let them pass by as they recite them;
they must penetrate their true meaning.
When the nature is empty and quiescent, this Dharma appears at that time. Because it is free from marks, it dwells in stillness; because it dwells in stillness, it does not engage with objects.

These words reveal the complete manifestation of the essence of the nature. Now, "when the nature is empty and quiescent" refers to the severance of the limits of past and future—the moment when not a single thought arises.
This single phrase, "this Dharma appears at that time," precisely manifests the principle of not relying on words and letters.
The Great Tradition of the Direct Pointing through the Plucking of the Flower refers to this very dharma right before one’s eyes;

it is manifested face-to-face at the very moment of the present thought. Indeed, our Buddha Tathāgata first attained it before Mount Bodhi upon seeing the morning star, and later revealed it by plucking a flower during the assembly at the Nirvāṇa Sūtra. Unintentionally, it has again appeared here...

This is where the Middle Way is pierced through. I have always said that while the First Patriarch used the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the mind, nothing is as direct and appropriate as this single phrase.

From the myriad explanations of the successive patriarchs—down to their raising of arms, rolling balls, picking up objects, pushing aside, brandishing whisks, striking with staffs, and shouting "Ho!"—none of these various pedagogical devices transcend this single phrase. Yet, this single phrase is truly...
It flows forth from within wondrous enlightenment; it is the gateway of the Great Dharani.

The two characters "total-holding" (zongchi) are *dhāraṇī* in Sanskrit, meaning that which can comprehensively encompass all phenomena, containing inexhaustible teachings, principles, practices, and fruits. Yet, this total-holding is without words or letters;
it merely constitutes a wondrous accord with the Buddha-mind, enabling one to understand the meaning of non-differentiation within the midst of differentiation.
Within the state of non-differentiation, one understands the meaning of differentiation.
When sentient beings awaken to this, they immediately attain the secret heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas and suddenly become identical with the Buddha-body.

They skillfully master the *dhāraṇī* of the languages of all sentient beings and are able to turn the fundamental wheel of Dharma. This is the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas; it encompasses all Buddha-dharmas.

Because there is nothing it does not fully encompass. Furthermore, it is called "mantra" (zhēnyán), and it is also named the "Secret Treasury" (mìmìzàng). It is called "secret" (bì) because it is not transmitted to those who are not suitable vessels;
it is called "esoteric" (mì) because it is profound, hidden, and difficult to know. Moreover, the secret itself is the manifest meaning: that which has not yet been awakened to is the esoteric.
To realize this is not secret. Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states that only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully exhaust the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
This sūtra also says that only Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas can know it.
Thus, for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is manifest; yet within the sphere of ordinary sentient beings, it is secret. If one wishes to attain its manifestation—
The secret fusion is thus. For now, it is well to take up a single phrase for study. However, from the very beginning, Śākyamuni was truly one whose compassionate heart was too earnest.
He further said: "Because one is free from marks, one dwells in stillness; because one dwells in stillness, one does not engage with objects.
This means that this present, manifest capacity is fundamentally free from the marks of birth and cessation, dependent origination, and even words and letters. It is only...
He dwells in reliance upon emptiness and stillness. Because he dwells in reliance upon emptiness and stillness, he does not act as a condition for any phenomena.
Upon realizing this, one finally understands why the man from the Pang family asked: "Who is it that does not consort with the myriad dharmas?
Mazu Daoshi said: "Wait until you can suck up all the water of the West River in a single mouthful."
I shall now tell you. If you wish to understand the essential meaning within the sutras, look first at this single phrase of Master Mazu:
"What is its intent? It says: "These are all dependently arisen phenomena;
these phenomena do not arise through conditions. Because causes and conditions are subject to arising and ceasing, they are non-existent; the nature of arising and ceasing is empty and quiescent."
This refers to the solitary existence of the essential nature (*dharmatā*). That is to say, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world arise from conditions.
Now, the Dharma I have spoken of—the entirety of reality manifesting in its own right—is that which cannot be produced by conditions.
Yet, all conditioned things arise and cease through their own characteristics based on causes and conditions. If not...
Since they arise from conditions, even the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions do not exist.

Since these characteristics are non-existent, one knows that the nature of this arising and ceasing is fundamentally empty and quiescent, and thus only the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) remains.

The nature of conditions is that which takes objects as its conditions; this is the fundamental nature of dependent origination. Therefore, the arising of phenomena is not [independent of] conditions, and the non-arising of conditions is likewise so.
This statement shows that the nature of phenomena transcends [duality]: the nature of all dependent origination is precisely the nature of the subject that perceives and the object perceived.
Thus, both these dual conditions—the perceiver and the perceived—originate fundamentally from conditions. Hence, one knows the arising of the nature of phenomena.
In reality, there is no dependence upon conditions; since those conditions do not exist, their arising cannot be apprehended either.
Ordinary beings take delusion and karma as conditions, while noble ones take responsive resonance as conditions. There are four meanings of conditioned arising (*pratītyasamutpāda*):

first, existence because of arising through conditions; second, emptiness because of arising through conditions; third, existence because of the absence of intrinsic nature; and fourth, emptiness because of the absence of intrinsic nature.

Among these four meanings, the latter two are taken as the reality. That which is empty because it is dependently originated and devoid of intrinsic nature is not the emptiness of nihilistic or non-existent views;
this is called "true emptiness. That which exists because dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature is not the existence of eternalistic or substantialist views;
this is "illusory existence. Furthermore, because dependent origination lacks intrinsic nature, there is no arising; because it lacks intrinsic nature...

Because it arises through conditions, it does not cease; furthermore, because one investigates its nature of non-arising, it is not produced. Because it can manifest the nature of non-arising, it does not cease.
This is what is called the true nature of dependent origination, the meaning of non-arising.

"Phenomena born of causes and conditions—these phenomena are themselves the causes and conditions; they possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, yet they are themselves without arising or ceasing.
This means that their nature is without arising or ceasing. That is to say, all things in the world are phenomena produced by causes and conditions.

Since these phenomena arise from such [conditions], they naturally belong to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Once they belong to causes and conditions, they possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
If the essence of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) did not belong to causes and conditions, then it would likewise be devoid of arising and ceasing.
That [Suchness] is the true mark of reality; fundamentally, it does not exist within arising and ceasing. At this time, all phenomena spontaneously give rise to arising and ceasing.

This statement means that, in essence, there is no arising or ceasing. To say that the nature of those phenomena has neither birth nor extinction, and that its essence remains as it is, is precisely True Suchness (Tathatā), the true mark of reality, which fundamentally does not possess arising and ceasing. However, at this time, all phenomena...
At all times and in all places, one spontaneously gives rise to various notions of emergence and disappearance;
yet how could there be a "self" therein?
Therefore, the ultimate pure source does not depend on the power of the multitudes; it is precisely within the subsequently attained state that one attains what was originally attained.

This statement expresses the non-duality of the original and the beginning; therefore, these two characters summarize the aforementioned principles and meanings to encompass the essential purport of this entire sutra.
The three characters "extremely pure original" (*jijing ben*) should be read as one phrase with one character per word. "Extremely" (*ji*) means ultimate.

"Purity" means luminous purity; "original" refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). These are words used to describe that which is beyond the full capacity of speech—meaning that it is difficult to exhaustively express.
It is said that for this reason, this is the ultimate, this is luminous purity, and this is precisely what is called original enlightenment.

However, when one observes through the wondrous discernment of awakening, the essential body (*dharmatā*) is revealed in its solitude; it is not produced by the power of the dependent origination of manifold phenomena.
That is, at the very place of the Vajra-mind-ground attained last by the Perfectly Awakened One, one attains that which is to be attained—the attainment of the self-nature of original enlightenment.
At that time, when the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha heard what the Buddha had spoken, his mind was filled with joy; as for the rest of the assembly, they were likewise without [doubt].
Regarding those who doubt: having understood the minds of the assembly, he spoke this verse.
This describes the absence of doubt; by speaking the verse, he brings the matter to a conclusion.
"I know the doubts in the minds of the assembly, which is why I have asked so earnestly. The Tathāgata, in his great kindness and compassion, has distinguished [the truth] without remainder."
This clarifies the request to turn the wheel of Dharma. [The interlocutor] says: "I know that the minds of the assembly harbor doubts;

therefore, with earnest and persistent entreaty, I put forth this inquiry. Now, the Buddha, out of great compassion, has crossed over the world and has skillfully distinguished the meanings of the aforementioned dharmas.
There is nothing left remaining.
All these two assemblies have attained complete clarity. Now, from this place of realization, I universally transform all sentient beings.

This clarifies the flow and transformation of the benefits of the Dharma. Previously, in the "Chapter on the Emptiness of True Nature," the two assemblies—the Great and the Small—were distinguished, namely the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
Now, all of these have attained clear understanding and enter together into the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, he himself says:
"I now benefit sentient beings from the place of realization. This is what is meant by having perfected one's own self-awakening and being able to awaken others.
"Other" means the same as the Tathāgata’s intention in appearing in the world.
Just as the Buddha’s great compassion does not abandon his original vow, he dwells within the afflictions while abiding in the stage of the only son.
This clarifies the great vow to benefit sentient beings. That is to say: the Buddha originally did not abandon his compassionate vows; I, too, shall act accordingly.

Furthermore, a Bodhisattva regards all sentient beings as if they were an only child. Since sentient beings now dwell within afflictions (*kleśa*), I too shall dwell within afflictions to transform and deliver them.
The section on the factors of perfect enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) concludes here; what follows belongs to the Great Vow.
The section on transformation is the section on circulation.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the assembly, saying: "This bodhisattva is inconceivable; he constantly possesses great compassion."
They uproot the suffering of sentient beings. If there are sentient beings who uphold this sūtra-dharma and uphold the names of these bodhisattvas, they shall not fall into the evil destinies;
all obstacles and difficulties will be completely extinguished.
This praises the benefit of sentient beings through the power of compassion, as well as the merit of the sutras in eliminating obstacles;
that is to say, the Dharma is so named because it equally possesses inconceivable perfuming, whereby one can distance oneself from evil and extinguish obstacles.
If there are sentient beings who uphold this sutra, being free from all other distracting thoughts and focusing their minds exclusively on this sutra, practicing it according to the Dharma,
at that time the Bodhisattva will constantly manifest transformation bodies to preach the Dharma for them, protecting these people and never abandoning them for even a moment.
May these people swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This reveals that such is the bodhisattva’s vow to manifest in person to protect the Dharma. However, those who uphold it must maintain single-minded mindfulness.
Cultivation must be in accordance with the Dharma. If one can do so, then the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all Buddhas will manifest before one in every thought-moment.
What distance could there then be from the Bodhi of the Buddhas?
"You bodhisattvas, when transforming sentient beings, must cause them all to practice such definitive Mahāyāna teachings;
this is specifically the admonition for you to follow, practice, and transform others."
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:

"The Tathāgata has spoken of the mass of merit of the Mahāyāna, which definitively severs the fetters and brings about the benefit of the realization of non-arising; it is inconceivable. What is the name of such a teaching?"

This is the praise for the request for the name of the Dharma. In the Sanskrit language, he is called Ānanda; here it is translated as "Joyous Celebration" (Qingxi). He was the Buddha’s maternal cousin.

He was named such because he was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment. At the age of eight, he left the household life under the Buddha and served as the Buddha’s attendant until he reached the age of thirty.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "After the Tathāgata had attained enlightenment, more than thirty..."
In the year [X], while staying in the city of Rājagṛha, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Who among you is able to receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures, provide for all the necessities required for his service, and yet not lose sight of one's own self-benefit? At that time, Kauṇḍinya...
“Śāriputra, all of you seek to serve as my attendants. The Buddha said, “You are already advanced in years and require an attendant yourself;
how then can you wish to serve me? Even when five hundred arhats likewise sought to serve him, the Buddha would not accept them.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered into meditative concentration and observed the mind of the Tathāgata; it was [resting] upon Ānanda...

It was a difficult situation, like the first rising of the sun casting its light upon the western wall. He then arose from his meditative concentration and, speaking with the Buddha’s intention, addressed Kāśyapa:
"Together with five hundred arhats, we request that you [Kāśyapa] invite Ānanda, for the Buddha intends to have you perform this task.
Ānanda said, "If such is the case, I must first seek three vows, just as the World-Honored One did."

"Therefore, I pray that you do not grant me these robes. I have accepted a separate invitation from a *dānapati*; please allow me not to comply with it. My coming and going shall be without fixed time;
let it be according to my own discretion. The World-Honored One has granted me three wishes; I shall now obey the command of the Saṃgha. The Buddha granted his permission.
Ānanda further said, "The Buddha should explain to me the Dharma he previously taught. The Buddha granted his permission to explain it once more.
He served as an attendant for more than twenty years, fully possessing the eight qualities and being able to uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
As for these eight qualities: his faculty of faith was firm and solid; his mind was upright and honest; his body was free from the suffering of illness; and he was always diligent and energetic.
He is endowed with mindfulness; his mind is free from arrogance; he has accomplished meditative concentration; and he is fully possessed of the wisdom born of hearing.
Therefore, the Buddha constantly refers to him as the "Treasury of Much Learning" (*bahuśrutakośa*) and the foremost in *dhāraṇī*. The Buddha further stated:
"The attendants of all past Buddhas were likewise endowed with these eight qualities. He also said: "When Ānanda hears what I teach, it is like pouring from one vessel into another."
Water: Place it in a vessel, and all its secret meanings can be fully understood.

Now, whenever the Buddha has finished preaching the Dharma within an assembly, Ānanda invariably requests that a name be given to it; for such is indeed his duty as the custodian of the treasury of the Dharma.
Regarding this present statement, [Ānanda asks about] the mass of merit and blessings of the Mahāyāna Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata.
To definitively sever the fetters and realize the benefit of the unborn primordial awakening (anādikāla-ajñāna) is truly inconceivable.
What name should it be called?
By receiving and upholding this sutra, how much merit will be obtained? I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain this for me.
This question concerns the merit obtained from upholding this sutra.
The Buddha said: "Good son, the name of this sutra is inconceivable; it is that which all Buddhas of the past have protected and remembered.
It enables one to enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s omniscience. If there are sentient beings who uphold this sutra, then in a single..."

Among all the sutras, there is nothing to be sought therein; this is the dharma of this sutra. It is the dhāraṇī of all dharmas, it encompasses the essentials of all sutras, and it is the fundamental tenet of all these sūtra-dharmas.
This is a praise of the merit of the sutra. Indeed, the *Avataṃsaka* is also known as the *Great Inconceivable Sutra*, and this sutra is likewise called "Inconceivable.

Furthermore, among the Dharma taught by the Buddha, sutras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* are protected by Śakra and Brahmā, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is protected by bodhisattvas; however, this sutra is inconceivable, for it is the realm of the Buddhas.
Therefore, they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas. What does "protected and remembered" mean? It means being able to cause sentient beings to enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Furthermore, it is said that those who uphold this sutra have already attained this single flavor of the *amṛta* (nectar) of *ghṛta* (clarified butter);
thus, among all other sutras, they have nothing further to seek. Again, it is stated that although the Dharma of this sutra is but one...

The *Weimojie jing* (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra). It encompasses the principles of the five flavors; though it is but a single scripture, it is able to subsume the essential outlines of more than three hundred assemblies of various sutras.
Now, that which has its veins and channels interconnected is called a "binding" (*xi*), while that from which a stream issues forth is termed a "source" (*zong*).
However, one must understand that all the teachings of the various sūtras are affiliated with this very Dharma and flow forth from within it.
For example, while the *Prajñāpāramitā* extensively practices the six perfections, they are merely matters found within the "Chapter on the Dharma of Signlessness" (*animitta-dharmapada*) herein.
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "All Buddhas, as well as the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas..."

Even Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi all emerges from this sutra; how much more so the Dharma of this sutra, which instantly transcends the ten stages and proceeds directly to the two types of Perfect and Wondrous Enlightenment.
As for the names of this sutra: it is called the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-sūtra*, also called the *Vajrasamādhi*, and also called the *Aparimitārthasiddhānta*.

Thus, there are three names according to their designations. Now, as for "Compendium of the Mahāyāna" (*Mahāyānasaṃgraha*), this name is established based on the Dharma; it carries the meaning of *prajñā* (wisdom).
It takes True Suchness (tathatā) as its essence. As for the Vajra Samādhi, it is named after its function; by employing both a metaphor and the dharma itself, it is fully revealed:
that which can crush what is firm and shatter delusions is the meaning of liberation, and it takes the clarification of the mind and the seeing of nature as its function.
As for the school of the Infinite Meanings (ananta-artha), it is named after its essence; it is able to encompass the One.
All phenomena are the foundation for all meanings; this is the meaning of the *dharmakāya*. Indeed, the *dharmakāya* can fully encompass all meanings and give birth to all phenomena.
If sentient beings realize the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, they will clearly understand the non-duality of the initial and fundamental awakenings (*ādikṣānti-bodhi* and *mūlabodhi*).
Therefore, this sutra takes the two awakenings—initial and fundamental—as its central tenet. Now, I establish this...
Third, it clarifies that the secret treasury of the three perfected virtues serves as the precursor to nirvana.
If there is anyone who receives and upholds this sutra, they are said to receive and uphold the teachings of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.
Such merit is like space: it has no boundaries and is inconceivable.
This clarifies that the merit is boundless. It is said that one who upholds this sutra upholds hundreds of thousands of Buddhas;
yet these hundreds of thousands of Buddhas do not transcend this Dharma. Furthermore, merit is compared to empty space, for there is nothing that surpasses it.
That which I entrust to you is none other than this sutra;

I specifically reaffirm this entrustment. To "entrust" (*zhù*) means to deposit a matter for the sake of future reliance; to "reaffirm" (*lèi*) means to sit together with the phenomena of that matter.
Now, the intent behind the Buddha’s entrustment is this: among all the treasuries of Dharma I have taught, this sutra alone is the most supreme.
"Indeed, the Tathāgata has preached all the sūtras and dharmas solely for the purpose of revealing this dharma of the Vajrasamādhi.
Ānanda asked: "What is the mental practice? And what kind of person is it that receives and upholds this sūtra?"
This distinguishes the inquiry into the nature of the faculties. First, one distinguishes their mental conduct, and subsequently, one distinguishes the person.
The Buddha said: "Good son, those who receive and uphold this sutra have minds free from gain and loss, and they constantly cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*)."

If one constantly delights in stilling the mind amidst worldly proliferation (*prapañca*), entering villages with the mind always in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and dwelling at home without attachment to the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), this clarifies their conduct.
Indeed, when the mind is free from gain and loss, it is detached from grasping and rejecting; thus, one constantly cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Thus one abides in non-retrogression; this may be verified as the reality of one’s mental conduct.
If one constantly delights in a tranquil mind regarding conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), then when encountering circumstances, one will not be turned by those circumstances.

When entering a village, if the mind remains constantly in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), then when encountering sensory objects, one will not be deluded by those objects. If one dwells at home, one does not become attached.
To dwell within the three realms of existence yet remain unstained by the dust of the world—by this one may determine the character and stage of such a person.
This is the sphere of practice for Bodhisattvas of the sixth and seventh stages of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Such a person will possess five kinds of merit in the present life: first, they will be respected by the multitude; second, their life will not be cut short by untimely death;
third, they will be able to skillfully respond to and refute heterodox arguments; fourth, they will delight in delivering sentient beings;
and fifth, they will be able to enter the noble path. Such a person as this shall uphold this sutra.
This clarifies the five blessings obtained in the present life. First, by upholding the Dharma for oneself, one will certainly receive respect;

by guarding oneself with the Way, one will certainly not suffer an untimely death. Second, for one's own enjoyment, one attains samādhi and clear right knowledge, thereby being able to discern heterodox doctrines;
with inexhaustible compassion and vows, one delights in delivering sentient beings. Third, for the enjoyment of others... [text fragment ends]
The former four are the practices of a bodhisattva within the causal stage; the latter is the ability to enter the noble path, which constitutes the fruit-virtue of a bodhisattva.

Such a person benefits both themselves and others in the present, is able to enter the noble path, and will certainly receive, uphold, and propagate this sutra to transform sentient beings. This is the way for us practitioners of the Way.
Truly fortunate! This must not remain unknown.
Ānanda asked: "If such a person were to deliver all sentient beings, would they be worthy of receiving offerings?
This question was posed to clarify whether or not he was fit to receive offerings, in order to sever the doubts of the world.
The Buddha said: "Such a person as this can serve as a great field of merit for sentient beings; they constantly practice great wisdom and expound both the provisional and the ultimate.
These are the Saṃgha of the Four Reliances."
This clarifies the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) of the Mahāyāna: namely, rely on the Dharma and not on the person; rely on the meaning and not on the words;
rely on wisdom (*jñāna*) and not on consciousness (*vijñāna*); rely on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not on the non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
Having attained these four reliances, one is able to constantly practice with great wisdom. Now, wisdom is divided into the provisional and the real. Real wisdom is the very essence of all Buddhas.
One attains wisdom (*jñāna*). All paths of verbal expression are severed. Expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is precisely the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);
it is able to establish transformation through skillful means (*upāya*). However, in reality, it is not expedient without being real, nor is it established without being real.

One must manifest both the expedient and the real together for them to constitute the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) of the Mahāyāna. The "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokadhātunirgama-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "When a Bodhisattva dwells..."
While abiding in nirvāṇa, he manifests birth and death; while ultimately in a state of quiescent extinction, he manifests the arising of afflictions;

while constantly entering deep meditative absorption, he manifests the enjoyment of sensual pleasures; and while always remaining far removed from the triple world, he does not abandon sentient beings.

This is the uncommon dharma of the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real, which does not depend on the instruction of another. Furthermore, it is said: "Although he knows all dharmas..."

There is no artificial fabrication, yet one does not abandon the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. Although one knows that awakening does not come from another and enters into the Dharma, one seeks all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) through various skillful means (*upāya*).
Although one constantly observes that there is no person (*pudgala*) and no self (*ātman*), [one continues to practice].

They teach and transform sentient beings without weariness or fatigue. Although they have already accomplished the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva without ceasing.
Although they know that all phenomena are ineffable, they turn the pure wheel of Dharma to bring joy to the minds of the multitude.
Although they manifest entry into great parinirvāṇa, they manifest [their presence] in all places.
Taking birth and being able to perform such a dharma that unifies the provisional and the real is the work of a Buddha.

What is now being expounded—this union of the provisional and the real—is precisely this same meaning. However, apart from the "Chapter on Leaving the World," this originally elucidates the path of constant practice for benefiting sentient beings after the fruit of wondrous enlightenment;
it is identical to the characteristics of the four reliances of the Mahāyāna, and not those of the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the supports (*niśraya*): first, begging for food; second, dwelling among burial mounds or at the foot of trees; third, wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*);
and fourth, consuming decomposed medicines. These are the four.
Regarding all offerings, even those consisting of one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain may be accepted; how much more so clothing and food?
This clarifies that both internal and external forms of giving are worthy of acceptance. Generally, the relinquishing of all parts of one's own body constitutes internal giving.

Clothing, food, and requisites constitute external giving (*bāhya-dāna*). As stated in the "Chapter on Dedication" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Most Supreme Wisdom (*Jñānavara*) offered his head and eyes as a gift, while the Bodhisattva Benefiting Others (*Upakāraka*) offered his marrow and flesh.

Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says that the Bodhisattva All Sentient Beings Delight to See (*Sarvasattvapriyadarśana*) gave up both arms, and the Bodhisattva Medicine King (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*) gave up... [his own body].
This refers to the body and so forth. For if even internal giving can result in receiving [retribution], how much more so external giving?

When a wise person receives food, they should cultivate the perception of revulsion, just as a hungry ghost in a vast wilderness eats the flesh of its own child, feeling only loathing and finding no pleasure at all.
Thus, by observing deeply, one comes to know that the world receives morsel-food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
This is the fault [of food]. As for "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), it refers to the segmented food of the desire realm that sustains the physical body.
Next, one contemplates "contact as nutriment" (*sparśa-āhāra*). It is like skinning and flaying oxen and sheep, or like various insects devouring [their prey].

Since there is a body, there is contact; if one craves the pleasure of contact, one will ultimately encounter painful contact. Thus, one knows that the affliction of contact is truly great. Furthermore, one contemplates "volition as nutriment" (*manaḥsañcetanā-āhāra*).
This nutriment of volition is like a great mass of fire; this volition is the seventh mental karma.
Because it arises from fundamental ignorance and non-awakening, it is metaphorically compared to a mass of fire. Yet, as soon as there is a cause for perception, this nutriment of volition exists.
Furthermore, observe the nutriment of consciousness: it is like three hundred clusters of bristling thorns standing in rows, impossible to approach, because of the existence of birth.

Thus, there is this consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*). These three types are all called "food" because they are able to nourish and benefit the sense faculties (*indriya*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the seeds of sentient beings.
These constitute the food of the three realms. The wise contemplate them in this way and do not give rise to thoughts of craving toward anything.
Therefore, when receiving food, regardless of whether it is good or bad, one should regard it as applying ointment to an ulcer.
It is merely medicine for a sore. Furthermore, it must be understood that a bhikṣu should take the joy of the Dharma as his food.
For instance, when the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (an alternative name for Wenshu) provided a rare meal for Śāriputra and others, he said:
"The food I have now prepared cannot be divided into portions; it cannot be swallowed; it is not composed of the three objects of the senses—scent, flavor, or touch."
Its substance is not comprised within the three realms, nor is it unconditioned. Such a wondrous food is the food of the Tathāgata;
it is not the food of cooked rice. Having heard this, Subhūti and Śāriputra were filled with the joy of the Dharma and both entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
One no longer consumes the food of the three realms; this is the meaning taught in the two sūtras on Prajñā and Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, a sūtra says: "All dharmas abide by means of food: in the eye, sleep is its food; in the ear, sound is its food;
in the nose, fragrance is its food; in the tongue, taste is its food; in the body..."
They take fine and smooth textures as their food; those in the mind take mental objects as their food; those in the Great Parinirvāṇa take heedfulness as their food.
Good son, such people as these are your spiritual friends and your bridge; how much more so, then, are ordinary persons?
"Not making offerings" clarifies that [the Buddha] is the excellent guide for those of the Two Vehicles.

However, while Ānanda attained only the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) at the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and although he realized the Dharma-body and awakened to the gates of the Buddha-dharma at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama*, he had not yet exhausted his outflows (*āsrava*). Upon reaching...
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is recorded that he was prophesied to become a Buddha;

although he could recollect the Dharma-treasuries of all past Buddhas and penetrate them without obstruction, his residual outflows (*āsrava*) were not yet exhausted. It was only after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the compilation of the Dharma-eye, that he finally attained the fruit of Arhatship.
This is why it is said here: "Such a person as this is your spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), for they are capable of leading you into the state of the noble ones."
Because he is the Way, he is your bridge and ford for the purpose of crossing over the ocean of the three realms of existence.
He is truly able to serve as teacher and guide for you followers of the Two Vehicles; how much more so should ordinary people of the mundane world not revere and serve him?
Ānanda said: "If one receives and upholds this sutra from such a person, and makes offerings to that person, how much merit will be obtained?
This is another question regarding the blessings and benefits of transmitting and upholding [the teaching].

The Buddha said: "Furthermore, if there were someone who were to take gold and silver filling an entire city and give it as a gift, it would not equal the merit of receiving and upholding even a single four-line verse of this sutra from such a person; it is inconceivable."
The merit of this is difficult to measure. Generally, giving with material wealth yields only the tainted blessings of the realms of humans and devas;
this has already been clarified in the preceding passage. There is no need to inquire as to how much merit is obtained. Hereafter, the text exclusively reveals the power of the upholder:
if one can uphold even a single verse from within this [text], one will immediately awaken to original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) and attain...
The wisdom-treasure of the Dharma King’s appearance in the world—how could it ever be compared to worldly treasures?
This merit and this virtue are truly immeasurable; they cannot be conceived by the mind nor discussed by the mouth.
Good son, those sentient beings who uphold this sutra will have their minds constantly in samādhi and will not lose their original mind.
This clarifies that they do not lose the awakened mind. It is said that when one person attains the Way, many people obtain benefit.
If one causes all sentient beings to uphold this sutra, they will certainly attain realization of this mind and remain constantly in samādhi; they will definitely not lose it.
This is its fundamental mind. In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when praising the merit of generating the bodhicitta, more than ten similes are cited in succession to compare it;
yet even these do not equal even a small fraction [of its merit]. This is because generating the mind is the manifestation of the essence of the fundamentally enlightened mind (*mūla-bodhi*).

However, at the very first moment of this manifestation, one attains the "path of seeing" (*darśana-mārga*) through a single thought-moment of resonance, whereby one has already severed the afflictions of the path of seeing.

Deluded, one must further cultivate the Way to seek the severance of the afflictions of thought (*sahakleśa*). Only then can one attain the state of not losing the original mind and abide eternally in the Way.

This is why the First Patriarch, Master Bodhidharma, came from South India to this land to transmit the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle and the One Mind, desiring to cause people to clarify the mind and see their nature, and furthermore to attain the Great Horse [of the Path].
The Master extensively propagated his Way, saying: "All phenomena are the phenomena of the mind. The myriad dharmas all arise from the mind; the mind is the root of the myriad dharmas.
Whatever forms one perceives are the perception of the mind itself. The mind does not exist as a mind of its own accord."

It exists because of form. If there are sentient beings of superior faculties who, upon encountering the instruction of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), comprehend it at the mere mention of the words, they do not pass through the successive stages and levels but immediately awaken to their original nature.
Are these proclamations not the teaching and guidance of Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage? Furthermore, it is said: "Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, all are [the Way]."
This is the inconceivable function: not grasping at good, not abandoning evil, and neither relying upon nor adhering to the two extremes of purity and defilement.

In the preceding thought, the subsequent thought, and the middle thought—moment by moment they do not depend upon one another; moment by moment they are quiescent. This is called the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
Is this not also the accomplishment of the inconceivable actions of body, speech, and mind by a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage?
Is it the practice of signlessness? Furthermore, Baizhang said: "The mind is like empty space; do not even form the thought of 'empty space.
Huangbo said: "Abandon everything—inner and outer, body and mind—so that it is like empty space, with nothing to grasp or cling to."
Thereafter, one responds to things according to their conditions, such that both subject and object are forgotten.
Linji said, "The moment you conceive a thought, you have already gone astray. Deshan said, "The mere flicker of a single thought is the very kin of Māra.
Are these statements not, in fact, the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) within the seventh stage? Observing this throughout...

Among the patriarchs of the past, there were none who did not attain such realization through these *samādhis*; only then could they be called true descendants of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, able to benefit sentient beings and engage with others.
However, in the present age, the Dharma-vehicle has declined, and we are unable to stem this falling tide.

Consequently, those who claim to have seen the Way are many, while those who truly cultivate the Way are few; those who discourse on principle are many, while those who truly penetrate the principle are few. This is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to as "deviant."
The Master preached the Dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This being precisely the time, how could it not be tragic?
If one loses the original mind, one must immediately repent. The method of repentance is that which brings about coolness and clarity.
This clarifies that by repenting for the loss of the [awakened] mind, one immediately attains coolness and clarity. However, this loss of mind is nothing other than this:
the student merely seeks a single awakening and considers it the end of the matter, thereby failing to engage in rigorous inquiry (*karada*).

Consequently, they follow along with worldly conditions, and after a long time, their old habits arise once more. Not only do they fail to sever the afflictions of thought (*sahakleśa*), but even the previously severed afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭikleśa*) arise again.
